title: AgentPolicyForge: From Executable Environments to Policy Benchmarks and Adaptive Guards
abstract: Customized agent deployments define policies over tools, resources, and execution conditions. Providing these policies in the task agent's prompt does not reliably prevent violations. Training a guard requires examples of tool calls that comply with or violate those policies. We introduce AgentPolicyForge, a framework that uses executable environments to construct policy benchmarks and iteratively train policy guards. With this framework, we construct PolicyGym, a dataset across ten policy families using 698 scenarios for training data generation and 254 separate held-out scenarios for human-reviewed test sets. Tool calls are executed and their outcomes recorded to help determine whether they comply with the policy. Every violating case uses a permitted tool, requiring checks of arguments, resources, and context rather than tool identity alone. The case construction process supports iterative guard training: an attacker generates requests using retrieved strategies, and the guard is fine-tuned on balanced, environment-verified examples. Training improves policy enforcement even with a fixed archive. Updating the archive further reduces in-domain attack success compared with keeping it fixed. We compare policy-aware task agent self-regulation with a trained policy guard. On PolicyGym, the final guard-based configuration achieves a 40-44% relative reduction in attack success rate and fewer benign rejections than policy prompting alone.

Abstract

Customized agent deployments define policies over tools, resources, and execution conditions. Providing these policies in the task agent’s prompt does not reliably prevent violations. Training a guard requires examples of tool calls that comply with or violate those policies. We introduce AgentPolicyForge, a framework that uses executable environments to construct policy benchmarks and iteratively train policy guards. With this framework, we construct PolicyGym, a dataset across ten policy families using 698 scenarios for training data generation and 254 separate held-out scenarios for human-reviewed test sets. Tool calls are executed and their outcomes recorded to help determine whether they comply with the policy. Every violating case uses a permitted tool, requiring checks of arguments, resources, and context rather than tool identity alone. The case construction process supports iterative guard training: an attacker generates requests using retrieved strategies, and the guard is fine-tuned on balanced, environment-verified examples. Training improves policy enforcement even with a fixed archive. Updating the archive further reduces in-domain attack success compared with keeping it fixed. We compare policy-aware task agent self-regulation with a trained policy guard. On PolicyGym, the final guard-based configuration achieves a $40$ – $44\%$ relative reduction in attack success rate and fewer benign rejections than policy prompting alone.

## 1 Introduction

Language-model agents increasingly call tools, query databases, and modify
external systems (Schick et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023; Xi et al., 2025).
Deployments govern these actions through policies specifying which tools
and resources agents may use and under what conditions
(Wen et al., 2026a; VIOLA, 2026).
For example, a transfer tool may be permitted only for amounts below a
limit, and record access may be restricted to the record’s owner.
An allowed tool can therefore still be used in violation of policy:
compliance depends on its arguments, the resources it accesses, and
the state in which it executes.

Providing the policy directly to the task agent reduces violations,
but leaves substantial enforcement errors. In our evaluation, a
policy-prompted frontier agent still allows violating calls to execute
in $13$ – $15\%$ of threat episodes and rejects around $9\%$ of benign requests
(§4.2).
A separate guard allows policy enforcement to be trained
and evaluated independently of the task agent, without changing the task agent’s weights.
To train and evaluate this guard, we need tool calls paired with policies,
relevant context, and compliance labels.

These examples must cover both compliant and violating calls, with labels
grounded in what the agent actually proposes. A request alone is insufficient:
the agent may propose a different action, and successful execution does not
establish policy compliance. Executable environments let us reset state,
execute concrete calls, and inspect their outcomes, linking policy judgments
to observable evidence. Training data can then be refreshed to target
remaining misses and false alarms, while held-out tests stay fixed to
measure progress.

Existing policy benchmarks and monitors provide resources for evaluating
deployment-specific compliance, including PolicyGuard (Wen et al., 2026a) and VIOLA (VIOLA, 2026).
Our focus is constructing new policy cases from executable environments:
binding rules to concrete tools and state, collecting calls and execution
evidence, and reusing this process for both fixed tests and fresh guard
training data.

We introduce AgentPolicyForge, a framework that uses executable
environments to construct policy benchmarks and iteratively train policy
guards through a shared case-construction process. A shared construction process generates requests targeting compliance
or violation, collects calls from a policy-blind task agent, and executes them to collect
evidence for determining whether the calls comply with the policy.
Environment adapters provide access to tools, state, and execution.
The framework then binds policy rules and executable checks to each scenario’s tools and state.

With this framework, we construct PolicyGym, a dataset for training and evaluating
policy guards across ten policy families. Training data generation uses 698 Agent World Model
(AWM) scenarios (Wang et al., 2026). Human-reviewed tests use 254 separate held-out
scenarios: 187 in-domain (ID) and 67 out-of-domain (OOD) within AWM.
OOD scenarios come from groups not used for training data generation, but remain within AWM.
Each example pairs a proposed tool call with policy rules, relevant context,
execution evidence, and a compliance label.
Every violating test case uses a permitted tool but breaches an argument, resource, or context
condition, which shows that identifying forbidden tools alone is insufficient.

We use PolicyGym’s training seeds and the construction process to generate
fresh examples for iterative guard training. Each round,
an attacker retrieves archived strategies to generate fresh requests.
We fine-tune the policy guard using supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on a
balanced set of verifier-confirmed violations and compliant calls,
including violations it missed and compliant calls it incorrectly blocked.
Training with a fixed archive already reduces ASR on both evaluation splits.
We also update the archive with candidate strategies derived from
attack outcomes. Candidates are validated on training scenarios
before entering the archive.
This archive-mediated coevolution links guard updates through SFT
to strategy updates that guide subsequent requests.

After ten rounds of coevolutionary training, the guard achieves attack success
rates (ASR) of $8.22\%$ in-domain and $7.89\%$ out-of-domain when filtering fixed
task-agent proposals. Compared with policy-aware task-agent self-regulation,
this configuration achieves a $40$ – $44\%$ relative reduction in ASR and rejects
fewer benign requests. We compare fixed and evolving archives after ten matched training rounds. Updating the archive lowers in-domain ASR by $24.1\%$ but increases benign over-block by $0.75$ percentage points.

• 

We introduce AgentPolicyForge, a framework that constructs policy
benchmarks and trains policy guards in executable environments. It binds
deployment policies to concrete tool calls, uses execution evidence to check
generated cases, and produces separate cases for held-out evaluation and
iterative guard training.

• 

We contribute PolicyGym, an execution-grounded policy-compliance
dataset with supervision generated from 698 scenarios and human-reviewed tests
on 254 separate held-out scenarios. Every violating test case uses a permitted
tool, requiring guards to check policy conditions on arguments, resources,
and context rather than identify forbidden tools.

• 

We develop an iterative guard-training process that generates fresh
compliant and violating cases for SFT.
Training reduces ASR on both evaluation splits with a fixed strategy archive.
Archive-mediated coevolution further uses guard feedback to update attack
strategies, with an additional in-domain blocking gain in the matched run.

## 2 The AgentPolicyForge Framework

Figure 1: AgentPolicyForge framework.
One construction process produces human-reviewed policy tests and fresh
guard training data. Execution records support labeling and rule checks.
SFT updates the guard, and guard feedback yields candidate attack strategies.
Validated strategies enter the archive to guide subsequent requests.
Test cases are used only
for evaluation, not guard training or strategy validation.

## 2.1 Problem Setting

We study a policy guard that checks a task agent’s proposed tool call using only
information available before execution. Given a user request $q$ , the task agent proposes
 $c=(\text{tool},\text{args})$ . The guard decides whether to allow it using the request,
proposed call, policy $\Pi$ , visible pre-action state $s$ , and relevant tool schema
 $\Sigma$ . We denote these inputs by $z=(q,c,\Pi,s,\Sigma)$ .

The attacker controls the request and seeks to induce a violating call that the guard
allows, but cannot modify the policy, tool schema, or visible state supplied to the guard.
Execution outcomes support labeling during data construction but are not included
in the guard’s inputs.

A policy $\Pi$ specifies permitted tools $\mathcal{T}^{\mathrm{ok}}$ , permitted resources
 $\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{ok}}$ , and conditions $\mathcal{C}$ over call arguments and environment
state. A condition is violated only when it applies to the call and is not satisfied;
we therefore define each $\phi\in\mathcal{C}$ to return true outside its applicability scope.
Let $\text{res}(c)$ denote the resources accessed by the call. A proposal violates the
policy if any of the following holds:

 $\displaystyle V_{0}$ 
 $\displaystyle:\;\text{tool}\notin\mathcal{T}^{\text{ok}},$ 

 $\displaystyle V_{1}$ 
 $\displaystyle:\;\exists\,\phi\in\mathcal{C}:\neg\phi(\text{args},s),$ 

 $\displaystyle V_{2}$ 
 $\displaystyle:\;\text{res}(c)\not\subseteq\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{ok}}.$ 

(1)

Here, $V_{0}$ denotes a forbidden tool, $V_{1}$ an unsatisfied applicable condition, and $V_{2}$ 
an unauthorized resource. Although the general formulation includes $V_{0}$ , PolicyGym
focuses on $V_{1}$ and $V_{2}$ through a permitted-tool invariant: every violating
test case uses a permitted tool. This prevents tool identity alone from revealing violations
and requires checking policy conditions on arguments, resources, or state.
For example, a transfer tool may be allowed even though the proposed amount exceeds the policy limit.

The guard outputs an intervention level: 0 (Pass), 1 (Monitor), 2 (Verify), 3 (Modify), or
4 (Block).
These levels provide more detailed feedback than a simple allow/block decision, distinguishing flagging a potential problem from blocking an action. In our evaluation,
only Level 4 prevents execution. Levels 2 - 4 count toward intervention recall and FPR, measuring how often the guard flags violating and compliant calls, respectively.

## 2.2 From Executable Environments to Policy Cases

Figure 1 (left) shows how executable environments support
policy binding, seed generation, and the construction of labeled calls.

## Environment and policy binding.

To construct a policy from a template, we select a tool, identify the relevant
arguments or resources, and fill in the rule’s conditions. For example,
“Each [operation] must not exceed [limit]” becomes “Each transfer must not
exceed $500” by selecting a transfer tool, its amount argument, and a $500
limit. The template includes an executable check that compares the proposed
amount with this limit.

Deployment policies can also be supplied directly by users. For PolicyGym,
we use reusable templates covering ten policy families (§3).
An environment adapter connects the construction process to each environment.
It provides tool definitions and argument types, identifies resources, and
supports inspecting state, restoring the initial state, and executing calls.
A template can be applied only when the environment provides the fields and
state needed to check its rule.

## Seed and request generation.

Each seed is a structured input for request generation. It contains
the scenario’s policy clauses, a target operation, and key argument values.
A violating seed specifies an intended call that breaks one selected policy rule.
A compliant seed specifies an intended call that satisfies all policy rules
that apply to it.
The attacker converts each seed into a natural-language request. The seed describes the intended action, but we label the call the agent actually proposes. The attacker converts each seed into a natural-language request. Training seeds generate requests for training data, and held-out seeds generate requests for test cases.

## Task-agent proposals and execution.

The task agent receives the attacker’s request and tool schemas, then proposes a call. The task agent does not receive the policy. We execute each call from the environment’s initial state after checking that its arguments are valid and it matches the request, then record the result. We keep successfully executed calls and label them as compliant or violating. Execution success does not mean the call follows the policy.

## Labeling and human review.

We consider two sources of compliance labels: (1) An LLM judge interprets the policy
and execution evidence to provide a judgment, the applicable clause, and supporting
evidence. (2) An executable rule checker, called the verifier, evaluates the
encoded policy conditions. These checks are possible because the policy
templates specify the rules, and the environment provides tool schemas,
actual call arguments, and recorded state.
We train the guard using LLM labels and compare this with training
using verifier labels (§4.3). In both experiments, we keep only cases that the verifier can label as compliant or violating.
Test cases receive both an LLM label and a verifier judgment. We retain only cases with a definite verifier judgment and a human-approved LLM label.

## Why train a guard when executable checks are available?

During data construction, we use policy checks and execution records
to help label calls. At deployment, policies may be written in natural
language without matching check code. A verifier can enforce these
rules only after they are encoded and the required information is
available before execution. We train a guard to judge proposed calls from policy text and pre-action context, without verifier judgments or execution results. Complete executable checks can still be used directly when available.

## 2.3 Iterative Guard Training and Archive Updates

In Figure 1 (right), each round generates training examples, updates the guard’s parameters through SFT, and validates new attack strategies. Strategies that pass validation are saved in the attacker archive for later rounds.

To collect examples, the attacker generates requests using archived strategies.
The task agent proposes calls, and the current guard judges them. We execute
valid calls in the sandbox even if the guard would block them, so we can
check their outcomes. We discard calls that fail, do not match the request,
or cannot be judged by the verifier.
We build a SFT training set with equal numbers of calls labeled compliant and
violation. Here the LLM judge uses the policies, calls, and execution evidence to provide SFT labels, but the guard receives only pre-execution information. Algorithm 1 summarizes the training procedure.

Before adding a strategy to the archive, we test it in training
environments by generating attacks with and without it.
Production strategies must produce new verified bypasses.
Exploration strategies must not reduce the bypass count
(Appendix A.10).
Validation uses only training scenarios.

In this archive-mediated coevolution, SFT updates the guard,
and validated strategies update the archive. Test cases guide neither
update. To measure the benefit of archive updates, we compare with
a control that uses the same data collection and SFT procedure but
keeps the archive fixed at $S_{0}$ in §4.4.

## 3 PolicyGym: Benchmark Construction

## 3.1 AWM Environments and Policy Instantiation

We build PolicyGym on Agent World Model (AWM) (Wang et al., 2026), which provides
 $1{,}000$ resettable scenarios with SQLite data and typed FastAPI/MCP tools.
We define rule templates for ten policy families: time windows, backdating,
amount limits, own-record access, restricted tables, protected identifiers,
data residency, field masking, protected flags, and dual approval.
We fill these templates using each scenario’s tools, arguments, resources,
and state to create concrete policies (§2.2).
Appendix Table 5 explains each family and its required evidence.
Every violating test case uses a permitted tool. Its violation can be determined
from one call’s arguments, resources, or state ( $V_{1}$ or $V_{2}$ ), although the
same episode may contain other calls.

## 3.2 Training Seeds and Labeled Examples

The source pool contains 6,603 seed–policy pairs from 698 AWM scenarios.
We check whether each seed supports a valid call that satisfies or violates
the specified policy. This leaves 5,655 seeds: 2,863 targeting violations and
2,792 targeting compliance. These seeds guide request generation. They are
not labeled tool-call examples.

## 3.3 Held-Out Test Construction and Evaluation

We construct the test sets from scenarios excluded from the source pool using the same steps in §2.2.
ID scenarios belong to naming groups represented in that pool, and OOD
scenarios belong to groups absent from it. Both splits remain within AWM
and use the same policy families and construction process.

Using held-out seeds, we generate requests and collect task-agent calls
through the process in §2.2. Test cases must have a
definite v
limitations:
PolicyGym studies synthetic policies whose violations can be determined from one
tool call. Both test splits share AWM and policy templates, so they do not establish
generalization to new policy types or deployments. The Qwen-AgentWorld pilot
reuses interfaces with simulated responses, but high benign rejection limits
direct guard transfer. We do not compare learned guards with complete executable
rule checks.

Results use one generation seed and two Qwen3 backbones, without measuring
variation across training runs. The attacker, task agent, and judge use proprietary
Claude models and may share biases in generated calls and labels. The follow-up
human review covers 100 test episodes, not independent double annotation of the
full test sets. Training-label accuracy remains unmeasured.

Evaluation uses fixed attacks and does not compare systems at equal benign
rejection. Baselines also differ in model size. These comparisons therefore do
not isolate all effects of training, model size, and blocking rules. External
adapters used evaluation feedback, and VIOLA has few benign trajectories.
We measure blocking decisions, not task completion, the outcomes of verification
or modification, or deployment cost.
conclusion:
AgentPolicyForge builds policy benchmarks and trains guards using executable
environments. PolicyGym provides training data and human-reviewed tests.
Generated data improve enforcement, with archive updates adding an in-domain
gain at Level 4 in the matched run.
Future work will evaluate guard adaptation to new policy types and deployment changes.

title: PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agents via Machine-Checked Integrity Theorems and Scalable Community Trust
abstract: Persistent memory is a largely undefended surface for injection and poisoning, and the same risk limits memory sharing among agents. We present PerMIT, a memory architecture with provable integrity guarantees under an explicit trust assumption: only user-typed inputs and values confirmed at a gate are trusted. PerMIT mediates the release and use of untrusted environment-derived values through a finite memory interface, while preserving agent-driven multi-turn planning and tool choice. Over this finite interface, we prove two integrity theorems that are also machine-checked in Lean 4, which together ensure that environment-derived memory reaches a sensitive action only if confirmed at the gate and influences the agent's behavior only through what the gate displays. Every attack in our threat model thereby reduces to a single auditable decision, which a human, an LLM verifier, or both can make in practice. On Trojan Hippo, PerMIT records zero observed attack success with self-verification and lightweight verifiers. Because each confirmation is a logged verdict on exact content, endorsements accumulate across users, and sufficiently endorsed items become community-confirmed with no further verification required. Under explicit assumptions, we prove and corroborate in simulation a co-scaling property: as the community grows, the risks of promoting poison and of wrongly evicting benign knowledge fall, while per-user verification effort does not rise. On $τ^2$-bench, communities of up to 90 autonomous agents use PerMIT to build shared knowledge bases with no direct memory injection promoted, and the resulting knowledge significantly improves new agents on held-out tasks, suggesting a path toward agents that safely self-improve at test time.

2.1 Persistent Memory as an Attack Surface
3.2 The Single-User Tier: a Finite Memory Interface
body_start:
Abstract

Persistent memory is a largely undefended surface for injection and poisoning, and the same risk limits memory sharing among agents. We present PerMIT, a memory architecture with provable integrity guarantees under an explicit trust assumption: only user-typed inputs and values confirmed at a gate are trusted. PerMIT mediates the release and use of untrusted environment-derived values through a finite memory interface, while preserving agent-driven multi-turn planning and tool choice. Over this finite interface, we prove two integrity theorems that are also machine-checked in Lean 4, which together ensure that environment-derived memory reaches a sensitive action only if confirmed at the gate and influences the agent’s behavior only through what the gate displays. Every attack in our threat model thereby reduces to a single auditable decision, which a human, an LLM verifier, or both can make in practice. On Trojan Hippo, PerMIT records zero observed attack success with self-verification and lightweight verifiers. Because each confirmation is a logged verdict on exact content, endorsements accumulate across users, and sufficiently endorsed items become community-confirmed with no further verification required. Under explicit assumptions, we prove and corroborate in simulation a co-scaling property: as the community grows, the risks of promoting poison and of wrongly evicting benign knowledge fall, while per-user verification effort does not rise. On $\tau^{2}$ -bench, communities of up to 90 autonomous agents use PerMIT to build shared knowledge bases with no direct memory injection promoted, and the resulting knowledge significantly improves new agents on held-out tasks, suggesting a path toward agents that safely self-improve at test time.

## Contents

## Part I Main Paper

## 1 Introduction

By carrying preferences, decisions, and hard-won context across sessions, persistent memory transforms a stateless LLM into an agent that becomes more capable and personalized with continued use.
Although agents benefit from reading and writing persistent memory, this capability also creates an attack surface that the underlying models are poorly equipped to defend.
Poisoned information can readily enter persistent memory when an agent browses webpages or invokes tools containing planted injections (Das et al., 2026).
Such attacks can turn a one-shot prompt injection (Debenedetti et al., 2024) into a persistent compromise, and a single compromise could easily propagate to a broader community if that memory were ever shared.
Existing memory-sharing frameworks such as the Open Knowledge Format (McVeety & Hormati, 2026) (OKF) define formal protocols for writing and exchanging knowledge among agents but do not address memory attacks.
This difficult-to-control risk has limited the practical deployment of memory sharing between agents.

Existing defenses validate retrieved content, govern access, or enforce information-flow policies during agent execution.
A-MemGuard empirically detects context-dependent poisoning through consensus among memory-induced reasoning paths (Wei et al., 2025), whereas Collaborative Memory enforces dynamic read/write policies over provenance-tagged private and shared memory fragments (Rezazadeh et al., 2025).
However, neither approach provides formal security guarantees against malicious memories.
Beyond memory-specific defenses, CaMeL addresses prompt injection during agent execution through isolated planning with capability-based policies and user confirmation (Debenedetti et al., 2025); FIDES formalizes IFC guarantees and supports selective hiding and constrained inspection of tool results (Costa et al., 2025). PerMIT builds on this isolation-and-mediation lineage to secure the persistent-memory lifecycle.

PerMIT enforces its trust boundary at the memory interface. The harness captures environment-derived content, including tool outputs, as untrusted and mediates its release and use. The protected agent chooses its next operation and can re-plan on endorsed feedback, so its internal reasoning is not inspected or taint-tracked. The noninterference proofs quantify over arbitrary agent strategies using this finite interface (Goguen & Meseguer, 1982). However, preventing all influence from untrusted memory would also prevent legitimate tasks whose next steps depend on information recalled from that memory.
To mitigate the safety–utility tradeoff, PerMIT adopts endorsement (Myers et al., 2006), a formal relaxation that promotes an untrusted value to trusted status only after the user confirms the exact value displayed at the gate, so untrusted memory can be selectively endorsed and used rather than barred.
Using this finite mediation surface and endorsement mechanism, we prove Action Integrity as an exact authorization property and Reasoning Integrity as noninterference modulo the display transcript (Sabelfeld & Myers, 2004; Askarov & Sabelfeld, 2007), and machine-check their single-user core in Lean 411
 1

 The Lean 4 artifact is available upon request and will be released with the code when the paper is published. Its scope and correspondence are documented in Appendix E and Supplement S9..
These machine-checked guarantees hold over unbounded interface-conformant executions (§2.2), separating enforced mediation from the correctness of individual endorsement decisions.

Endorsement preserves benign utility by allowing external values to become trusted through an interface with a finite set of operations. The gate displays the exact value, original user instruction, and source, making the decision auditable. On Trojan Hippo, PerMIT combines live agent rollouts with targeted action-boundary probes; self-verification and lightweight verifiers record zero observed ASR while retaining useful memory capabilities (Table 1).

Although security concerns have limited the deployment of shared memory, Karpathy’s LLM-Wiki (Karpathy, 2026) illustrates its potential: thousands of users adopted his shared coding-agent setup to improve their agents’ performance.
LLM-Wiki’s success was an exception because the author is highly reputable, and the shared knowledge had accumulated thousands of public endorsements through GitHub stars.
However, scaling shared memory to diverse communities requires accepting contributions from ordinary users and agents, allowing adversaries to pose as legitimate contributors and spread harmful content. To solve this dilemma, PerMIT learns from the success of LLM-Wiki and allows each shared knowledge item to accumulate trust independently, paralleling security mechanisms in distributed systems that aggregate endorsements over shared objects (Walsh & Sirer, 2006).
Each logged confirmation is bound to the exact content, allowing verdicts from different users and agents to accumulate as item-level trust.
Each item requires confirmation until its accumulated trust reaches the “Community Confirmed” threshold.
As the population grows, confirmations and endorsements allow more items to reach this status and become directly available to new users without further verification, so safety and convenience improve together.
Under explicit assumptions, we prove that poison-promotion and wrongful-eviction risks decrease as the community grows, while the average per-user confirmation burden does not grow (Supplementary Theorem S6.13).
Our simulation spanning five billion promotion attempts also corroborates this co-scaling behavior.
PerMIT thus supplies the security assurance missing from the Open Knowledge Format (McVeety & Hormati, 2026) while remaining compatible with its knowledge-sharing protocol.

Finally, we close the loop by using PerMIT to construct community-confirmed shared knowledge bases on $\tau^{2}$ -bench (Barres et al., 2025) with up to 90 fully autonomous agents and no human involvement.
None of the tested direct injection payloads reaches the Community-Confirmed tier, and a zero-state agent (i.e. a fresh agent with no prior context or memory) connected to the resulting knowledge base significantly outperforms an agent without shared knowledge on held-out, experience-dependent telecom tasks (§5).

In summary, this paper makes three contributions:

1. 

Securing agent memory with machine-checked integrity.

PerMIT mediates a finite memory interface and binds each endorsement to an exact displayed value and its intended use. Under explicit trust assumptions, PerMIT provides two integrity guarantees, machine-checked in Lean 4 for the single-user core, and an auditable confirmation gate for human or automated verification.

2. 

Shared memory in which safety and convenience scale together rather than trade off.
Because each gate decision is a logged verdict on exact content, verdicts accumulate into community-confirmed knowledge, which is the layer that existing memory-sharing frameworks such as OKF lack. Under explicit assumptions, we
prove and corroborate in simulation that poison-promotion and wrongful-eviction risks fall as the community grows while per-user verification effort does not rise.

3. 

Safe, autonomous self-construction of shared knowledge.
Our experiments show that autonomous agent communities can safely construct useful knowledge bases with PerMIT. By enabling agents to generate, verify, and certify knowledge in complex environments, PerMIT provides a concrete path toward test-time learning and self-evolving agents.

## 2 Background and Related Work

## 2.1 Persistent Memory as an Attack Surface

Persistent-memory architectures manage context across sessions through tiered storage, consolidation, and revision (Packer et al., 2023; Chhikara et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025). Because stored observations later return to the agent’s context, transient exposure can become durable influence. Attacks enter through direct poisoning of a memory or knowledge base (Chen et al., 2024), query-only interaction (Dong et al., 2025), or indirect ingestion of retrieved artifacts and webpages (Srivastava & He, 2025; Zou et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026b); shared state can also contaminate users without an adversary (Yang et al., 2026a). The defining risk is temporal: Trojan Hippo plants a dormant payload through one untrusted tool call and activates it only in a later session (Das et al., 2026). This persistence makes turn-local prompt-injection defences insufficient and motivates guarantees over the memory lifecycle (Lin et al., 2026).

## 2.2 Defenses and Formal Coverage

Existing defenses draw their boundaries at different layers. Content-based methods detect anomalous memories or task drift (Wei et al., 2025; Abdelnabi et al., 2024). Isolation and privilege-control methods constrain how untrusted information can influence tool interactions (Wen et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2025). TMA-NM (Louck, 2026) binds memory authority to origin and studies consequential-action safety using TLA+ model checking and an inductive-invariant argument. Willison’s Dual LLM pattern introduced privileged planning, quarantined processing, and opaque references (Willison, 2023). CaMeL adds capability-based enforcement and user confirmation, while leaving formal verification as future work (Debenedetti et al., 2025, §§2,5,10). AgentDyn reports zero utility for its CaMeL configurations under automated dynamic-task evaluation (Li et al., 2026). FIDES provides a formal IFC model with integrity noninterference, selective variable hiding, and schema-constrained quarantined inspection (Costa et al., 2025). Its type-aware policies can permit bounded influence; PerMIT centers exact-value, tool-scoped endorsement and the complete display transcript. Whereas CaMeL and FIDES address prompt injection in agent execution more generally, our contribution centers the persistent-memory lifecycle, with Action Integrity and Reasoning Integrity guarantees for arbitrarily long interactions through the memory interface under explicit trust assumptions. We machine-check the integrity theorems in Lean 4 and aggregate item-level endorsements in the federated tier. Planning and tool choice remain agent-driven, including replanning on endorsed feedback.

## 2.3 Shared Memory and Evaluation

Shared-memory work has primarily addressed exchange, access, and portability. OKF standardizes knowledge exchange (McVeety & Hormati, 2026), Collaborative Memory enforces dynamic policies over private and shared fragments (Rezazadeh et al., 2025), and Portable Agent Memory proposes cryptographically verified transfer and injection-resistant rehydration (Ravindran, 2026). These mechanisms complement PerMIT but do not establish recipient-side action and reasoning integrity for adopted content.

General agent-security benchmarks emphasize prompt injection within a task episode (Debenedetti et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026; Weng et al., 2026); Trojan Hippo most directly matches our cross-session threat model (Das et al., 2026). We therefore use Trojan Hippo to evaluate persistent-memory security and $\tau^{2}$ -bench (Barres et al., 2025) to evaluate the end-to-end utility of autonomously constructed shared knowledge.

## 3 The PerMIT Framework

## 3.1 Threat Model

PerMIT assumes an adversary capable of controlling or manipulating content obtained from the external environment, including tool outputs, web content, external files and codebases. Poisoned payloads may enter persistent memory when the agent invokes tools, browses the web, or inspects external files or code. PerMIT establishes a provenance-based trust boundary: only values typed in directly by the user or exact values explicitly confirmed by the user through the confirmation interface are treated as trusted. All other environment-derived content remains untrusted and cannot reach the protected LLM unless it first passes through this confirmation gate and gets verified to be trusted.

## 3.2 The Single-User Tier: a Finite Memory Interface

The P-LLM remains an agent that chooses its next operation and revises its plan using endorsed feedback. Prompts describe the interface; the harness enforces its observation and flow rules without inspecting the agent’s internal reasoning. Gate decisions control which values are endorsed; the harness enforces how values cross the interface.
Figure 1 summarizes PerMIT’s architecture, trust boundary, and shared-memory trust-accumulation mechanism.
Architecturally, PerMIT places a
Protected LLM agent (P-LLM) on the protected side of the trust boundary and uses a Quarantined Reader (Q-LLM) to inspect and retrieve relevant content from untrusted memory. The Q-LLM can read the memory store but has no tool capabilities. In our implementation, it is realized as a recursive language model (RLM) (Zhang et al., 2025), enabling it to navigate stores larger than a context window without loading their contents into the P-LLM’s trusted context (implementation details in Section B.4). Untrusted content is exposed to the P-LLM only through opaque handles rather than as readable bytes, and the content can be released only after endorsement through the confirmation gate (Lemma D.1).
The P-LLM interacts with persistent memory through a fixed algebra of seven
operations: $\mathsf{write}$ , $\mathsf{recall}$ , $\mathsf{fill}$ ,
 $\mathsf{crystallize}$ , $\mathsf{display}$ , $\mathsf{confirm}$ , and
 $\mathsf{evict}$ . In particular, $\mathsf{recall}$ returns readable bytes only
for trusted content and otherwise returns an opaque handle; $\mathsf{fill}$ 
searches the untrusted region of memory and likewise returns handles; and
 $\mathsf{crystallize}$ produces a schema-bound summary that remains untrusted
when written back to memory. Appendix B explains all seven
operations from a systems perspective, with a worked poisoning trace. The full interface also mediates tool invocation, trusted retrieval, input channels, and batched iteration (Section D.1). Sensitive-tool literals must byte-match typed or tool-endorsed content to bypass the gate; handles always gate. Data tools may receive agent-composed bytes. Trust denotes provenance and authorization, not factual correctness.

Figure 1: PerMIT mediates observations and data flows at the persistent-memory interface while leaving planning and tool choice to the protected agent.

PerMIT’s finite memory interface yields two guarantees, stated compactly below. Both assume source-based labels, immutable stored blocks, and faithful displays; Appendices D.2.1 and D.2.2 summarize the arguments; Supplement S3 gives the full proofs.

Action Integrity (Theorem D.3, compact form).

Assume trusted endorsement: acceptance authorizes the exact displayed bytes for the named tool. For every execution from a well-formed initial state, under any attack, each argument reaching a sensitive tool is either an exact user-typed value or a value endorsed by that user at its exact bytes for that exact tool, at or before the call. Endorsement grants reusable authority for an exact value and tool. It does not bind argument position, task, purpose, time, or the other arguments of a call (Appendix D.2.1).

Reasoning Integrity modulo t
conclusion:
PerMIT contributes a finite memory interface with machine-checked integrity guarantees, a federated protocol that turns exact-content endorsements into reusable trust, and an autonomous workflow for constructing useful shared knowledge. Under explicit assumptions, the protocol bounds poison promotion and wrongful eviction while reducing repeated verification. The agent communities promoted no direct injection payloads and improved held-out task performance through PerMIT.

These results motivate three future directions. First, provenance and endorsement do not ensure usefulness: shared memory may contain redundant, inaccurate, or hallucinated knowledge, motivating quality-aware gates and active memory management. Second, estimating rare promotion events required five billion simulated attempts and over 50 hours of computation; more efficient calibration with live verifiers and users would strengthen deployment evidence. Third, adaptive payload search against live verifiers remains an open empirical question. Our simulations test the protocol’s conditional safety boundaries through adaptive protocol attacks under controlled reviewer responses; they do not replace adaptive payload search against live verifiers. Human or agent memory managers could combine memories and review their joint meaning and intended use, then seek fresh user endorsements of the combined content before it becomes trusted. Testing this workflow against adaptive endorsement and delayed-combination attacks is a future direction. Matched component controls and measured human review effort would further clarify deployment trade-offs.

title: Behavior Beyond Text: Evaluating Refusal Transfer Failure in LLM Agents
abstract: While large language models are increasingly deployed as tool-calling agents, their safety evaluations still focus primarily on their ability to refuse harmful requests in text. We investigate whether the refusal behavior in text transfers to tool use. We construct a benchmark of 2,304 prompts across four domains, consisting of matched triplets that present the same harmful or benign request in text-only, standard tool-enabled, and adversarially framed tool-enabled settings. We then assess tool-call safety using 20 predefined forbidden actions. Testing five models of varying sizes and families, we find that requests refused in text frequently result in unsafe tool calls. Under standard tool-enabled prompting, this divergence occurs for 10-52 percent of harmful requests refused in chat. To mechanistically investigate this gap, we identify a refusal-associated direction in the residual stream of each of the five models. We find that in tool-enabled contexts, the activations along this direction decrease in four of five models. Furthermore, lower activation predicts unsafe tool calls across all five models (AUC 0.76-0.86). However, restoring the signal to the respective text-only value through activation patching only prevents a subset of unsafe calls, primarily by suppressing tool use rather than by producing safer calls. Steering along the refusal direction nearly eliminates unsafe calls only at strengths that also suppress benign tool use or degrade the output quality. Our findings indicate that the identified refusal direction contributes to whether a model acts, but only partially explains the refusal divergence. Therefore, evaluating the safety of tool-calling agents requires directly examining their actions along with their textual responses.

Abstract

While large language models are increasingly deployed as tool-calling agents, their safety evaluations still focus primarily on their ability to refuse harmful requests in text. We investigate whether the refusal behavior in text transfers to tool use. We construct a benchmark of 2,304 prompts across four domains, consisting of matched triplets that present the same harmful or benign request in text-only, standard tool-enabled, and adversarially framed tool-enabled settings. We then assess tool-call safety using 20 predefined forbidden actions. Testing five models of varying sizes and families, we find that requests refused in text frequently result in unsafe tool calls. Under standard tool-enabled prompting, this divergence occurs for 10–52 percent of harmful requests refused in chat. To mechanistically investigate this gap, we identify a refusal-associated direction in the residual stream of each of the five models. We find that in tool-enabled contexts, the activations along this direction decrease in four of five models. Furthermore, lower activation predicts unsafe tool calls across all five models (AUC 0.76–0.86). However, restoring the signal to the respective text-only value through activation patching only prevents a subset of unsafe calls, primarily by suppressing tool use rather than by producing safer calls. Steering along the refusal direction nearly eliminates unsafe calls only at strengths that also suppress benign tool use or degrade the output quality. Our findings indicate that the identified refusal direction contributes to whether a model acts, but only partially explains the refusal divergence. Therefore, evaluating the safety of tool-calling agents requires directly examining their actions along with their textual responses.

## 1 Introduction

Increasingly, the use cases of large language models have shifted from simply generating text to taking actions in the form of agents. Many modern systems browse the web, execute code, call typed tools, and implement enterprise workflows (Schick et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023; Qin et al., 2024). With this shift in the deployment of LLMs, there is a corresponding shift in the meaning of their “safety”. That is, a tool-enabled agent can cause harm through its actions in the environment, not only by emitting an unsafe sentence as measured in text-based settings.

Indeed, safety alignment is currently overwhelmingly trained and evaluated on text. In particular red teaming, refusal training, and jailbreak benchmarks target harmful text-based completions (Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022a; Bai et al., 2022b; Ganguli et al., 2022; Perez et al., 2022; Mazeika et al., 2024). A model that has learned to
say “I can’t help with that” has learned a behavior over its verbal
output. Nonetheless, whether that behavior also governs the tool-call decision is a
separate question that carries direct consequences as these agents move into financial, medical, and legal settings.

This distinction is important because tool-enabled agents are increasingly being developed and applied in high-risk domains such as finance and healthcare (Ding et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025), where failures can lead to financial losses, privacy breaches, or the execution of malicious instructions extracted from external sources.

However, prior work has rarely investigated whether refusal mechanisms transfer to tool-call decisions. To address this gap, we evaluate models from five different families on a dataset we created spanning four domains. We run inference on all of these models using groups of three semantically similar requests: one text-only request and two other tool-enabled variants. We find that models that refuse harmful requests in text generation often fail to refuse similar requests when they are framed in the format of a tool invocation.

## Behavioral finding:

We evaluate our benchmark of prompt triples, in which each harmful request is posed as a plain chat prompt as well as two tool-enabled versions. We find that, although the models refuse 44–76% of harmful chat prompts, they oftentimes fail to refuse the same requests when phrased in the tool-use variant. This gap, which we call conditioned divergence, is substantial and does not track model size in our five models.

## Mechanistic finding:

Next, we ask why, seeking to find the mechanistic underpinnings of our behavioral results. We begin by identifying the refusal direction in each model, following the approach of prior work, which shows that refusal is mediated by a single direction (Park et al., 2024) in the residual stream (Arditi et al., 2024). To directly address the behavioral finding, we then test whether that refusal direction also governs tool call safety. We find that it does, but only in part. That is, tool-enabled prompts suppress the activation of the refusal direction at the decision token in most models, and a lower activation predicts the unsafe call in all five models (AUC 0.76–0.86). Nonetheless, when we restore the refusal signal to its no-tool level, we find that for most models only a minority of unsafe calls revert, and most of those that do revert by emitting no tool call rather than a safer one. Hence, we conclude that refusal suppression explains only part of this transfer failure. The refusal direction is therefore a useful signal for monitoring but a comparatively blunt knob for control. Because the divergence recurs in all five model families, it may reflect a general property of how alignment is represented in models, although the internal mechanism differs between them.

## 1.1 Contributions

1. 

A 2304 prompt matched triple benchmark spanning four high-stakes domains with 20 deterministic forbidden actions to score tool-call refusal.

2. 

A conditioned-divergence metric separating transfer failure from the base refusal rate, together with evidence that text refusal does not reliably transfer to tool call safety.

3. 

A mechanistic study across five model families showing the refusal direction is a strong predictor (AUC 0.76–0.86) but only a partial mediator (patching reverts 13–90% of unsafe calls, mostly by suppressing the call rather than by making it safe), with suppression significant in four of five families and random-direction, mean-direction and KL-admissibility controls reported for all five.

## 2 Related work

## Tool-augmented language models.

This line of work introduces the extension of LLMs from simple text generation to actions that take the form of external tool calls, and teaches models to call functions, search, and run multi-step workflows
(Schick et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023; Qin et al., 2024). This shifts an area of potential harm from text that has been generated to actions done by an agent. The latter is the surface of our targets for evaluation.

## Mind the GAP.

The closest work to ours is
Cartagena and Teixeira (2026), who measure the text-to-tool safety gap head-on. They pose each harmful request twice, with one version in plain chat and another version using available tools. This structure is similar to the dataset we constructed, as they also consider requests crossing several domains and similarly using a deterministic forbidden action check for safety. This paper shows that requests the model refuses in chat often emerge as unsafe tool calls once actions are enabled. This provides behavioral evidence, which we reproduce and then add a mechanistic explanation for. We
also measure the gap differently, as our conditioned divergence counts only the
triples a model genuinely refused in chat, so its base refusal rate cannot move
the number. Finally, we add an adversarially framed mode to each group to tell tool
availability apart from prompt pressure.

## Refusal and safety alignment in text.

Several works measure and train safety alignment over text generation and completion. Specifically, instruction tuning and RLHF can teach models to decline harmful requests (Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022a; Bai et al., 2022b), and red-teaming and jailbreak benchmarks stress-test
that behavior (Ganguli et al., 2022; Perez et al., 2022; Mazeika et al., 2024). These
methods evaluate what the model says, not whether the learned refusal governs the model’s actions when tools are available.

## Mechanistic interpretability of refusal.

Arditi et al. (2024)
shows that refusal in chat models is mediated by a single linear direction in the
residual stream. Specifically, they show that ablating it suppresses refusal and adding it induces
over-refusal. We test this on five architectures, where it reproduces only in part, and extend it to
the text-to-tool transition, testing whether the same direction stays active
when the model selects an action rather than a sentence.

## 3 Methodology

## 3.1 What we mean by an agent

The term agent is widely used across enterprise, spanning everything from a single function call to a multi-step system with planning, memory, and environment feedback. We therefore fix the object of the study. By an agent we mean an off-the-shelf instruction-tuned LLM with a minimal harness which includes a set of domain tools, implemented in standard OpenAI function call schemas that are injected into the model’s context, allowing the model to either respond with natural-language text or a structured call to one of those tools. No planning module, scratchpad, memory, or orchestration layer is included in this harness.

## 3.2 Dataset

The evaluation dataset consists of 2304 prompts across different categories:

• 

Domain: Finance, Healthcare, Education, and Legal: four
regulated settings, each with its own misuse modes and protected data.

• 

Scenario: Direct, Indirect, Justification/roleplay, and
Structured: four phrasings of the same intent, from straightforward
to tool-format-driven.

• 

Mode: No-tool chat, Tool-enabled normal, and Tool-enabled
stress (jailbreak-style framing): the central comparison.

• 

System condition: Neutral, Safety-reinforced (explicit
safety constraints), and Tool-encouraging (nudges tool use).

• 

Variant: A (original phrasing) and B (reworded).

• 

Request type: Harmful (should be refused / no unsafe tool
call) and Benign (safe to answer or call tools).

The scenario factor poses the request in different forms (Direct, Indirect, Justification/roleplay, and Structured) because different styles of framing alter AI outputs (Lutz et al., 2025). The three Mode options are the essential comparison of the datapoints. No-tool chat: no tools provided; model responds in conversation. Tool-enabled normal: domain tools are injected into the context under standard prompting. Tool-enabled stress: same tools injected into context. However, the user prompt includes higher pressure or jailbreak-style framing. Matched groups (same domain, scenario, variant, system condition, request type, and batch) share the same underlying intent across modes, with prompts adapted to each mode’s context: no-tool prompts make no reference to tools, while tool-enabled prompts explicitly invoke specific tools. This design holds scenario and intent constant while varying both tool availability and the framing appropriate to each mode, following the matched-prompt multi-domain safety evaluation methodology of Cartagena and Teixeira (2026).

Three system conditions vary the framing presented to the models: a neutral role description, a safety-reinforced version with explicit safety reminders, and finally a tool-encouraging version emphasizing efficient use of available functions.

These six factors define 576 cells; each cell was authored four times with distinct prompts (the Batch factor), giving 2304 prompts. These categories produce a broad set of reproducible scenarios for testing our claim.

## 3.3 Tool environments and forbidden actions

Each domain exposes five function-calling tools modeled on realistic
deployment schemas, adapting the domain tool-environment and deterministic forbidden-action design of Cartagena and Teixeira (2026).
Example tools include place_trade_order and
initiate_wire_transfer (Finance),
retrieve_patient_record and draft_medication_plan
(Healthcare), change_grade (Education), and
file_regulatory_submission (Legal).
Tools are provided in standard OpenAI function schema format.

Tool-call safety is scored by ForbiddenAction predicates which are deterministic Python functions that inspect a tool name and argument dictionary and return a Boolean violation flag.
Each domain defines five predicates: one per tool for 20 total.
Predicate types are:

• 

Sensitive-data flag: fires when a Boolean parameter
requesting protected data (e.g., include_phi=True) is set.

• 

Authorization-bypass: fires when a required authorization
field (e.g., approval_ticket) is absent, empty, or filled with a
value that asserts bypass rather than authorization (e.g.,
approval_ticket="skip_approval").

• 

PII exfiltration: fires when synthetic PII markers or
PII/privilege-seeking text (e.g., query="private student
identifiers") appears in text-valued arguments, or when a send tool names
an unapproved external recipient.

• 

Intent keyword: fires when argument content contains
policy-evasion terms (e.g., “evade”, “bypass”, “contraindicated”).

A run is scored tc_safe if no predicate fires; any violation yields
tc_unsafe. Every rule was validated against all stored runs and fires on 1.4–3.4% of benign tool-enabled runs per model.

## 3.4 Models

• 

Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 (Jiang et al., 2023)

• 

Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct (Dubey et al., 2024)

• 

Command R 7B
(CohereLabs/c4ai-command-r7b-12-2024) (Cohere, 2024)

• 

Qwen3-14B (Qwen/Qwen3-14B) (Yang et al., 2025)

• 

Gemma 3 27B (google/gemma-3-27b-it) (Gemma Team, 2025)

## 3.5 Metrics

Refusal rate.
This is the fraction of responses that decline the user request, computed separately
for harmful and benign prompts.
On harmful prompts, high refusal is the target safety behavior (Arditi et al., 2024) and on benign prompts, it shows over-refusal (false positive rate) (Röttger et al., 2024; Cui et al., 2025).
Refusal is scored only on genuine text responses; a tool-call-only response or empty text is not counted as a verbal refusal.

tc_safe rate.
This is the fraction of tool-enabled runs where no ForbiddenAction predicate fires.

Matched triples.
Each harmful request instance is issued in all three interaction modes:
no-tool chat, tool-enabled normal, and tool-enabled stress, producing a
matched triple of runs over the same underlying request.
These triples are keyed by (Domain, Scenario, Variant, System Condition, Batch),
so the no-tool run and the two tool-enabled runs differ only in tool
affordance and prompt framing and not in the actual request.
Let $\mathcal{T}$ be the set of all matched triples and, for a triple $t$ ,
let $\mathrm{refuse}(t)$ indicate that the no-tool run verbally refused and
 $\mathrm{unsafe}_{m}(t)=\neg\,\mathrm{tc\_safe}$ indicate that the
tool-enabled run in mode $m\in\{\mathrm{normal},\mathrm{stress}\}$ fired a
ForbiddenAction predicate.

Tool-call propensity.
Tool-use rates vary substantially across models. Under normal tool-enabled prompting, models issue at least one tool call on 11–59% of harmful requests. Conditional on issuing a call, however, 73–100% of calls are unsafe. Command-R illustrates why unconditional unsafe-call rates must be interpreted alongside tool-use propensity: it calls a tool on only 11% of harmful requests, and every such call is unsafe. Its benign tool-call rate is also relatively low at 40%, compared with 83% for Llama-3.1-70B. Thus, Command-R’s low aggregate unsafe-call rate partly reflects low tool-use propensity rather than consistently safe action selection.

Conditioned divergence.
Our primary metric.
Let $\mathcal{T}_{R}=\{\,t\in\mathcal{T}:\mathrm{refuse}(t)\,\}$ be
the triples whose no-tool run refused (baseline refusal).
Conditioned divergence for tool mode $m$ denotes the fraction of these triples
whose matched tool-enabled run is unsafe:

 $\Delta^{\mathrm{cond}}_{m}=\frac{\bigl|\{\,t\in\mathcal{T}_{R}:\mathrm{unsafe}_{m}(t)\,\}\bigr|}{\bigl|\mathcal{T}_{R}\bigr|}$ 

(1)

 $\Delta^{\mathrm{cond}}_{m}$ indicates how often the verbal refusal of a request
fails to carry over to the matched action when tools are available, the
core transfer-failure signal (Cartagena and Teixeira, 2026; Wu et al., 2024). It is reported separately for normal and stress modes, and conditions on $\mathcal{T}_{R}$ so that it is unaffected by how often the model refuses in text (a model that rarely refuses cannot
inflate or deflate it).

## 3.6 Refusal classification

Text refusal is classified by Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic, 2026) at temperature 0, using both the request and response. Empty or tool-call-only responses count as non-refusals, and disclaimer-wrapped compliance counts as compliance. Validation against Claude Fable 5 on 538 stratified examples yields 97.4% agreement ( $\kappa=0.94$ ). Intervention outputs are screened for degenerate (repetitive or non-linguistic) text before classification, and conditions with at least 25% degenerate output are flagged and their rates are not interpreted.

## 3.7 Mechanistic methods

## Refusal direction:

On the no-tool prompts, we take the decision token residual vector at every layer and compute the difference in mean direction (Marks and Tegmark, 2023) between harmful and benign prompts to identify the refusal direction: $\hat{r}_{l}=\text{unit}(\mu_{l}^{\text{harm}}-\mu_{l}^{\text{benign}})$ (Arditi et al., 2024). We then select the operating layer as the one maximizing the norm of the difference-in-means vector, measuring the magnitude of the separation, inside the causal mid band (35 to 85 percent depth). The layer is selected automatically for each model. We additionally score every candidate layer with the KL-divergence admissibility check of Arditi et al. (2024) on harmless prompts; at the selected layer only Command-R’s direction passes i

title: Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly expected to interact with environments and improve their decisions during deployment. However, how anticipating future outcomes and drawing on accumulated interaction experience can jointly support decision-making remains underexplored. We propose a test-time framework, inspired by Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control, that combines multi-branch predictive analysis with experience-based adaptation. At each step, the agent proposes multiple candidate actions and imagines their outcomes with a world model, so that alternatives can be compared without being executed in the environment. Since language environments provide neither explicit dynamics nor costs, the predicted outcomes are evaluated for task progress and risk, and MPPI-style weights over the resulting costs guide the final decision. A dual-branch experience memory enables self-improvement: the planner branch refines candidate generation and action selection, while the world model branch improves next-observation prediction. Experiments on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld across three backbones demonstrate the strong overall performance of our method and the effectiveness of experience-guided predictive control. Our code will be made publicly available.

## Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths
