headings: Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths
body_start:
Abstract

Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly expected to interact with environments and improve their decisions during deployment.
However, how anticipating future outcomes and drawing on accumulated interaction experience can jointly support decision-making remains underexplored.
We propose a test-time framework, inspired by Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control, that combines multi-branch predictive analysis with experience-based adaptation.
At each step, the agent proposes multiple candidate actions and imagines their outcomes with a world model, so that alternatives can be compared without being executed in the environment.
Since language environments provide neither explicit dynamics nor costs, the predicted outcomes are evaluated for task progress and risk, and MPPI-style weights over the resulting costs guide the final decision.
A dual-branch experience memory enables self-improvement: the planner branch refines candidate generation and action selection, while the world model branch improves next-observation prediction.
Experiments on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld across three backbones demonstrate the strong overall performance of our method and the effectiveness of experience-guided predictive control. Our code will be made publicly available.

## 1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) agents interact with environments by interpreting observations and taking actions to accomplish tasks.
Long-horizon tasks require them to sustain progress under incomplete observations, where poor decisions can lead to repeated failures or wasted interactions.
Building agents that make reliable decisions over extended interactions therefore remains a central challenge.

Prior work improves interactive decision making in several complementary ways.
ReAct interleaves reasoning with environment feedback (Yao et al., 2023b), but commits to a single proposed action at each step, which may miss useful alternatives.
Search-based methods instead explore multiple reasoning or action paths at inference time (Yao et al., 2023a; Zhou et al., 2024; Hao et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2026), but their cost grows with the breadth and depth of the search.
A separate line improves agents through retrieved reflections and trajectory-derived action advantages (Shinn et al., 2023; Li et al., 2026a).
These directions motivate exploring a few alternatives before acting, without executing them, together with experience gathered through interaction.
This also resembles how people mentally simulate a few alternatives before choosing (Gilbert and Wilson, 2007; Vul et al., 2014): the agent imagines the outcomes of several candidate actions (Hafner et al., 2020; Gu et al., 2025), which avoids the interaction steps and potential irreversible consequences of trying them in the environment.
Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control offers a concrete recipe for this pattern: it samples a finite batch of candidate trajectories, weights them by predicted costs with exponential (Gibbs) weights, executes only the next action, and replans (Williams et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2017).

Language environments, however, provide neither explicit dynamics nor costs.
A language world model can supply the missing dynamics by predicting the outcome of each candidate action (Hao et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026), but better next-observation prediction does not necessarily yield higher task success (Zhang et al., 2026).
We therefore couple prediction directly with decision making: the agent predicts the outcomes of several candidate actions, an evaluator assigns costs for task progress and risk, and MPPI-style weights summarize these costs for a final controller that selects or synthesizes the action to execute.

To make both the candidates and their predictions more reliable over time, we further introduce a dual-branch experience memory for self-improvement.
The planner branch uses accumulated experience to improve candidate generation and action selection, while the world model branch improves next-observation prediction, so that a single stream of interaction experience improves both what is proposed and what is predicted.
Both branches operate through retrieved textual context, with policy and world model parameters frozen.
Our analysis bounds the agent’s per-step regret in terms of three error sources, namely limited candidate coverage, errors in action selection, and inaccurate next-observation predictions, which motivates the two branches.

Experiments on ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021) and ScienceWorld (Wang et al., 2022) demonstrate the strongest overall success-rate performance among the evaluated methods across three backbones.
Our main contributions are:

• 

We propose a test-time, MPPI-inspired framework that improves a bounded predict–select–replan decision loop with experience: a world model predicts the outcomes of a few candidate actions, and a dual-branch memory improves both candidate generation and selection and next-observation prediction.

• 

We provide a theoretical analysis showing that the weighting rule is optimal under a KL-regularized objective, and that the per-step regret is bounded in terms of candidate coverage, action selection, and next-observation prediction errors, which motivates the two memory branches.

• 

Experiments on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld across three backbones demonstrate the strongest overall success rate performance among baselines. We also provide ablation studies and a computational cost analysis.

## 2 Related Work

## LLM agents.

LLM agents choose actions from textual or visual observations (Wu et al., 2025a; Wu et al., 2025b) in a loop.
ReAct (Yao et al., 2023b) and SayCan (Ahn et al., 2022) ground actions in environmental feedback or available skills, ADaPT (Prasad et al., 2024) decomposes tasks, and further methods support lookahead through branching or retrieved information (Yao et al., 2023a; Zhou et al., 2024; Koh et al., 2024; Holt et al., 2026).
In traditional control, a related perspective also uses lookahead: model-predictive control (Camacho and Bordons, 2007) plans over a finite horizon, executes only the first action, and replans from the new observation.
MPPI further weights sampled trajectories by their predicted costs (Williams et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2017).
We adapt MPPI’s strategy of predicting and weighting multiple candidates to language agents through world model prediction, replacing its continuous control update with a discrete action update driven by language models, and thus call our framework MPPI-inspired.

## World models for agent planning.

World models can estimate how actions change an environment before they are executed.
Dynalang (Lin et al., 2024), RAP (Hao et al., 2023), WebDreamer (Gu et al., 2025), and IMPLEMENT (Song et al., 2026) simulate action outcomes with language-based or lightweight world models; while ITP (Liu et al., 2026), WKM (Qiao et al., 2024), and WorldEvolver (Zhang et al., 2026) add adaptive lookahead, structured knowledge, or retrieved experience.
Qian et al. (Qian et al., 2026) and Li et al. (Li et al., 2026b) study how well agents use forecasts and whether LLMs can serve as text-based world models.
More recently, MemWM (Wang et al., 2026) trains a world model with offline-built memory to evaluate the candidates.
Unlike them, we keep all models frozen and use experience gathered during interaction in two branches that improve next-observation prediction and candidate generation and selection.

## Self-improving agents.

Experience-based methods improve later decisions by retaining information from prior interactions, building on memory systems (Park et al., 2023; Packer et al., 2023; Chhikara et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025; Sumers et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2026).
Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023), ExpeL (Zhao et al., 2024), ERL (Allard et al., 2026), and ReasoningBank (Ouyang et al., 2026) distill feedback or trajectories into experience, Voyager (Wang et al., 2024) and AWM (Wang et al., 2025) retain skills or task procedures, AdaPlanner (Sun et al., 2023) and JitRL (Li et al., 2026a) revise plans or action preferences from retrieved experience, and Memento (Zhou et al., 2025), ACE (Zhang et al., 2025), and Dynamic Cheatsheet (Suzgun et al., 2026) adapt through episodic memory or evolving contexts instead of fine-tuning (Wu et al., 2026).
These methods improve what the agent proposes; our dual-branch memory also improves what it predicts, so a single stream of interaction experience sharpens both the candidates and the forecasts used to choose among them.

Figure 1: Overview of our method. At step $t$ , the proposal policy takes the goal, history, and observation and proposes $K$ candidate actions $a_{t}^{(k)}$ . The world model predicts the next observation $\hat{o}_{t+1}^{(k)}$ of each candidate, the evaluator scores task progress and risk to give costs $C_{t}^{(k)}$ , and MPPI-style weights summarize these costs for the final controller, which decides the executed action $a_{t}$ . After execution, the transition updates both experience branches. The planner branch labels it as success, failure, or ignore and summarizes the first two into $M_{t}^{\mathrm{cand}}$ and $M_{t}^{\mathrm{final}}$ , retrieved by the proposal policy and final controller in future steps; the world model branch updates its episodic and semantic memory $M_{t}^{\mathrm{world}}$ , retrieved by the world model in future steps.

## 3 Problem Formulation

We consider a language agent solving a long-horizon interactive task with goal $g$ and an interaction budget of $T$ steps.
At step $t$ , the agent receives an observation $o_{t}$ and has interaction history $h_{t}=(o_{1},a_{1},\ldots,o_{t-1},a_{t-1})$ .
It acts from context $x_{t}=(g,h_{t},o_{t})$ . Its policy $\pi(\cdot\mid x_{t})$ defines a distribution over language actions, and the action at step $t$ is generated according to:

 $a_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x_{t}),\qquad a_{t}\in\mathcal{A}.$ 

(1)

After $a_{t}$ is applied, the environment generates the next observation according to:

 $o_{t+1}\sim P_{\mathrm{env}}(o^{\prime}\mid h_{t},o_{t},a_{t}).$ 

(2)

Our objective is to maximize the probability of completing the task within the interaction budget:

 $\pi^{\star}=\arg\max_{\pi}\Pr(\text{success by }T\mid g,\pi).$ 

(3)

In control, Model-Predictive Control (MPC) plans over a finite horizon $H$ by selecting the candidate action sequence $\mathbf{a}=(a_{t},\ldots,a_{t+H-1})$ with the lowest expected predicted cost:

 $\mathbf{a}^{\star}=\arg\min_{\mathbf{a}}\bar{J}_{t}(\mathbf{a}),$ 

(4)

where $\bar{J}_{t}$ is the expected cost of the model-predicted trajectory (Camacho and Bordons, 2007; Rawlings et al., 2017; Li et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021).
MPC executes only the first action and replans after the next observation.
Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) (Williams et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2017) approximates this search by sampling candidate trajectories and favoring those with lower predicted costs with Gibbs weights.
This predict-and-replan cycle suits our agent tasks, where each action shapes later decisions.
Inspired by MPPI, we develop a test-time framework for language agents that uses a world model to evaluate multiple candidate actions and guide decision-making.
The next section presents our method in detail.

## 4 Method

We first describe the test-time loop: a world model predicts outcomes for up to $K$ proposed actions, and MPPI-inspired weighting of task-conditioned costs guides a final controller to select or synthesize an action before replanning from the new observation.
We then describe how dual-branch experience memory improves planning and grounds future forecasts.

## 4.1 MPPI-Inspired Decision Loop

At time step $t$ , the agent receives the goal, interaction history, current observation, and action protocol.
Let $M_{t}^{\mathrm{P}}$ denote the planner experiences retrieved for this decision, which will be introduced in Sec. 4.2 in detail.
The proposal module first reasons over the context, and then emits up to $K$ atomic candidate actions.
The resulting candidate set is represented as:

 $\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{t}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\{a_{t}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{N_{t}},$ 
 $\displaystyle 1\leq N_{t}\leq K,$ 

(5)

 $\displaystyle a_{t}^{(k)}$ 
 $\displaystyle\sim q_{\pi}(a\mid x_{t},M_{t}^{\mathrm{P}}),$ 
 $\displaystyle k=1,\ldots,N_{t}.$ 

Here $q_{\pi}$ denotes the proposal policy, $K$ is the maximum number of candidates, and $N_{t}$ is the number generated at step $t$ .
This adapts MPPI’s candidate sampling to language actions: instead of adding perturbations to a continuous control sequence, the proposal policy generates candidate actions that could advance the task, gather information, or recover from failures.

Next, for each proposal, the world model receives the goal, current observation, candidate action, and retrieved world model memory $M_{t}^{\mathrm{world}}$ .

It predicts a one-step textual observation of the action’s immediate consequence:

 $\hat{o}_{t+1}^{(k)}\sim\hat{P}(o^{\prime}\mid g,o_{t},a_{t}^{(k)},M_{t}^{\mathrm{world}}).$ 

(6)

We use one-step prediction rather than multi-step rollouts to simplify the architecture and control computational cost.
We denote the resulting candidate-specific imagined transition by

 $\hat{\tau}_{t}^{(k)}=(g,h_{t},o_{t},a_{t}^{(k)},\hat{o}_{t+1}^{(k)}),$ 

(7)

which bundles the task context, proposed action, and predicted outcome used to evaluate that candidate.
In classical MPPI, candidate trajectories are evaluated by a numerical cost function.
For language agents, we instantiate this cost-evaluation stage through textual outcome prediction and evaluation of task progress and risk.
A language evaluator maps each imagined transition to a bounded predictive cost:

 $C_{t}^{(k)}=C_{\psi}(g,h_{t},o_{t},a_{t}^{(k)},\hat{o}_{t+1}^{(k)})\in[0,100],$ 

(8)

where lower cost indicates greater predicted usefulness for the goal.
The evaluator considers expected task progress, information value, and whether the predicted outcomes are consistent with the available evidence.
To account for uncertainty in predicted costs, we optimize a distribution $\mathbf{w}$ that favors low-cost candidates while retaining alternatives.
We denote its regularized objective by $\mathcal{F}_{t}(\mathbf{w})$ and its minimizing distribution by $\mathbf{w}_{t}^{\star}$ ; the objective combines weighted predictive cost with a KL penalty from uniform weighting.

Proposition 1 (Optimal candidate weighting).

For $N_{t}\geq 1$ candidates with finite costs, let $\Delta_{N_{t}}$ denote the probability simplex and $u_{t}^{(k)}=1/N_{t}$ the uniform reference. For $\lambda>0$ , consider

 $\displaystyle\mathbf{w}_{t}^{\star}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\arg\min_{\mathbf{w}\in\Delta_{N_{t}}}\mathcal{F}_{t}(\mathbf{w}),$ 

(9)

 $\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{t}(\mathbf{w})$ 
 $\displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{N_{t}}w^{(k)}C_{t}^{(k)}+\lambda D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbf{w}\|\mathbf{u}_{t}),$ 

The objective has a unique minimizer

 $w_{t}^{(k)\star}=\frac{\exp(-C_{t}^{(k)}/\lambda)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N_{t}}\exp(-C_{t}^{(j)}/\lambda)}.$ 

(10)

For every $\mathbf{w}\in\Delta_{N_{t}}$ ,

 $\mathcal{F}_{t}(\mathbf{w})-\mathcal{F}_{t}(\mathbf{w}_{t}^{\star})=\lambda D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbf{w}\|\mathbf{w}_{t}^{\star})\geq 0.$ 

(11)

The minimizing distribution is the standard Gibbs cost-tilted form underlying MPPI (Williams et al., 2017), which also admits a free-energy interpretation of bounded-rational choice (Ortega and Braun, 2013).
The proof is in Appendix B.
Proposition 1 shows that candidate weights depend on cost differences scaled by $\lambda$ : smaller $\lambda$ emphasizes the lowest predicted costs, whereas larger $\lambda$ retains more balanced influence across candidates.
Our main configuration uses $\lambda=10$ .
We use $w_{t}^{(k)}=w_{t}^{(k)\star}$ below.
The weights then guide the final controller, which also receives the goal, trajectory, observation, candidate set, predicted outcomes, and retrieved planner experiences.
We denote its action-generation step by

 $\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{t}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\{(\hat{o}_{t+1}^{(k)},w_{t}^{(k)})\}_{k=1}^{N_{t}},$ 

(12)

 $\displaystyle a_{t}$ 
 $\displaystyle\sim\pi_{\mathrm{final}}(\cdot\mid x_{t},\mathcal{A}_{t},\mathcal{E}_{t},M_{t}^{\mathrm{P}}),$ 

where $\pi_{\mathrm{final}}$ is the final controller.
It generates an action, selecting a proposed action or synthesizing a new atomic action when useful.
The controller executes only the selected action in the real environment.
It then appends the resulting observation to the trajectory and repeats the process from the updated context.

## 4.2 Dual-Branch Experience Memory

The weighting in Proposition 1 depends on both the proposed actions and the accuracy of their predicted costs.
It cannot assign weight to a useful action absent from the candidate set, and inaccurate forecasts can favor unsuitable candidates.
Moreover, optimal candidate weights do not guarantee an optimal final action, since action selection is performed by a separate controller.
Our dual-branch memory aligns with these limitations: the planner branch targets candidate coverage and final action selection, while the world model branch adapts forecasts to environment-specific dynamics.

Proposition 2 (Coverage, cost error, and selection).

Fix a nonempty candidate set, its uniform reference $\mathbf{u}_{t}$ , and $\lambda>0$ .
Let $\bar{C}_{t}(a)$ denote a reference cost for any action $a$ , with $\bar{C}_{t}^{(k)}=\bar{C}_{t}(a_{t}^{(k)})$ , and let $\mathbf{C}_{t}$ be the predictive costs, with

 $\max_{k}|C_{t}^{(k)}-\bar{C}_{t}^{(k)}|\leq\epsilon.$ 

(13)

Define $\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{t}$ by replacing $\mathbf{C}_{t}$ with $\bar{\mathbf{C}}_{t}$ in Eq. (9), and let $\bar{\mathbf{w}}_{t}$ minimize $\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{t}$ .
The predic
limitations:
First, world model accuracy is important because predicted outcomes determine candidate costs and can change the controller’s action preference.
Our current dual-branch adaptation relies on retrieved textual experience while keeping model parameters frozen. More capable mechanisms for improving world model accuracy and adapting to changing dynamics remain an important direction for future work.
Second, evaluating multiple candidates requires additional world model and evaluator calls at test time.
This increases inference latency and cost as the candidate set grows, motivating more computationally efficient ways to obtain useful candidate comparisons.

Ethical considerations. Our experiments are conducted entirely in text-based simulated environments and involve no human subjects or personal data. If such an agent were deployed in real environments, inaccurate world model predictions could lead to unsafe actions, so human oversight would be needed.
conclusion:
We presented a self-improving, test-time MPPI-inspired framework for language agents performing long-horizon tasks.
The framework predicts the outcomes of several candidate actions with a world model before acting, and uses MPPI-style weights to summarize their costs for the final decision.
A dual-branch experience memory enables self-improvement: planner memory refines candidate generation and selection, and world model memory improves next-observation prediction.
Experiments on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld demonstrate the strongest overall performance across three backbones, with measured computational costs remaining practical for the evaluated tasks.

title: Back Up Before You Regret: Measuring Backup Awareness and Automating Backup in Coding Agents
abstract: Coding agents now complete tasks autonomously, modifying real-world state such as artifacts, software environments, and configurations along the way. Yet they show limited backup awareness: recognizing that an action will modify state that may later be needed, and preserving it beforehand. To evaluate backup awareness, we introduce RegretBench, a benchmark of 205 executable tasks grounded in regret moments reported on platforms such as X.com, GitHub, and Stack Overflow, where users explicitly regretted not preserving state they later needed. Across six frontier models, agents complete 86.1% of tasks on average yet back up before these moments in only 15.2%, showing that task completion ability does not imply backup awareness. Because it is hard to predict which changes will be regretted, we propose BackUpper, a harness plug-in backup layer that checks every tool call and preserves affected state before modification. It combines rule-based strategies for common operations with a lightweight subagent for complex cases, and its rule table can expand with subagent decisions over time. On RegretBench, BackUpper covers every regret moment action and restores states with 92.2% average similarity to the original. Achieving this costs only $0.014 per task, with 7x fewer tokens than the main-agent self-backup baseline. When users have preferences on what to back up, BackUpper can also narrow its scope accordingly, matching human annotations on whether an action is worth preserving with an 84.5% F1 score. These results suggest that agents can keep actions reversible at low cost while respecting users' preferences.

Figure 1: Agents act on real-world state without preserving it, leaving users regretting the loss of state they later need. To evaluate whether agents back up before acting, we construct RegretBench, the first benchmark grounded in 205 real-world regret moments, and find that frontier agents back up in only 15.2% of tasks. To close this gap, we propose BackUpper, a plug-in backup layer that intercepts every tool call and covers every regret moment action, with restored state reaching 92.2% average similarity to the original.

## 1 Introduction

As coding agents grow stronger, users increasingly delegate to them operations that modify real-world state, such as artifacts, software environments, and configurations \citepli2026tool, trivedi2024appworld. Such operations can go wrong, and even when they complete as requested, users may later need the original state and regret not preserving it \citepzhong2026don, hasan2026breaks. Anticipating such regret, experienced users back up state before making changes \citepzeelenberg2007theory, abowd1992giving. A senior engineer, for instance, clones the environment before upgrading its dependencies. Yet today’s agents act without preserving the state they modify \citephasan2026breaks (Figure 1). To support reliable execution, agents should likewise recognize that this state may later need to be restored, and preserve it beforehand.

However, current backup mechanisms cover only part of this need. Mainstream harnesses back up only the workspace or edits made through built-in tools (Table 1) \citepnousresearch2025hermes, anthropic2025claudecode, openai2025codex, openclaw2025openclaw, wang2025openhands, so state modified through external tools or remote services is preserved only if the model backs it up itself. Yet existing research largely overlooks pre-action backup and focuses instead on reconstructing lost state afterwards \citeptan2025recoverybench, zhang2026webrollback, li2026human, which is often infeasible once the original state is destroyed. Whether agents exhibit backup awareness, recognizing an action will modify state that may later be needed and preserving it beforehand, thus remains unexplored.

Evaluating backup awareness requires identifying meaningful backup needs, yet whether the original state will be needed depends on unknown future uses. We therefore draw on documented regret moments from platforms such as X.com, GitHub, and Stack Overflow, where users lost state and explicitly regretted not backing it up. From 205 such moments, we construct RegretBench, the first benchmark for evaluating coding agents’ backup awareness, with each moment turned into an executable multi-turn task using real-world environments and interaction trajectories. Across six frontier models, agents complete 86.1% of tasks on average but back up state before regret moments in only 15.2%. GPT 5.6-Sol in Codex does so in just 5.9% of tasks, and DeepSeek V4-Pro in Hermes in only 2.9%. These findings highlight that backup awareness remains limited in current agents and that dedicated backup support is needed.

To provide this support without retraining, we propose BackUpper, a lightweight, plug-in backup layer for coding agents.
Since regret moments are hard to predict, BackUpper acts like an experienced user and treats every state-modifying tool call as worth backing up by default. It applies rule-based strategies to operations with clear modification semantics, such as DELETE, and delegates complex or ambiguous ones, such as running a script, to a lightweight subagent. In both cases, backup is handled outside the main agent’s context, keeping its history clean and its focus on the original task. On RegretBench, BackUpper backs up every regret moment action, and the state restored from its backups reaches 92.2% average similarity to the original. Achieving this costs only $0.014 extra per task, with 31.7% lower backup latency than main-agent self-backup. Given stated user preferences, BackUpper narrows its backup scope accordingly, reaching 84.5% F1 across three personalized modes. It also improves with use: subagent backup decisions can be distilled into reusable rules, doubling rule-based coverage after 30 tasks.

Our contributions are as follows:

1. 

We analyze the native backup mechanisms of five mainstream agent harnesses, showing that none covers state modification through external tools or remote services.

2. 

We introduce RegretBench, the first benchmark for evaluating backup awareness in coding agents, with 205 executable tasks grounded in real-world regret moments. Evaluations across six frontier models show that agents complete 86.1% of tasks on average yet back up before regret moments in only 15.2%.

3. 

We design BackUpper, a training-free, plug-in backup layer that covers every regret moment action and restores state with 92.2% average similarity, at only $0.014 per task and $7\times$ fewer tokens than main-agent self-backup. Given stated user preferences, it narrows its backup scope with an 84.5% F1 against human annotations.

## 2 Related Work

Agent State Modification and Native Protection.

Beyond editing code, coding agents now install packages, update databases, manage emails, and reconfigure services \citepli2026tool, trivedi2024appworld.
We use state to refer to the artifacts, environments, and configurations these operations affect. Existing harnesses protect this state only in the agent’s working directory, which we call the workspace, or via native tools. As shown in Table 1, Hermes \citepnousresearch2025hermes and Codex \citepopenai2025codex snapshot the workspace, Claude Code \citepanthropic2025claudecode and OpenHands \citepwang2025openhands save files before native edits, and OpenClaw \citepopenclaw2025openclaw runs scheduled local backups. None of these covers external state, such as local files outside the workspace or remote services \citepanthropic2024mcp, wu2026mcpmark. In contrast, BackUpper operates at the tool-call level, covering state wherever it lives.

State Recovery and Reversibility.

A related line of work studies how agents recover after failures. RecoveryBench \citeptan2025recoverybench evaluates resuming from states left by failed attempts. GA-Rollback \citepli2025generator and WebRollback \citepzhang2026webrollback detect errors and roll back or revisit earlier steps, while BackBench \citepli2026human incorporates human preferences into recovery. However, post-hoc recovery may be difficult or infeasible once the original state is destroyed \citepzhang2026webrollback, li2026human. RegretBench therefore evaluates whether agents preserve state before acting, and BackUpper automates this preservation.

Backup Needs and Regret.

Regret arises when a different choice would have led to a better outcome \citepzeelenberg1999anticipated. In computing, it often follows the loss of state the user later needs \citepzhong2026don, hasan2026breaks. Since what will be needed is rarely known in advance, experienced users make reversibility a habit \citepwunder2025achieving, kljun2016toward, while users without this habit struggle to recover \citepwunder2025achieving, holtervennhoff2024mixed. Agents now act on users’ behalf, but whether they share this backup awareness remains underexplored. Building on this link between regret and backup, RegretBench grounds its tasks in real-world regret moments, where users later wished they had backed up before an action.

## 3 Benchmark: RegretBench

We construct RegretBench in two steps (Figure 2). First, we collect reports of regret moments and identify what action caused the loss, what state was lost, and what the user later needed to recover. Second, we combine each case with a real-world environment and interaction trajectory to create an executable multi-turn task. We place the affected state outside native harness backup coverage, so that any backup behavior reflects the agent’s own backup awareness.

Sourcing Regret Moments.

We source 205 regret moments from platforms such as X.com, GitHub, and Stack Overflow. These moments arise from actions taken by users or agents, ranging from explicitly destructive operations to routine ones. From each report, we extract the triggering action, the affected state, and the user’s subsequent need. For example, one user sought to revert an ipykernel upgrade after it broke existing code \citephg628193hg2021revert: the action is the upgrade, the affected state is the previous package version, and the need is to restore it (Figure 2, “Regret Moment”).

Constructing Executable Tasks.

Since reports rarely include execution context, we pair each moment with a real-world environment and human–AI conversation. As the middle and right of Figure 2 show, the upgrade report is combined with the sidetable repository \citepmoffitt2020sidetable, an executable project with tests, and a SWE-chat dependency-update conversation \citepbaumann2026swe. At turn 5, the user requests the ipykernel upgrade, which replaces the installed traitlets outside the workspace and leaves no copy of its prior state unless the agent backs it up first. By placing the regret moment action within a multi-turn task, the setup resembles a real-world conversation rather than an isolated request. Task assembly is assisted by Claude Opus-5 and GPT 5.6-Sol. After construction, we manually verify every task for executability and consistency with the reported loss.

Figure 2: RegretBench construction pipeline. From each documented regret moment, we extract the triggering action and affected state, then embed them into a real-world environment and interaction trajectory. In this example, upgrading ipykernel silently replaces the installed traitlets; the agent completes the request but leaves no copy of the previous version for later recovery.

## 3.1 Benchmark Statistics

(a) Regret moment sources in RegretBench, spanning Social & Community (e.g., X.com), Creation & Productivity (e.g., GitHub), and Records & Media (e.g., The Register), reflecting diverse backup needs.

(b) Pairwise cosine similarity of task-level instruction embeddings. Lower values indicate higher diversity. Numbers under each tool name denote task counts; Browser tasks span GitLab, OwnCloud, and Reddit.

Figure 3: Source and instruction diversity in RegretBench.

Tools and Data Sources.

RegretBench contains 205 tasks across five tools (Figure 3(b)). The tools are Terminal for local system operations through the native shell, SQL for databases through PostgreSQL-MCP, Browser for web applications through Playwright-MCP, Email for communication through Email-MCP, and DevOps for cluster management through Kubernetes-MCP. Regret moment sources fall into three categories (Figure 3(a)): social discussions and community support on platforms such as X.com and Reddit (Social & Community, 39.0%), software development and collaborative file management on platforms such as GitHub (Creation & Productivity, 44.4%), and archival preservation and media reports of data loss from sources such as Archives.gov and The Register (Records & Media, 16.6%). Together, they capture diverse backup needs across personal and organizational settings. To assess instruction diversity across RegretBench tasks, we concatenate all instructions in each task and compute pairwise cosine similarity between the resulting embeddings. Average similarity is 0.240 across tools and 0.208–0.439 within each tool (Figure 3(b)), indicating that tasks span varied contexts.

## 4 Benchmark Evaluation

Models and Configuration.

We evaluate six frontier models: Claude Opus-5 \citepanthropic2026opus5 and Claude Sonnet-5 \citepanthropic2026sonnet5 in Claude Code \citepanthropic2025claudecode, GPT 5.6-Sol \citepopenai2026gpt56sol and GPT 5.6-Terra \citepopenai2026gpt56terra in Codex \citepopenai2025codex, and Gemini 3.7-Flash \citepgoogle2026gemini37flash and DeepSeek V4-Pro \citepdeepseek2026v4pro in Hermes \citepnousresearch2025hermes, all with default thinking effort. We standardize harness-level protection to workspace snapshots, so any backup beyond the workspace reflects the agent itself.

Judges and Metrics.

Following \citetxue2025an, we use two LLM judges, both powered by Claude Sonnet-5. The task judge determines whether the agent fulfills all user requests across turns, and we report Task Pass Rate (PR) as the percentage of tasks marked as fulfilled. The backup judge evaluates each out-of-workspace (OOW) modification, an action that changes state outside the workspace, and counts it as backed up if the agent preserved sufficient information for recovery before execution (Appendix D.1). Based on its judgments, we measure backup awareness from two angles. Regret Moment Backup Rate (RMBR) is the percentage of tasks whose regret moment action is backed up, measuring coverage of documented recovery needs. Out-of-Workspace Backup Rate (OWBR) is the percentage of all OOW modifications backed up, measuring how broadly the agent preserves state beyond regret moments. This section mainly reports PR and RMBR, while Section 5 uses OWBR. We further validate the backup judge against human annotations, showing 95.3% agreement (Appendix B.4).

(a) Agents complete tasks but rarely back up. All six models pass 81.5–92.2% of tasks, yet RMBR averages only 15.2%, with four models below 10%.

(b) Agents make 30.1–58.9 tool calls per task, and Claude Opus-5, with the highest RMBR, spends 8.9% of them on backups.

Figure 4: PR and RMBR (a), and average tool calls per task (b) on RegretBench.

Main Results.

Figure 4(a) presents PR and RMBR across six frontier models. (1) Task completion ability does not imply backup awareness. All six models pass most tasks, yet RMBR averages only 15.2%. Across all runs, 72.0% complete the task as requested without backing up the regret moment state (Appendix B.5). This indicates that agents are capable of fulfilling immediate requests but often overlook recovery needs documented in real user experiences. (2) Even the strongest model leaves backup gaps. Despite achieving the highest PR and RMBR, Claude Opus-5 still fails to back up the regret moment state in 35.6% of tasks. These results highlight the need for backup support beyond models’ own awareness.

Execution Length and Main-Agent Self-Backup Overhead.

Figure 4(b) shows that agents make 30.1–58.9 tool calls per task on average, indicating that RegretBench tasks are multi-step and reflect realistic workflows. Within these trajectories, self-backup adds notable overhead: Claude Opus-5, the model with the highest RMBR, spends 8.9% of its tool calls on backups. Each of these calls is issued by the main model with its full context, so the cost scales with the main model’s price and context length. This motivates offloading backup from the main agent (Section 5).

(a) RMBR of three models across three harnesses. Rates vary by at most 5 points within each model.

(b) RMBR vs. Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index across three GPT generations.

Figure 5: Harness and model generation ablations on a 60-task subset of RegretBench.

Backup awareness varies more across models than across harnesses.

To test whether harness design affects backup behavior, we run Claude Opus-5, GPT 5.6-Sol, and DeepSeek V4-Pro in each of Claude Code, Codex, and Hermes on a 60-task subset, with harness protection standardized as in the main configuration. RMBR remains stable across harnesses but differs sharply across models (Figure 5(a)): 68.3–73.3% for Opus, 5.0–8.3% for Sol, and 0–1.7% for DeepSeek. This further suggests that the low backup rates in Figure 4(a) reflect limited backup awareness in the models. Improving it thus calls for either training the model or adding support ou
conclusion:
Coding agents increasingly modify state that users may later need, yet whether they preserve it beforehand has remained largely unexamined. We introduced RegretBench, the first benchmark for evaluating this backup awareness, grounded in 205 real-world regret moments. Frontier models complete 86.1% of its tasks but back up before regret moments in only 15.2%, showing that task completion ability does not imply backup awareness. Rather than relying on models to anticipate such moments, we proposed BackUpper, a plug-in layer that by default preserves state before any tool call modifies it. It covers every regret moment action, and its backups restore state to 92.2% average similarity to the original at only $0.014 per task, using 7 $\times$ fewer tokens than main-agent self-backup. In comparison, Post-hoc Recovery restores only 33.8% at over 450 $\times$ the cost. BackUpper also adapts to user preferences without degrading task performance, and can grow with use. These results suggest that keeping agent actions reversible is practical today. Looking forward, we hope the RMBR signal from RegretBench helps model developers internalize backup awareness, so that agents themselves recognize when state is worth preserving.

Future Directions.

First, regret moments could be mined directly from human–AI conversation logs, since a user’s request to revert or recover state signals that the earlier state was needed. Second, the large gap between Claude Opus-5 and other models suggests that backup awareness may be learnable rather than an inherent limitation, thus RMBR could serve as a training signal to close this gap. Third, BackUpper backs up every state-modifying call by default because regret is hard to predict. Future work could learn to predict which actions are likely to be regretted from regret moments such as those in RegretBench, allowing BackUpper to skip low-risk actions and further improve efficiency. Fourth, since BackUpper operates at the tool-call level, it could be extended to other agents that modify external state, such as computer-use and web agents.

title: D-Skill: Distilling Teacher Knowledge through Agent Skills
abstract: Frontier language-model agents excel at complex tasks, but high inference costs make transferring their capabilities to smaller models essential. Traditional knowledge distillation achieves this through parameter updates, requiring access to the student's weights and additional training compute while encoding the transferred knowledge implicitly in the parameters. We introduce D-Skill, a framework that treats the teacher as a black box and distills its behavioral advantage into an interpretable natural-language skill by analyzing paired rollouts and identifying behavioral divergences and agreements. The resulting lessons are consolidated offline, with any compatible skill-update backend, into a skill document that is provided to the student at inference time. D-Skill constructs the skill entirely offline from fixed trajectories, without labels, further environment interaction, or weight updates after rollout collection. Across SpreadsheetBench-Verified, ALFWorld, and chess puzzles spanning multiple teacher-student pairs, D-Skill closes 75%-95% of the teacher-student gap without touching model weights. After a single offline pass over the paired traces, D-Skill outperforms one-epoch SFT baselines and remains competitive with multi-epoch SFT. Under the same model family, the resulting student also incurs 5.7x-8.3x lower inference cost per task than the teacher. Our results demonstrate that natural-language skill distillation offers a performant, interpretable, and efficient alternative to weight-based capability transfer.

body_start:
Abstract

Frontier language-model agents excel at complex tasks, but high inference costs make transferring their capabilities to smaller models essential.
Traditional knowledge distillation achieves this through parameter updates, requiring access to the student’s weights and additional training compute while encoding the transferred knowledge implicitly in the parameters.
We introduce D-Skill, a framework that treats the teacher as a black box and distills its behavioral advantage into an interpretable natural-language skill by analyzing paired rollouts and identifying behavioral divergences and agreements.
The resulting lessons are consolidated offline, with any compatible skill-update backend, into a skill document that is provided to the student at inference time. D-Skill constructs the skill entirely offline from fixed trajectories, without labels, further environment interaction, or weight updates after rollout collection. Across SpreadsheetBench-Verified, ALFWorld, and chess puzzles spanning multiple teacher–student pairs, D-Skill closes 75%–95% of the teacher–student gap without touching model weights. After a single offline pass over the paired traces, D-Skill outperforms one-epoch SFT baselines and remains competitive with multi-epoch SFT. Under the same model family, the resulting student also incurs 5.7×–8.3× lower inference cost per task than the teacher. Our results demonstrate that natural-language skill distillation offers a performant, interpretable, and efficient alternative to weight-based capability transfer.
††footnotetext: Code is available at https://github.com/shuo-yuan/D-Skill.

## 1 Introduction

Figure 1: D-Skill closes the gap at a fraction of its cost.
D-Skill closes 84% of the teacher-student gap at $8.3\times$ lower inference cost on SpreadsheetBench-Verified. Teacher: GPT-5.6 Terra; student: GPT-5.6 Luna.

Frontier agents can reliably solve complex agentic tasks
(OpenAI, 2026b; Anthropic, 2026a; Jimenez et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024; Merrill et al., 2026), but their high inference costs (Chen et al., 2023b) make it desirable to transfer their capabilities to cheaper student models (Hinton et al., 2015; Hsieh et al., 2023; Zeng et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2023a; Chen et al., 2024; Kang et al., 2026). Classical knowledge distillation performs this transfer by updating the student’s
parameters using supervision such as the teacher’s output distribution
(Hinton et al., 2015; Kim and Rush, 2016; Gu et al., 2023), complete teacher-generated trajectories (Ho et al., 2023; Hsieh et al., 2023; Zeng et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2023a; Chen et al., 2024; Kang et al., 2026), or teacher evaluations of student-generated samples
(Agarwal et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2023).
Despite differences in supervision, these approaches impose several constraints: weight access is required, excluding many proprietary API-served models; backpropagation adds substantial computational cost; and sufficient training data is needed for the student to generalize. Moreover, the transferred knowledge is encoded in the model’s parameters, making it difficult to inspect, revise, or correct after training (Meng et al., 2022; Yao et al., 2023).

Recent work has shown that skills, natural-language artifacts encoding reusable task knowledge, strategies, and procedures, can substantially improve agent performance without modifying model weights (Anthropic, 2025a; Ni et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026).
Because skills remain external to the model, they are portable across deployments and can be inspected or edited after construction (Anthropic, 2025a).
Existing skill-generation methods are generally not organized around the teacher–student relationship central to distillation. Teacher-driven methods compile stronger-model trajectories or teacher-generated modules without conditioning the transfer on the target student’s behavior (Ni et al., 2026; Fu et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025). Student-centered methods instead learn from the target agent’s own experience, including contrasts between successful and failed rollouts, without a matched stronger-agent reference (Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Suzgun et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026). D-Skill instead constructs a student-targeted skill by comparing teacher and student trajectories collected on the same tasks. We ask whether their behavioral differences can be distilled, in a single offline pass over fixed traces, into an external textual update.

We propose D-Skill, a method for distilling model capabilities into a skill by comparing paired teacher and student rollouts. For each unlabeled task, we obtain one rollout from each model, either through fresh execution or from previously saved traces. A difference analyst extracts lessons from both divergences and agreements between the two behaviors. Divergences identify states in which the student behaves differently from the teacher and pair the student’s behavior with the teacher’s alternative, while agreements identify shared strategies that should be preserved. These lessons are consolidated into a single skill, which is loaded into the student’s context at inference time. Once the rollouts have been collected, D-Skill requires no answer keys, labels, held-out evaluation, or further environment interaction. The teacher and student contribute only through their fixed traces: neither is queried or fine-tuned during analysis and consolidation, and no model weights are modified.

We evaluate D-Skill on SpreadsheetBench Verified, ALFWorld and chess puzzles using different teacher-student pairs with different model families. As presented in section 4.1, across all three benchmarks and different teacher-student settings, D-Skill closes $83.4\%$ to $89.3\%$ of the teacher–student performance gap on SpreadsheetBench Verified, $84.6\%$ to $94.6\%$ on ALFWorld, and $75.3\%$ to $87.7\%$ on chess puzzles. This transfer also yields substantial inference-cost savings: in the GPT-5.6 Terra–Luna setting, the D-Skill student costs $8.3\times$ less per task than the teacher on SpreadsheetBench Verified and $5.7\times$ less per episode on ALFWorld (see section 5.3). We further compare D-Skill with supervised fine-tuning and find that it provides stronger transfer after a single pass over the teacher corpus while attaining performance comparable to multi-epoch fine-tuning (Section 5.2). These results demonstrate that textual skill distillation can match weight-based transfer in the evaluated setting while producing an artifact that remains readable, editable, and portable. In summary, this paper makes the following contributions:

• 

We formulate skill distillation as an alternative to weight-based knowledge distillation, encoding transferred capabilities in an external, interpretable artifact that requires neither weight access nor gradient-based training.

• 

We introduce D-Skill, a simple yet effective method that distills paired teacher and student rollouts by identifying their behavioral divergences and agreements and consolidating the resulting lessons into a reusable skill. After rollout collection, the method requires no labels, held-out evaluation, or further environment interaction.

• 

We demonstrate across three benchmarks and multiple teacher–student pairs that D-Skill closes most of the performance gap. In addition, it also outperforms the evaluated skill-learning baselines while retaining substantially lower inference cost than the teacher.

## 2 Related Work

## Knowledge distillation.

Knowledge distillation trains a compact student to match a stronger teacher’s
predictions (Bucilă et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015), extended to sequence-level
imitation (Kim and Rush, 2016), compressed language models (Sanh et al., 2019),
and on-policy variants that supervise the student’s own rollouts to close the
train–inference mismatch (Gu et al., 2023; Agarwal et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026).
Throughout, two assumptions persist: the transfer medium is parameters
(gradient updates, so closed-weight students are out of reach), and the signal
is distributional (logits or token-level divergences, requiring white-box teacher
access and a shared tokenizer). D-Skill relaxes both: knowledge is retained as an
explicit textual skill consumed in context by black-box students, and the signal is the behavioral contrast between teacher and student trajectories on shared tasks.

## Skill and memory-augmented agents.

A complementary line of work equips agents with persistent memories or skills—external artifacts carried across tasks and consulted at inference time. Reflexion stores reflections on past failures (Shinn et al., 2023), Voyager builds libraries of executable skills through exploration (Wang et al., 2023), and subsequent work consolidates trajectories into procedural memory (Wang et al., 2024; Fang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). SkillGen contrastively induces and validates skills from an agent’s successful and failed rollouts (Ma et al., 2026). Teacher-driven approaches instead transfer stronger capabilities: Trace2Skill compiles stronger-model trajectories into textual skills (Ni et al., 2026), while AgentDistill packages teacher-generated procedures as reusable MCP modules (Qiu et al., 2025).
D-Skill instead constructs a student-targeted skill by directly comparing teacher and student trajectories.
D-Skill addresses this gap by contrasting teacher and student trajectories, producing guidance targeted to their behavioral differences.

## Automatic textual optimization.

A third line improves a text artifact through iterative textual updates: APE and OPRO
search over instructions with LLM proposers (Zhou et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2024),
Promptbreeder evolves prompts self-referentially (Fernando et al., 2023),
DSPy compiles multi-stage pipelines by tuning their prompts against a validation metric
(Khattab et al., 2023), and TextGrad backpropagates natural-language critiques as
“textual gradients” (Yuksekgonul et al., 2024). The same machinery has recently
been applied beyond instructions: GEPA evolves prompts by reflecting on execution
traces (Agrawal et al., 2026), and SkillOpt optimizes a portable skill file through
gated patch-style edits validated on held-out tasks (Yang et al., 2026), one
instance of a growing family of self-evolving skill methods (Jiang et al., 2026).
These methods treat text as an optimizable artifact, typically using task evaluation
to select or refine updates. D-Skill follows the same broad paradigm but focuses on
teacher–student distillation: it derives textual updates from behavioral contrasts
between a stronger teacher and a target student on matched tasks. D-Skill thus extends
automatic textual optimization to capability transfer while remaining compatible with
different skill-update backends.

## 3 Method

Figure 2 summarizes D-Skill, which consists
of three stages: rollout collection, difference analysis, and skill update.
No stage computes a gradient or requires access to the parameters of either
model. Collecting fresh rollouts requires the teacher and student to interact
with the task environment; when saved traces are available, this interaction
can instead have occurred during an earlier execution. In either case, all
subsequent analysis and skill construction operate offline on fixed traces.

## 3.1 Problem Setup

Let $\mathcal{T}=\{t_{1},\ldots,t_{n}\}$ be a set of unlabeled tasks sampled from
a task distribution $\mathcal{D}$ , and let $\pi_{S}$ and $\pi_{T}$ denote a
student and a stronger teacher policy operating in the same task and action
space. Given paired trajectories
 $\{(\tau_{S}(t),\tau_{T}(t)):t\in\mathcal{T}\}$ , our objective is to construct a
natural-language skill $s$ such that the skill-conditioned student $\pi_{S}^{s}$ 
improves over the original student without modifying its parameters. If
 $J(\pi)$ denotes expected task performance, we quantify the transfer by the
fraction of the teacher–student gap closed:

 $\operatorname{GapClosed}(s)=\frac{J(\pi_{S}^{s})-J(\pi_{S})}{J(\pi_{T})-J(\pi_{S})}.$ 

## 3.2 Rollout Collection

Figure 2: 
Ground-truth-free skill distillation from paired rollout traces.
(1) Rollout: Paired teacher and student traces are obtained
from fresh rollouts or saved executions.
(2) Difference analysis: A Difference Analyst Agent compares
the fixed traces without answer keys, labels, or further
environment interaction, extracting divergence and
agreement items.
(3) Skill update: A Consolidation Agent converts the lessons
into patches, merges them, and applies the update to SKILL.md.

For each task $t\in\mathcal{T}$ , we collect one trajectory from each model,
 $\tau_{S}(t)$ and $\tau_{T}(t)$ , recording the actions issued and the observations
returned. The paired trajectories are the unit of supervision; no later stage analyzes either trajectory in isolation.
The two policies attempt each task independently, with neither conditioned on the other’s behavior. When trajectories are collected specifically for D-Skill, both policies interact with the task environment through ordinary execution; alternatively, trajectories may be retrieved from logs of prior executions, allowing distillation to begin directly from saved traces. The two trajectories need only correspond to the same task and use a shared action interface. Once the trajectories have been collected, D-Skill operates fully offline: neither $\pi_{S}$ nor $\pi_{T}$ is invoked again, and skill construction requires no further environment access, ground-truth labels, rewards, or evaluation feedback.

## 3.3 Difference Analysis

In the second stage, a difference analyst agent $\mathcal{A}$ converts each
paired student and teacher trace into a set of structured, reusable
lessons. The analyst can inspect the actions and observations recorded in
the traces, but it has no access to answer keys, labels, or additional environment interaction.

Rather than asking the analyst to compare the trajectories freely, we require it to examine each pair along a predefined set of behavioral dimensions. These dimensions cover, for example, what information each agent gathered before acting, how it selected and executed actions, how it responded to errors or unproductive intermediate observations, and how it verified the final result. This shared schema makes lessons comparable across task pairs and discourages the analyst from emphasizing superficial differences in naming, phrasing, or reasoning style. Each lesson must cite concrete evidence from the paired traces and express a task-general principle rather than an instance-specific correction. Details about the prompt for the analyst can be found in appendix B.

For each trajectory pair, the analyst produces at most three lessons, ranked by their anticipated usefulness on future tasks, and assigns each to one of two classes: a divergence lesson identifies a behavioral difference between the two agents, specifying the student’s behavior, the teacher’s alternative, and a reusable instruction intended to address the gap; an agreement lesson identifies a behavior shared by both agents that is judged worth preserving in the distilled skill.

## 3.4 Skill Update

To construct the final skill document, we use a modified version of the
Trace2Skill consolidation backend (Ni et al., 2026) as the D-Skill consolidator. We retain its map–reduce–apply procedure but adapt its input to consume the structured
divergence and agreement lessons produced by our difference-analysis
stage. The complete lesson pool is shuffled and partitioned into $k$ chunks, which are
processed sequentially to update the skill document.
For each chunk, a consolidation agent $\mathcal{C}$ performs three phases.
In the map phase, it independently converts each lesson into a
candidate patch to the current skill, such as appending to an existing
section, replacing existing content, or creating a new section. In the
reduce phase, it merges the patches by removing duplicates,
resolving conflicts, and generalizing related rules. Finally, in the
apply phase, the merged patch is deterministically incorporated into
the current skill before the next chunk is processed.

We use this adapted Trace2Skill backend throughout our experiments. D-Skill’s
output from the preceding stage is a general pool of structured lessons, so
other compatible skill-updating backends could be substituted without
changing the rollout-collection or difference-analysis stages, more details can be found in section 4.2.

limitations: D-Skill has three main limitations. First, it requires a capable analyst at distillation time: replacing the analyst with the weaker student substantially reduces the fraction of the gap closed (Table 3), although this is a one-time rather than per-inference cost. Second, loading the distilled document increases inference cost relative to the bare student by adding input tokens and, in some cases, inducing additional interaction steps, even though the resulting agent remains substantially cheaper than the teacher. Third, D-Skill can transfer only capabilities that can be expressed as instructions and executed by the student. It can improve procedures such as planning, verification, and tool use, but cannot supply fundamental capabilities the student lacks, such as deeper calculation, perception, or sufficient underlying model capacity.
conclusion:
We introduced D-Skill, a method that distills the behavioral gap between a black-box teacher and student into a natural-language skill by contrasting paired rollouts on the same tasks. Once the trajectories are collected, D-Skill operates fully offline, requiring no further policy queries, environment interaction, labels, rewards, evaluation feedback, or weight updates. Across SpreadsheetBench Verified, ALFWorld, and chess puzzles, D-Skill closes $82$ – $95\%$ of the teacher–student performance gap across multiple model families while retaining a substantial inference-cost advantage over the teacher.
D-Skill also provides stronger one-pass transfer and remains competitive with multi-epoch SFT when using the same teacher-trajectory corpus, without gradient updates or access to the student’s weights. Together, these results demonstrate that natural-language skill distillation is a practical, interpretable, and inference-efficient alternative to weight-based capability transfer in the evaluated domains.

title: Simply Logical -- The First Three Decades
abstract: This paper charts the evolution of the Prolog textbook Simply Logical -- Intelligent Reasoning by Example from print with runnable programmes on a 3.5-inch diskette published in 1994, via various intermediate online versions, to the fully interactive online edition available today. Our aim is to investigate -- from both the writer's and the reader's perspectives -- the potential impact of technology on educational materials. The three authors of this paper present three distinct and complementary points of view, which come together to shape an interactive online book that offers an immersive learning experience. Peter describes the philosophy behind the original book and experiences teaching from it. Jan demonstrates how contemporary web programming has enabled a fully interactive realisation of the book's philosophy. Kacper reports how different technologies can be adopted to build a versatile authoring toolkit that underpins the interactive online edition of the book. Collating these distinct yet coherent perspectives allows us to reflect on future opportunities for interactive Prolog teaching materials arising from the continuous development of web technologies. The insights we offer should be of interest to teachers of Prolog as well as those wanting to find out about the latest educational technologies.

## Simply Logical –
The First Three Decades

Peter Flach

Affiliation: Intelligent Systems Laboratory, University of Bristol, United Kingdom

E-mail {peter.flach, k.sokol}@bristol.ac.uk

Kacper Sokol

Affiliation: Intelligent Systems Laboratory, University of Bristol, United Kingdom

Jan Wielemaker

Affiliation: SWI-Prolog Solutions b.v., Netherlands

headings: 2 Interactive Prolog in the Browser (Jan Wielemaker)
body_start:
Abstract

This paper charts the evolution of the Prolog textbook Simply Logical – Intelligent Reasoning by Example
from print with runnable programmes on a 3.5-inch diskette published in 1994, via various intermediate online versions,
to the fully interactive online edition available today. Our aim is to investigate – from both the writer’s and the reader’s perspectives – the potential impact of technology on educational materials. The three authors of this paper present three distinct and complementary points of view, which come together to shape an interactive online book that offers an immersive learning experience. Peter describes the philosophy behind the original book and experiences teaching from it. Jan demonstrates how contemporary web programming has enabled a fully interactive realisation of the book’s philosophy. Kacper reports how different technologies can be adopted to build a versatile authoring toolkit that underpins the interactive online edition of the book. Collating these distinct yet coherent perspectives allows us to reflect on future opportunities for interactive Prolog teaching materials arising from the continuous development of web technologies. The insights we offer should be of interest to teachers of Prolog as well as those wanting to find out about the latest educational technologies.

Keywords: 
Education Learning Textbook Interactive Prolog SWI-Prolog SWISH Artificial Intelligence Logic Programming

## 1 The Paperback (Peter Flach)

As a beginning lecturer at Tilburg University in the early 90s of the previous century I started teaching a module on Artificial Intelligence (AI), then an emerging specialist topic within the still young discipline of computer science.
Initially using a general AI textbook [10] I started devising practical exercises and coursework assignments in Prolog, which I had come across a couple of years before. These grew into a set of lecture notes that eventually became the Simply Logical – Intelligent Reasoning by Example book [8]. I ended up publishing with John Wiley after I had a chat with a representative at a conference; they were very helpful and even suggested the title. I was fortunate in finding Bob Kowalski willing to write a foreword, in which he very graciously wrote that my book relieved him of the temptation to write a revised edition of his own book, Logic for Problem Solving [9].

Rather than trying to cover all of AI, which even then had grown into a diverse field, I decided to focus on reasoning in various forms: deductive, inductive, reasoning with natural language, reasoning with incomplete information, etc., which approach is captured by the “intelligent reasoning” part of the book’s title.
The “by example” moniker reflected the didactic philosophy: teaching by showing, learning by doing.
Every AI technique discussed was accompanied by a Prolog programme implementing it. These programmes served two didactic purposes. By running them, the student could get a feeling what a particular technique is all about. But perhaps more importantly, the declarative reading of each programme was an integral part of the explanation of the technique it implemented. For the more elaborate programmes, special attention was paid to their stepwise development, explaining key issues along the way.
My hope was that the reader would mount the accompanying 3.5” diskette into their computer, and try out the Prolog programmes alongside reading the book. While this was perhaps optimistic back then, the online format available today integrates the “showing” and “doing” sides of the educational coin very well, as will be demonstrated below.

I still use Simply Logical in my lectures as an introduction to both logic programming and AI. Treating the subjects side by side allows for some pretty powerful examples, such as a resolution prover for full clausal logic as a demonstrator for breadth-first search. Rather than modernising the text I have opted for modernising the demonstrators and programming assignments.
For example, the natural-language question-answering programme described in Chapter 7 of the book, which nowadays we would call a chatbot, was developed into an Amazon Alexa skill. This demonstrates the power of a hybrid system consisting of speech-to-text and text-to-speech components enabled by deep learning, and a logical engine in the middle capable of explainable logical reasoning.
Other material developed over the years includes a Prolog-driven agent that needs to solve a logical puzzle while moving around in a grid world and a Reveal.js slide deck that can be used for self-study and trying out Prolog programmes without leaving the browser. The latter is based on SWISH, which Jan introduces in the following section.

## 2 Interactive Prolog in the Browser (Jan Wielemaker)

Crucial for realising the fundamental philosophy behind Simply Logical is the ability to
run code interactively in the browser. Modern browser and service
technology allows for several designs:

1. 

Have Prolog in a sandbox (such as a virtual machine or container) on a server
and provide ways to submit a programme and view its output. An
example of this approach can be found at
Coding
Ground.

2. 

Have a web service with dedicated support for Prolog that
offers a sandboxed Prolog execution environment. SWISH11
 1

 https://swish.swi-prolog.org/ – SWI-Prolog for SHaring [16] – is implemented based on this paradigm.

3. 

Execute Prolog in the browser. Some Prolog systems are written
directly in JavaScript, thus enabling them to be run in the browser, e.g.,
Tau-Prolog.
Another solution is to compile Prolog to JavaScript [13].
Alternatively, Web Assembly (WASM) offers a low-level
virtual machine for the browser, which
allows running
more traditional C-based Prolog implementations; for example, Emscripten provides a Clang-based
compiler suite that targets WASM, underpinning implementations such as the Ciao
Playground and
SWI-Prolog WASM port.

The first category typically provides a batch-style
interaction, making it difficult to adapt for (online and interactive) educational resources; the latter two approaches are more suitable in this respect.

SWISH,
originally developed by Torbjörn Lager, is based on
Pengines – an
architecture to access Prolog on a remote server –
and consists of
a monolithic multi-threaded SWI-Prolog server. Its user interface is written in
JavaScript with server-side assistance for semantic highlighting,
feedback on predicates, template insertion and other user-focused features.
Pengines underlies Prolog execution, which
takes place in a sandboxed environment that consists of
a Prolog thread and a temporary module. Executing a query (1) transfers
the code and query to the server; (2) starts a thread and creates a
temporary module; (3) loads the code into the module; and (4) executes
the code. This operationalisation allows for rich interaction with the client, e.g.,
“read” from the client, ask for alternative solutions or trace
through the programme in a manner similar to traditional Prolog tracers. Other
noteworthy features of SWISH include:

• 

The ability to store programmes on the server under Git-style version management. Programmes can either be private or visible to the public, and may include each other.

• 

Availability of render plugins that allow rendering Prolog terms – e.g., as tables or graphics that represent chess boards, charts and graphs
– using modern web browser technology.

• 

An R Project interface
offering access to R’s algorithms and chart outputs.

• 

Notebook format allowing for rich interactive
pages that provide a sequence of HTML, Markdown,
programme and query cells.

SWISH has proved to be an invaluable resource for the Prolog community, including educators.
It facilitates (Prolog) learning, code discussion and exchange as well as shared access to data for data science.
After its launch in 2014 the
system quickly gained popularity as an alternative to local
installations of Prolog systems used for exercises in Prolog classes at
schools worldwide.
As of December 2022, it hosts over 150,000 programmes and nearly 15,000 notebooks, many of which in several versions.
It sustains on
average hundreds of concurrent users, peaking at over one thousand users, usually towards the end of each academic cycle. Notably, teachers started adapting their
educational materials and course workflows to SWISH for more than just
a convenient online Prolog execution environment. Some wrote course material as SWISH notebooks.
Others use SWISH notebooks for exercises;
they organise the content as questions, background data,
example queries and, sometimes, skeleton or partial solutions. A student then forks the notebook, completes it,
saves it and sends the link with the completed notebook to the teacher.

As interactive in-browser programming exercises were gaining in
popularity, I began to wonder whether we could do something similar
to teach Prolog as a programming language.
With Learn Prolog Now! [2]
being one of the more popular online (and later paperback [3]) Prolog books, I
experimented with making it interactive.
Learn Prolog Now! is written in LaTeX, which is then converted to
an unintelligible HTML code used to publish the online version. Because of that, I built the interactive version [4] by using a
rewriting proxy server.
This is a Prolog programme that:

1. 

uses SWI-Prolog’s HTML parser and generator to parse the original pages;

2. 

identifies the code blocks that represent programmes and queries;

3. 

re-writes the programme fragments into new HTML elements
that connect each programme to relevant queries, allowing these pairs to
be transformed into an embedded SWISH instance; and

4. 

inject JavaScript into the page to make the page – specifically, the code boxes – interactive.

While side-stepping the need to manually edit the book source, this automation is far from perfect.
Observing this particular use case of SWISH, nevertheless, motivated Peter and Kacper to make Simply Logical similarly interactive.
They decided to
manually identify the programmes and queries as it was clear
that given the available technology it is impossible to do so programmatically with
acceptable precision.

## 3 The Online Edition(s) (Kacper Sokol)

The book was first made freely available in 2007, when the copyright reverted back to Peter, who decided to release its PDF and associated programmes online through a dedicated web page. In 2015, as a pilot, most of the original book source – written in a now obsolete version of MS Word – was ported to a collection of messy HTML files replete with superfluous markup;
the figures were extracted as non-standard EMZ files and later converted to the more modern Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) format. This provided a canvas for transforming a static web page into an online, interactive resource using SWI-Prolog’s SWISH platform.

From then on, the manual process of identifying Prolog code listings and their associated queries took place, with appropriate HTML code being embedded by hand to display interactive SWISH code boxes. Each SWISH box initially renders the programme as text, as in the original book.
Opening the box reveals a tripartite widow with an editable code listing (pulling in additional code as required), pre-populated Prolog queries, and an answer pane as shown in Figure 1. Two decades after publication of the original book, technology had caught up sufficiently to support the envisaged didactic philosophy, which was an almost revelatory experience. The first release had thus seen the light of day.

Figure 1: Interactive SWI-Prolog code box based on SWISH. A code listing (top) can be turned into an interactive code box (bottom) by pressing the “play” button in its top-right corner.

The script responsible for rendering SWISH code boxes was elaborate enough to streamline certain tasks.
Prolog queries displayed in the text were assigned unique IDs, which allowed them to be dynamically imported into relevant code boxes upon launch. Both interactive programmes and static code listings could also be tagged, providing an opportunity to import code into interactive boxes at run time. To give the book a fresh look and feel and prepare its presentation for a range of modern devices – desktop and laptop computers, tablets and mobile phone screens – the HTML content was adapted to the Bootstrap framework. The book was split into four HTML files: Part I, Part II, Part III and Appendix, complemented with an index page, with the source hosted on GitHub22
 2

 https://github.com/simply-logical/simply-logical/. The second release of the book’s online version was built with Jekyll to generate static web pages, which were hosted on GitHub Pages under the dedicated https://book.simply-logical.space/ domain.

However, the main text was now written in HTML, which was still fairly limiting, especially when it comes to authoring (new or derived) content.
With Markdown being much simpler to write, edit and maintain as well as more human-readable and covering all of the markup needs, I started porting and cleaning the source.
In the process, the diversity of the book’s building blocks – text, figures and code listings – sparked an idea for a bespoke content generation system where the resources are split into prime elements that can be reused to compose new material.
Initially, this novel workflow relied on Jekyll, which proved to be limiting and prompted me to embark in late 2018 on developing a bespoke content generation platform.
Its prototype, while versatile, required the source documents to be extensively annotated, making the authoring experience overly complicated and stalling the project.

When Jupyter Book [6] arrived in early 2020 it rekindled my hope for a modular version of Simply Logical. The platform allowed composing content from diverse building blocks and offered nearly all of the required functionality, apart from support for SWISH code boxes. While based on the Sphinx Python documentation generation engine, it nonetheless could be extended with a custom plugin. This encouraged me to finalise the separation, conversion and cleaning of the book content, and to begin developing the necessary Jupyter Book extensions. The result is a highly modular design, where the book is split into a collection of files based on their type: text, exercise, solution, code and figure. All of these materials are published on GitHub under the permissive Creative Commons (BY-NC-SA) licence, which allows easy reuse, incorporating into bespoke courses, or adapting into alternative educational resources such as practical training sessions. This release marked the third instalment of the online edition [7].

From a technical perspective, the latest version is realised through a collection of bespoke Jupyter Book plugins (that also work with Sphinx) spanning functionality specific to SWI-Prolog [17].
These extensions were later adapted to be compatible with the cplint [14] and ProbLog [5] probabilistic programming languages. Specifically, I developed and released sphinx-prolog33
 3

 https://github.com/simply-logical/sphinx-prolog/, which among other things allows to embed interactive SWI-Prolog and cplint code boxes based on their respective SWISH implementations. The sphinx-problog44
 4

 https://github.com/simply-logical/sphinx-problog/ extension offers analogous functionality for ProbLog facilitated by the online execution environment underpinning the code examples published as part of the ProbLog website.

Including a SWISH code box is as simple as writing a specially-formatted Markdown code block, an example of which is shown in Listing 1. This element is assigned a unique ID (swish:0.1), and its content can either be provided verbatim (optional :- content.) or loaded from a file. Through its optional parameters it is possible to:

•

•

•

if Prolog queries are included directly in the code via a specially-formatted query block (lines 13–15 in Listing 1), hide them from the users prior to launching the code box (hide-examples).

## 4 Discussion and Outlook

Developing Jupyter Book plugins and building authoring environments for interactive Prolog content set us on a path to further explore alternative technologies for composing diverse (interactive) training resources. As a proof of principle we created a prototype of a new publishing workflow in which multiple artefacts such as online documents, slides and computational notebooks can be generated from a unified collection of source materials [15]. This contrasts with much of current practice, where authoring environments are limited to individual publishing artefacts, for example, LaTeX or MS Word documents, and PowerPoint or Keynote slide decks.
