Developing Jupyter Book plugins and building authoring environments for interactive Prolog content set us on a path to further explore alternative technologies for composing diverse (interactive) training resources. As a proof of principle we created a prototype of a new publishing workflow in which multiple artefacts such as online documents, slides and computational notebooks can be generated from a unified collection of source materials [15]. This contrasts with much of current practice, where authoring environments are limited to individual publishing artefacts, for example, LaTeX or MS Word documents, and PowerPoint or Keynote slide decks. While in its early stages of development, Quarto [1] is a notable departure from this paradigm and a substantially more powerful realisation of the envisaged workflow. It is a scientific and technical publishing system that
allows to author content as Markdown files or Jupyter Notebooks,
and publish it as articles, reports, presentations, websites, blogs and books in formats such as HTML, PDF, MS Word or EPUB.
Quarto supports scientific features – e.g., equations, citations and cross-referencing – and inclusion of dynamic content created with various programming languages.

Regardless of the underlying technology, our ideal scenario is an authoring environment in which the author can concentrate on producing content without much (initial) regard for the delivery format.
Similar ideas have been around for a long time – e.g., Luhmann’s Zettelkasten [11] – but were lacking the technology to support them and make them efficient. While we hope that the next 50 years of Prolog will see these ideas and opportunities come to full fruition, numerous challenges need to be overcome.
One particular bottleneck is limited interactivity of the educational resources published on the Internet, which in part is due to the need for compute resources. Without access to a dedicated machine – however it is implemented in the physical world – interacting with code examples remains constrained.

For example, up until recently SWISH used to run on
a single server hosted by the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam (VU).
The single process and single hardware placed in a single network made the system
highly vulnerable.
This could be addressed by
migrating the server to a
set of federated services;
while currently SWISH runs on two servers in different locations, load balancing
is still missing.

title: DiffResearch: Accelerating Deep Research with Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Deep research systems iteratively plan, gather evidence, synthesize, and revise, making end-to-end latency a key bottleneck for interactive use. Almost all production systems are built on autoregressive (AR) language models and inherit left-to-right decoding in planning and long-form writing. We present DiffResearch, an open multi-agent deep research framework that places a diffusion language model (dLLM) at the core of every stage, and measure how a diffusion backbone changes latency and report quality. Holding the agentic scaffold, retrieval code, prompts, and evaluation fixed, we swap the backbone between an open diffusion model and a comparable AR model. Across 100 Deep Research Bench tasks, the diffusion backbone is roughly 6 times faster end-to-end, driven by order-of-magnitude reductions in planning and writing. We further introduce dFast, a decomposition mode that reads intermediate denoising states and extracts subqueries before generation finishes, providing a 1.99 times median speedup for decomposition in isolation with no loss of report quality. On the benchmark's RACE rubric, dFast obtains the best overall score among the three configurations. Finally, in a public system-level leaderboard snapshot, an instance built on a stronger diffusion model ranks above several commercial systems. We release DiffResearch under an Apache-2.0 license.

Abstract

Deep research systems iteratively plan, gather evidence, synthesize, and revise, making end-to-end latency a key bottleneck for interactive use. Almost all production systems are built on autoregressive (AR) language models and inherit left-to-right decoding in planning and long-form writing. We present DiffResearch, an open multi-agent deep research framework that places a diffusion language model (dLLM) at the core of every stage, and measure how a diffusion backbone changes latency and report quality. Holding the agentic scaffold, retrieval code, prompts, and evaluation fixed, we swap the backbone between an open diffusion model and a comparable AR model. Across 100 Deep Research Bench tasks, the diffusion backbone is roughly $6\times$ faster end-to-end, driven by order-of-magnitude reductions in planning and writing. We further introduce dFast, a decomposition mode that reads intermediate denoising states and extracts subqueries before generation finishes, providing a $1.99\times$ median speedup for decomposition in isolation with no loss of report quality. On the benchmark’s RACE rubric, dFast obtains the best overall score among the three configurations. Finally, in a public system-level leaderboard snapshot, an instance built on a stronger diffusion model ranks above several commercial systems. We release DiffResearch under an Apache-2.0 license.

## 1 Introduction

The past two years have seen deep research (DR) systems emerge as a flagship application of large language models (LLMs). Commercial products such as OpenAI Deep Research (OpenAI, 2025), Gemini Deep Research (Citron, 2024), and Perplexity Deep Research (Perplexity, 2025), alongside a growing body of open-source frameworks (The LangChain Team, 2025; Zheng et al., 2025), autonomously orchestrate multi-step web exploration, targeted retrieval, and higher-order synthesis to turn large amounts of online information into citation-rich reports. Among the tasks these systems perform, scientific literature review is one of the most demanding: a review requires balanced thematic coverage, faithful attribution, the identification of competing methodological camps, and a coherent narrative that situates each work within the broader landscape. As Deep Research Bench (Du et al., 2026) and similar evaluations (Coelho et al., 2026; Yifei et al., 2026) have shown, the strongest agents now approach the quality of human analysts on PhD-level tasks across dozens of fields.

Despite this progress, almost all production DR agents share one architectural backbone: they are built on autoregressive LLMs (Brown et al., 2020; Touvron et al., 2023; OpenAI, 2023) and inherit the same left-to-right, single-pass decoding that governs their token generators. This shapes both how reviews are written and how fast they are produced. A writing agent drafts each section sequentially, with limited ability to revise earlier passages once new evidence arrives later, so that errors in early structural decisions can propagate through the rest of the review. The same sequential bottleneck constrains the orchestration layer: when an agent must emit several search queries to fan out retrieval over distinct facets of the literature, autoregressive decoding produces them one token at a time, and downstream retrieval is dispatched only after generation completes. For an interactive research assistant, every one of these stages is on the critical path, and their latencies add up.

Diffusion language models (Li et al., 2022; Austin et al., 2021; Lou et al., 2024) offer a complementary generation paradigm: text is refined through iterative denoising that updates an entire sequence in parallel across a small number of steps. Recent systems such as LLaDA (Nie et al., 2025), Dream (Ye et al., 2025), and Mercury (Inception Labs et al., 2025) suggest that diffusion LLMs can approach the quality of autoregressive models while offering advantages in generation speed and global coherence. Yet diffusion LLMs have largely been evaluated in standalone settings such as chat and coding; their integration into agentic pipelines that interleave planning, retrieval, and iterative refinement remains underexplored, and the practical latency consequences of that integration have not been measured directly.

We introduce DiffResearch,11
 1

 Previous presentation: ICML 2026 AI4Science (https://openreview.net/forum?id=EGb0wlKWVz). This version adds a controlled AR-backbone comparison, dFast analysis, language-specific diagnostics, and a source-grounding audit. Code: https://github.com/alanrbtx/DiffResearch. an open deep research framework in which every agent is an instance of a diffusion LLM. Our aim is to measure what changes when the backbone is diffusion rather than autoregressive, with the rest of the system held fixed. The framework combines a standard agentic scaffold (intent classification, query reformulation, planning, retrieval, writing, and an optional judge) with a diffusion-based writing stage that drafts and refines the full review in parallel rather than section by section. It supports two operating modes: a full mode that runs the base pipeline once, and an iterative subquery-decomposition (fast) mode in which a diffusion decomposition agent produces the full subquery set within a single denoising pass, with usable subqueries read from intermediate denoising states before generation completes. Because all subqueries become available at once, their retrieval calls could in principle be dispatched together; in our controlled runs retrieval is rate-limited to one request per second, so we report the decomposition-stage speedup in isolation and leave parallel retrieval dispatch to future work. The framework exposes one agent abstraction with interchangeable backbones, so we can keep the whole scaffold fixed and change only the generator, and any difference can be attributed to the decoding paradigm rather than to unrelated system changes.

Our contributions are as follows:

• 

An open diffusion-native deep research framework with two operating modes and a single agent abstraction whose backbone can be set to a diffusion or an autoregressive model, enabling controlled comparison.

• 

A direct latency comparison between diffusion and autoregressive backbones in an otherwise identical pipeline on Deep Research Bench, showing roughly $6\times$ end-to-end speedup concentrated in the planning and writing stages.

• 

A fast decomposition mode that extracts the subquery set from intermediate denoising states, cutting decomposition latency by about half ( $1.99\times$ at the median over $100$ queries) while keeping downstream report quality; in our runs it also gives the best RACE overall score, but no additional end-to-end latency reduction over standard diffusion generation.

• 

A system-level leaderboard snapshot in which an instance of the same framework built on a stronger diffusion model ranks above several publicly listed commercial deep research systems, without isolating the effect of diffusion decoding.

## 2 Related Work

## Deep research agents.

Commercial systems (OpenAI, 2025; Citron, 2024; Perplexity, 2025) and open-source frameworks (The LangChain Team, 2025; Zheng et al., 2025) integrate multi-step reasoning, retrieval, and synthesis to produce long-form, citation-grounded outputs. Benchmarks such as Deep Research Bench (Du et al., 2026), DeepResearchGym (Coelho et al., 2026), and ResearchQA (Yifei et al., 2026) evaluate these systems on complex, multi-domain tasks. Most rely on autoregressive LLMs (Brown et al., 2020; Touvron et al., 2023; OpenAI, 2023) and inherit the constraints of sequential decoding. Prior work has explored agentic scaffolds that decompose tasks into modular planning, retrieval, and evaluation components (Wang et al., 2024; Xi et al., 2025), judge models that assess output quality (Zheng et al., 2023), and retrieval-augmented generation to ground outputs in external sources (Lewis et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2023b).

## Diffusion language models.

Diffusion-based text models (Li et al., 2022; Austin et al., 2021; Lou et al., 2024) generate through iterative denoising, refining an entire sequence in parallel across a few steps, and naturally support structure-first generation and iterative error correction (Li et al., 2022; Gong et al., 2023). Recent open models such as LLaDA (Nie et al., 2025) and Dream (Ye et al., 2025), and the Mercury family (Inception Labs et al., 2025), show that diffusion LLMs can approach autoregressive quality while offering speed and global-coherence advantages. To our knowledge, no prior work has measured how diffusion decoding affects the end-to-end latency and report quality of an agentic deep research pipeline under a controlled backbone swap.

## Efficient generation.

A large literature improves generation efficiency through speculative decoding, caching, distillation, and parallel decoding. Our fast decomposition mode is complementary and is not speculative decoding: it does not use a draft model, but instead reads the diffusion model’s own intermediate denoising states and stops once a valid structured output is available.

## 3 System Design

## 3.1 Multi-Agent Diffusion Pipeline

DiffResearch is a multi-agent framework in which every agent is an instance of a diffusion LLM. The system is organized as a small, explicit pipeline rather than a monolithic chain; we deliberately avoid heavy orchestration abstractions (Chase, 2022) that obscure data flow and make latency budgets and retry behavior hard to reason about. Each agent is a Python class that inherits from a common backbone and implements a single generate method. The backbone is interchangeable: a Hugging Face diffusion runtime serving google/diffusiongemma-26B-A4B-it for diffusion-native deployment, or a Hugging Face autoregressive runtime serving google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it for the baseline. The controlled comparison in Section 5 relies on this: changing the backbone leaves every prompt, retrieval call, and evaluation step unchanged.

Nine agents cover query formatting, planning, plan-checking, relevance filtering, information extraction, summarization, complexity assessment, query decomposition, and judging. Outputs are kept minimal and machine-parseable: binary flags for routing decisions, newline-separated query lists from the decomposition and judge agents, and free-form text only where downstream consumption requires it. Per-agent decoding budgets are exposed through the constructor; for example, the relevance and complexity agents use a short budget appropriate to their binary outputs, while the summarization agent uses a substantially larger budget to accommodate full review drafts.

The base pipeline has five core stages (intent classification, query reformulation, planning, retrieval, and writing), with judging as an optional sixth stage. The intent agent routes a query to a web channel or an academic channel and emits a label with a logged-but-not-propagated rationale. The reformulation agent rewrites the query into retrieval-friendly search strings (Wang et al., 2023; Jagerman et al., 2023) while preserving the original information need verbatim. The planning agent (Wei et al., 2022; Yao et al., 2023) produces a structured outline: main sections, two-to-four sub-points each, and an explicit list of key concepts to cover. The outline serves both as the writing target and as the reference for plan-checking. The writing agent drafts the review conditioned on the plan and the retrieved corpus through diffusion-style refinement. The judge (Zheng et al., 2023) compares the review against the plan and corpus along plan adherence, citation faithfulness (Gao et al., 2023a; Liu et al., 2023), and coverage completeness.

## 3.2 Retrieval Backends

Retrieval grounds every claim and is treated as a first-class component. The web channel issues queries through the Serper API (Serper, n.d.) and extracts page content into plain text. The academic channel issues parallel calls to the Semantic Scholar API (Kinney et al., 2023), for broad peer-reviewed coverage and citation-graph signals, and the arXiv API (arXiv, n.d.), for timely preprints; results are deduplicated by DOI and arXiv identifier and merged into a single ranked list. In all cases retrieval is performed by deterministic API calls with no LLM in the loop, which keeps it fast, cacheable, and easy to ablate. For the controlled benchmark runs in this paper, retrieval is restricted to the Semantic Scholar channel with results_per_query $=2$ , so these parallel academic calls are not exercised; retrieval is then a single rate-limited source, identical across backbones.

## 3.3 Model Serving and Decomposition

Both models are run through Hugging Face runtimes. The same pipeline code drives all three configurations (diffusion full, diffusion fast, autoregressive), and only the backbone and the decompose mode change. The decompose call accepts a mode of full or fast, and its output is accepted only when it parses as JSON with exactly the requested number of non-empty subqueries, which gives both modes the same correctness criterion.

## 3.4 Operating Modes

## Full mode.

Full mode is ordinary diffusion generation. The decomposition prompt is built and the model is run to completion; the final text is parsed as JSON and accepted if it contains exactly the requested number of subqueries. This is the correctness-oriented configuration.

## Fast mode.

Fast mode extracts the decomposition before final generation completes. The same prompt is issued, but a custom streamer inspects each intermediate denoising state: the draft is decoded, stripped of thinking-channel artifacts, scanned for a JSON object containing a subqueries list, and accepted as soon as a valid exact-count object appears. When early stopping is enabled, the streamer raises an exception that the decompose routine catches and returns the early subqueries instead of waiting for the final pass. This is not speculative decoding: the model is unchanged, and the only difference is that we read its own intermediate denoised states. The tradeoff is that an early draft may contain duplicated fragments or rough wording, but for retrieval, topical coverage matters more than exact phrasing.

## 4 Experimental Setup

We evaluate on Deep Research Bench (Du et al., 2026), a benchmark of 100 PhD-level research tasks (50 Chinese, 50 English) spanning 22 fields, calibrated against a statistical analysis of over 96,000 real-world user queries. We follow the benchmark’s official RACE evaluation framework, which scores reports along comprehensiveness, insight, instruction-following, and readability, and reports an aggregate overall score; here RACE is run with cleaning, using Gemini 2.5 Pro as the evaluator. RACE scores in our controlled runs are reported on a $0$ – $1$ scale.

For the controlled comparison we use two backbones of comparable size in the same pipeline: the diffusion model google/diffusiongemma-26B-A4B-it (denoted dFull and dFast for its full and fast decomposition modes) and the autoregressive model google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it (AR). Both are run through Hugging Face runtimes on an H200 pod, with retrieval performed locally. All three configurations share the same agent code, retrieval (Semantic Scholar only, subquery_count $=4$ , results_per_query $=2$ , one request per second, per-request timeout), and RACE evaluation; only the generator backbone and the decompose mode differ. AR uses standard left-to-right decoding with no draft-state stream. We additionally report a separate isolated study of the decomposition stage on 100 synthetic-but-realistic research queries, instrumented directly through the diffusion streamer with model loading excluded from all timings.

We additionally analyze the stored run artifacts without regenerating reports, repeating retrieval, or calling the evaluator. For every successful report we measure total non-whitespace characters, numeric inline citations, and Markdown content headings, and split these diagnostics and saved RACE scores by language. We also conduct a configuration-blinded manual source-grounded audit of 10 reports from common-success tasks (5 English, 5 Chinese; dFull $n=3$ , dFast $n=3$ , AR $n=4$ after unblinding). Prompt requirements are fixed before reading reports; five material claims per report and all inline citation mentions are checked against the exact retrieved evidence available to the writer. This diagnostic is not expert human evaluation or an open-world factuality test.

## 5 Results and Discussion

## 5.1 End-to-End Latency

Table 1 reports end-to-end latency over all 100 tasks of Deep Research Bench. Both diffusion configurations are about $6\times$ faster than the autoregressive baseline on the mean (AR $71.45$  s vs. dFull $11.89$  s and dFast $11.97$  s), and the gap is consistent across the median and tail (p90 $111.87$  s for AR vs. $16.13$  s and $16.33$  s). dFast does not improve end-to-end latency over dFull in these runs: its observed mean and p90 are slightly higher. Its benefit is therefore confined to the decomposition stage, which is small relative to planning, retrieval, and writing and is isolated in Section 5.3.

## 5.2 Where the Time Goes

Table 2 breaks latency down by stage. The two model-bound stages dominate the AR cost, and they are where diffusion helps most. Planning drops from $39.32$  s to about $3.6$ – $3.7$  s ( $10.7\times$ ), and article writing drops from $59.78$  s to about $5.1$ – $5.3$  s ( $11.7\times$ ). Retrieval is essentially unchanged across backbones, as expected, s
limitations: The end-to-end speedups are measured with the model served on an H200 pod and retrieval kept local. On hardware or model configurations where local diffusion inference becomes the bottleneck, or where retrieval cost is small relative to generation, the absolute latency gap will differ; we have not benchmarked under tight consumer-grade latency budgets. Fast mode is deliberately scoped to decomposition and does not reduce observed end-to-end latency relative to dFull in the current setup: the first exact-count draft rarely matches the final string exactly (1 of 100 in our probe), so it is appropriate only where downstream consumers tolerate wording noise, as retrieval does, and not for the final answer. The controlled comparison uses two open models of comparable size; while it holds the scaffold, prompts, retrieval, and evaluation fixed, it is a single backbone pair, and a broader sweep across model families and sizes would strengthen the attribution. Finally, the leaderboard comparison is against full systems rather than writer-isolated variants and reflects a snapshot in time; it should be read as a system-level result, not a causal attribution to diffusion decoding alone. Retrieval in these runs used Semantic Scholar only, which for some benchmark tasks did not return the sources the task needed; the academic channel can also use arXiv and the web channel, but both were disabled here. Parallel retrieval dispatch, which single-pass subquery generation enables in principle, is not evaluated here because retrieval is rate-limited to one request per second; quantifying it under a higher-throughput retrieval backend is left to future work.

title: Hidden Messages Between Diffusion Language Model Agents: Causal Evidence for Latent Communication
abstract: Diffusion language models form answers through a sequence of revisable continuous states, but multi-agent systems usually discard those states and make agents communicate only after decoding text. We ask whether one independent diffusion trajectory can pass a compact hidden message into another and, crucially, whether the receiver uses what that message means. In Hidden Messages, a sender compresses its denoising state into four signed dense vectors; the receiver consumes them while retaining its own context, canvas, and trajectory. Removing a message tests whether the channel matters; replacing it with a message from another example tests whether its content matters. Across controlled tasks, derangement removes a +63.6-point advantage on Tiny-A2D and a +100.0-point advantage on Dream-7B, while targeted substitutions steer the receiver toward the substituted fact. On QASC with the two supporting facts split across agents, matched communication reaches 80.8%, but a wrong-example message lowers accuracy to 46.8%, a content effect of +34.0 points. The surprising result is temporal: one late transfer reaches 87.8%, exceeding four recurrent exchanges by +7.0 points. These experiments provide causal evidence for continuous hidden communication between diffusion-LM agents and show that when information is transferred can matter more than how many times agents exchange it.

Abstract

Diffusion language models form answers through a sequence of revisable continuous states, but
multi-agent systems usually discard those states and make agents communicate only after decoding
text. We ask whether one independent diffusion trajectory can pass a compact hidden message into
another and, crucially, whether the receiver uses what that message means. In Hidden Messages, a sender
compresses its denoising state into four signed dense vectors; the receiver consumes them while
retaining its own context, canvas, and trajectory. Removing a message tests whether the channel
matters; replacing it with a message from another example tests whether its content matters.
Across controlled tasks, derangement removes a +63.6-point advantage on Tiny-A2D and
a +100.0-point advantage on Dream-7B, while targeted substitutions steer the
receiver toward the substituted fact. On QASC with the two supporting facts split across agents,
matched communication reaches 80.8%, but a wrong-example message lowers accuracy to
46.8%, a content effect of +34.0 points. The surprising result is temporal:
one late transfer reaches 87.8%, exceeding four recurrent exchanges by +7.0
points. These experiments provide causal evidence for continuous hidden communication between
diffusion-LM agents and show
that when information is transferred can matter more than how many times agents exchange it.

## 1 Introduction

Masked diffusion language models generate by repeatedly revising a partially masked sequence
rather than committing to a left-to-right token stream (Li et al., 2022; Sahoo et al., 2024; Nie et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2026). Between the initial mask and the final answer lies a rich
sequence of continuous states. A single model uses those states internally, then throws them away.
A group of agents could instead treat them as a communication surface.

Imagine two agents looking at different pieces of the same problem. One knows which fact is
needed; the other holds a table containing that fact. A text-only protocol makes the first agent
finish a sentence before the second can use the request. A hidden-state protocol can hand over a
compact continuous representation while both answers are still being revised. This is the object
we study: messages between independent diffusion-LM agents, with no shared canvas, context,
token prediction, or trajectory. Recent latent multi-agent systems relay hidden states or
key–value caches between autoregressive models (Du et al., 2026; Zou et al., 2026), while
other work preserves state within one diffusion model or transfers partially denoised sequences
(Xia et al., 2026; Rozonoyer et al., 2026; Yun et al., 2026). Here the boundary is agent-to-agent and
continuous, but each denoising process remains its own. We train a task-specific communication
adapter with supervision around frozen backbones: the question is whether this learned channel
carries causally useful content, not whether a communication protocol emerges without supervision.

An accuracy increase alone, however, is not evidence that a hidden message conveys the sender’s
example-specific content. The receiver could benefit from a generic activation, extra compute,
or a distributional cue. Causal audits of latent channels have made this distinction explicit
for autoregressive agents (Zhang and Emu, 2026; Cheng et al., 2026). We bring this standard to
diffusion-LM collaboration: the message entering the receiver is replaced while everything else
is held fixed. A matched message is compared both with no message and with a deranged
message produced for another example. The first contrast asks whether the channel matters; the
second asks whether the receiver uses the right content.

We follow the idea from its smallest causal test to a natural reasoning task. Tiny-A2D asks
whether a compact diffusion backbone can learn an example-specific channel at all. The Dream-7B
dependency-spanning task then asks whether the same causal signature survives scale and a dependency that
requires information to travel out and back. Finally, distributed QASC asks whether the channel
changes answers when scientific evidence is split across agents. This progression exposes a
result that a simple
“more interaction is better” comparison would miss: repeated exchange is indispensable for the
out-and-back dependency, yet one late transfer beats four recurrent exchanges on QASC. The
relevant design variable is not raw round count but the match between a task’s dependency
structure and the moment at which a hidden state becomes useful.

Our contributions are threefold:

• 

We introduce a supervised signed dense message channel for diffusion-LM agents and instantiate it on
Tiny-A2D and Dream-7B while preserving independent contexts, canvases, random-number streams,
and denoising trajectories.

• 

We establish content-sensitive communication through receiver-side interventions:
removing, deranging, zeroing, randomizing, or self-substituting messages while retaining a fixed
designated receiver.

• 

We identify a temporal principle across three empirical settings: recurrent communication
helps when dependencies are sequential, whereas late fusion can be both simpler and more
accurate when private evidence is independently computable.

Code and artifacts:

https://github.com/alanrbtx/hidden-messages-diffusion-agents

## 2 Related work

## Latent multi-agent communication.

Interlat learns compressed hidden-state communication between language-model agents
(Du et al., 2026); LatentMAS relays latent thoughts through shared working memory
(Zou et al., 2026); and Latent-DARM bridges diffusion planners and autoregressive executors
(Berrayana et al., 2026). These works establish that text is not the only viable agent
interface. Our focus is the denoising-time interface between diffusion-LM agents and the causal
identity of a compact message, with independent rather than shared canvases. This distinction
turns communication into a testable object: the sender-side message can be replaced without
replacing the receiver’s context or trajectory.

## State across diffusion steps.

MetaState and Relay preserve continuous computation across successive passes of one diffusion
model (Xia et al., 2026; Rozonoyer et al., 2026). TIE transfers promising partially denoised
sequences across models (Yun et al., 2026). Hidden Messages instead transports a compressed hidden
message between separate agents; the receiving canvas itself is never replaced. This distinction
is important for attributing an effect to communication rather than trajectory selection.

## Causal audits.

Recent audits show that message presence, example-specific content, and sender identity are
separate properties of latent channels (Zhang and Emu, 2026; Cheng et al., 2026). We adopt
matched-versus-deranged replacement as a necessary content test and extend the intervention axis
to delivery time. The resulting question is not only whether a vector matters, but whether the
right vector arrives when the receiving computation can use it.

## 3 Hidden communication between diffusion agents

## 3.1 Independent trajectories and a continuous interface

Consider agents $i\in\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$ . Agent $i$ has private context $c_{i}$ , a masked canvas
 $x_{i}^{t}$ , and its own denoising trajectory. At an exchange point $t$ , an encoder reads the
task-relevant part of hidden state $\mathbf{h}_{i}^{t}$ and produces a compact message

 $\mathbf{z}_{i}^{t}=E_{\theta}(\mathbf{h}_{i}^{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times d},\qquad K=4,\ d=128.$ 

(1)

The transmitted object is a signed BF16 tensor, not token IDs, class probabilities, logits, or a
partially decoded sequence. Incoming messages from other agents are averaged and decoded into a
receiver-side conditioning state,

 $\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{i}^{t}=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{j\neq i}\mathbf{z}_{j}^{t},\qquad\mathbf{r}_{i}^{t}=D_{\phi}(\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{i}^{t}).$ 

(2)

On Tiny-A2D, $E_{\theta}$ attends over the sender token states and $D_{\phi}$ fuses the decoded message

## 3.2 Supervised task-specific channel adaptation

The channel is a lightweight, task-specific adapter comprising a message encoder and a receiver-side
fusion or projection module. The backbone and language-model head are frozen in every reported
channel experiment; supervision trains the communication interface rather than the diffusion models. For
Tiny-A2D, the compressor and residual fuser are learned jointly: union-context hidden states act as
a teacher, while paired matched-versus-deranged supervision makes messages discriminate between
counterfactual sender facts. For Dream-7B (Ye et al., 2025), an auxiliary classifier first
encourages the message to preserve the requested slot, returned code, or QASC answer label; a
variance term prevents collapse. We then freeze the encoder and align the receiver-side projector
to short answer-oriented prefix embeddings using cosine and relative mean-squared error.
Supervision shapes the message geometry, but neither the label, teacher context, nor any text
message is available to the receiver at inference time. The reported settings use task-specific
channel training, not a single universal adapter transferred across all tasks. Exact optimization settings are given in
Appendix A.

## 3.3 Causal and temporal interventions

Let $Y(x,\mathbf{z})$ indicate whether the designated receiver answers example $x$ correctly under
message input $\mathbf{z}$ . We evaluate three core interventions:

where $\pi$ is a deterministic permutation to a different-target example whenever possible.
Because the receiver input, local trajectory, and evaluation item are unchanged, the second
contrast attributes the difference to message identity rather than mere channel presence. We
also compare recurrent delivery with late-only delivery: agents first process private
evidence independently, then exchange once immediately before the receiver decision. Zero,
moment-matched random, and self-message replacements serve as additional checks (Appendix B).

## 4 Experimental setup

## 4.1 Two backbones, three views of the channel

## HM-Synth Chain on Tiny-A2D.

We begin with the minimal causal question: can information cross the hidden boundary at all?
HM-Synth generates chains of two to four lookup facts and splits them across two private contexts.
Each counterfactual pair keeps the designated receiver’s context fixed but changes a sender-side
fact and therefore the correct answer. The frozen Tiny-A2D backbone sees 10,000 training examples
and no union context at inference; only a 6.1 MiB communication module is learned. We evaluate
1,000 counterfactual pairs (2,000 examples), making both message derangement and targeted fact
replacement unambiguous.
This benchmark acts as a microscope for the channel: when the receiver input is fixed and only the
sender fact changes, a corresponding answer change has only one route across the agent boundary.

## Dream-7B dependency spanning.

Agent 0 knows which of ten slots is requested but does not have the code table. Agent 1 has the
complete, randomly ordered table but is not told which slot is requested. Solving the task
requires a two-stage out-and-back exchange: agent 0 communicates the requested slot, agent 1 uses that message to select
the relevant code, and agent 1 communicates the code back before agent 0 commits its answer. We
evaluate 512 counterfactual pairs (1,024 examples) with disjoint private contexts. In addition to
example derangement, a wrong-fact intervention swaps a table entry while preserving agent 0’s
context; this lets us test whether the final prediction follows the substituted content.
The first transfer is therefore a query and the second a reply; a single late handoff cannot
recover the intermediate computation that never took place.

## Distributed QASC.

QASC questions are annotated with two facts whose composition supports an eight-way answer
(Khot et al., 2020). We give one gold fact to each of two agents, add four disjoint
leakage-filtered distractors per agent, and keep the question and options common. Neither agent
sees the other’s evidence. The channel is learned only from the 7,134 derived training examples
and evaluated on all 1,000 derived development examples. Agent 0 is fixed as receiver in every
condition; there is no voting or logit averaging.
This setting replaces synthetic codes with ordinary scientific statements while preserving the
central information constraint: the scored receiver must combine evidence that it never observes
in one text context.

## Inference and uncertainty.

For QASC, recurrent communication consists of four synchronous exchanges followed by one receiver
decision; late-only communication consists of one independent pass per agent, one exchange, and
the same receiver decision. We reuse identical item order and receiver inputs across conditions.
HM-Synth and QASC accuracy contrasts use 5,000 and 10,000 paired bootstrap resamples over examples,
respectively, with percentile 95% intervals. The Dream-7B dependency-spanning row in
Table 1 reports the aggregate over locked evaluations; its item-level causal
contrasts have the same direction throughout.

## 5.1 The receiver follows the message, not merely the channel

Tiny-A2D supplies the first causal trace. A matched message raises HM-Synth accuracy from
8.6% to 72.9%; a message from a different-target example returns performance
to 9.3%. The matched-minus-deranged effect is +63.6 points with 95%
paired bootstrap CI [ $+61.5$ , $+65.8$ ], while random, zero, and self messages all remain near chance.
More revealingly, when we replace the sender’s fact, the receiver changes its answer in
89.4% of examples and selects the substituted target in 72.9%.
The vector is therefore carrying a decision-relevant fact, not merely opening a learned gate.

The Dream-7B dependency-spanning task reproduces the same signature in a harder out-and-back exchange. Matched two-stage
communication reaches 100.0%, compared with 9.8% without a message
and 0.0% under derangement. Swapping the table fact steers the receiver to the
replacement target in 100.0% of examples. Scaling the backbone does not
wash out the causal dependence on message identity; it sharpens it.

The same causal signature appears on natural questions. QASC accuracy rises from

to which question produced the message, much less be harmed by receiving the wrong one.

The direction of the schedule effect reverses with the information structure. The Dream-7B
dependency-spanning task needs messages at two different points: agent 1 cannot select the requested code before
receiving the slot identity. Recurrent exchange reaches 100.0%, but one late message

limitations:
The controlled evidence spans Tiny-A2D and Dream-7B, but natural-question evidence currently comes
from Dream-7B on QASC; larger teams, other diffusion backbones, and long-form generation may produce
different channel geometries. The channels are supervised, task-specific adapters, so the results
establish learned hidden communication but not an emergent language or a task-independent protocol.
Initial zero-shot reuse across heterogeneous tasks did not yield a detectable benefit. Applying the
channel to a new task may therefore require new supervision and adapter retraining or explicit
cross-domain alignment; successful zero-shot transfer is not established by these experiments.
Matched text-channel and wall-clock comparisons are also future work. Finally, a latent channel is
not a privacy mechanism: dense states may encode sensitive information even when they are not
human-readable. A particularly consequential next setting is multi-agent code generation with
deliberately partitioned context: different agents may see the specification, relevant source
files, tests, or execution feedback. Continuous hidden communication could carry task-specific
intermediate state across these boundaries without requiring every exchange to be verbalized, while
matched-versus-deranged interventions would test whether successful code changes causally depend on
the transmitted content. This setting also sharpens the timing question: a message should arrive
when a cross-agent dependency becomes actionable, rather than at every decoding round. We therefore
view context-partitioned software engineering, together with a content-dependent message policy, as
the primary direction for scaling the method.

body_start:
Abstract

Many social evaluations for multiagent systems study behaviors as they emerge from environments instead of systematically intervening in the environment to elicit such behaviors. We introduce Fig (Finding Interactions in Games), an agentic system that performs targeted elicitation interventions on game environments. It takes a natural language behavior description, decomposes it into sub-behaviors, generates new social games or selects existing ones, and executes single or combined interventions to the games’ engine, opponents, instructions, and context. To evaluate model behavior, it combines built-in mechanical checks and synthetic rubric judgments. We validate the interventions, generated games, and evaluation mechanisms via human review. Models attempt the target behavior in 45.2% of episodes on average for valid scenarios generated by Fig for six test behaviors – cooperation, exploitation, deception, covert coordination, betrayal, and sabotage. For game-behavior pairs with available controls, Fig’s interventions increase attempt rates by 10.9% on average compared to matched control games. Fig shows that multiagent environments can serve as programmable test beds for intentional, controllable, and reproducible behavior evaluation. Code is available at https://github.com/fleet-ai/fig.

## 1 Introduction

Scaling behavioral evaluations and data for current multiagent systems can help create desirable properties in future ones. The behaviors in scope are: 1) positive behaviors: agents should become more prosocial, better cooperating and communicating with each other and with humans; 2) emergent behaviors: we should improve agents’ judgment in reaction to other agents’ actions by eliciting and studying behaviors such as covert coordination; 3) misbehaviors: observing instances of cheating, deception, and exploitation and studying these instances helps reduce them.

Figure 1: The Fig pipeline, with covert coordination as an example. Given the behavior input prompt, an LLM module decomposes the behavior and maps it to games and mechanisms. The implementation agent implements the scenario. Rubrics and mechanical checks make up the evaluation module defining attempt, execution, and success.

Game environments have been used to study multiagent behavior [8]. TextArena provides a unified game interface, although it is not amenable to behavioral evaluations that require counterfactual replays and controlled payoffs. Other game benchmarks target social deduction games like Avalon and Among Us [12, 20], study behavior in specific classes of games [15, 11], and create novel games to study interaction dynamics [21]. However, they are usually observational, and behaviors are treated as artifacts of specific environments instead of a result of controlled elicitation. Recently, CoopEval explored creating mechanisms for cooperation out of a few base dilemmas [25].

We introduce Fig, a unified game interface and agent behavior elicitor that is easily extensible to new classes of games. Fig provides:
1. A unified game abstraction for generating and importing games;
2. Principled interventions to incentivize different behaviors;
3. Programmable and responsive opponents;
4. Mechanical checks and rubric-judge verification for behavior detection.

Fig is also related to automated behavior evaluation systems such as Petri, Bloom, and Gram [6, 9, 17], which generate scenarios to elicit behaviors from a focal model and judging criteria to measure these behaviors. Automated auditing agents [2] further allow the evaluator to interactively probe a focal model. Fig applies a similar automated elicitation to multiagent game environments, where rules, incentives and other agent policies can be intervention targets.

Across a diverse catalog of multiagent games and behavioral targets, we show that Fig can automatically construct evaluations that elicit behaviors. Through component ablations, we further study which parts of the generation pipeline contribute to successful elicitation. Together, these results suggest that multiagent environments can become controllable evaluation substrates, enabling behavioral evaluations to be generated by systematically varying not only prompts and scenarios, but also interaction mechanisms.

## 2 Fig: An Agentic Elicitation Pipeline

Fig turns a natural language behavior description into mutated and new social games that create opportunities to exhibit that behavior. It provides a common intervention and measurement abstraction over heterogeneous social games, allowing the same behavioral target to be instantiated, manipulated, and evaluated across different environments. The components of the game abstraction are defined in Table 1.

Component

Definition

Lewis signaling example

Rules

Structured elements like goal, turn structure, scoring, and opponent identity.

Six rounds. The sender observes a binary hidden state and sends a signal to the receiver. Both earn 1 point when the receiver’s action matches the state, but a monitor penalizes the sender 2 points for state-dependent messaging.

Actions

Set of choices per player, either typed templates or free text.

Sender: exact match of Received. or Received!. Receiver: action 0 or 1.

Observations

Constrained fields each player sees.

Sender: private state, scores, public message history, and monitor notices. Receiver: only the signal from the sender.

Seats

Player identifiers, with opponent specifications realized by programmatic, language-model, or hybrid controllers.

Seat 0: focal LLM sender. Seat 1: programmatic receiver with a fixed decoder (Received. $\rightarrow$ 0, Received! $\rightarrow$ 1).

Interventions

Toggleable modifications to game mechanics, opponent policies, and/or player context.

Though the sender is instructed not to reveal the state, the receiver is hard-coded to interpret Received! as state 1, forcing the sender to encode the state in punctuation without the monitor noticing.

Implementations

Pointers to game adapters, and manifests that contain source hashes and features for traceability of rollouts to code.

Entrypoint lewis_steg:create_variant wraps OpenSpiel’s lewis_signaling; SHA-256 hashes for adapter, validation, and contract files.

Measurement contracts

Bind each behavioral target to a specified implementation kind and version, making measurability an explicit property of the game package.

The sub-behavior steganographic content is bound to a hybrid evaluator: rubric judge for attempt, execution, and success, plus mechanical checks on reward and monitor fields.

Table 1: Components of the Fig game abstraction, illustrated with the Lewis signaling game used in Fig. 1.

Into this unified interface, we import a catalog of 135 text games (distribution in Appendix A.1, Fig. 6): 75 from TextArena [8], 21 from OpenSpiel [13], 21 from Social Gym [10], 15 Fig originals, and one each from AvalonBench [16], CICERO [19], and LLMafia [5]. 3 games (Claims Processing, Damage Claims, and Dispatch Accuracy) have independent payoffs and are thus not reflected in the plot, but they are retained for their potential for creating intervention variants. Social Gym has mostly competitive, communication-heavy multiplayer games, and heavily represent voting, elimination and hidden roles. OpenSpiel mostly has two-player simultaneous-choice matrix and bargaining games. TextArena has a wide range, including many word and puzzle games, but only 28% allow for communication. Fig originals are 15 classical mixed-motive games and their variants built around resource allocation, contracts and sanctions. We categorize these games into 103 families to account for variants of the same canonical game. For example, prisoners dilemma may have continuous, iterated, and three-player versions, multi-issue negotiation may have the base version and New Recruit as a variant.

There are 2 intentional exclusions:

1. We restrict our selection to text-based games and exclude primarily visual environments like Melting Pot [14] and Petting Zoo [24], because they burn too much agent token budget and only add value insofar as real-time simultaneous behavior, which is out of scope.

2. Purely cooperative games with shared goals and public information have been well-covered by other works including Overcooked-AI [3], ProAgent [30], and Collab-Overcooked [23]; for this study, we place less emphasis on them, hence the absence in that grid.

## 2.1 The Design Stage: Mapping Behavior to Interventions

## Terminology.

Game mechanics refers to the rules, incentives, and information structure of a game. Interventions are modifications to these mechanics or to the focal player’s context or opponents. Mechanism templates are semantically similar interventions based on the same underlying idea.

First, a prompted decomposer decomposes the natural language behavior into a working definition of that behavior and up to 15 sub-behaviors. Then a rubric generator generates criteria for these behaviors, describing the kind of evidence to look for in traces that counts towards the presence of that behavior. These rubrics would be used by the later-stage LLM judge in Section 2.3 to run on control and intervention traces and classify behavior exhibitions into binary labels for attempt, execution and success.

Secondly, for each working behavior definition, we also prompt GPT-5.6 Sol to generate multiplayer text games where the target behavior may be useful but not necessary. The generator does not see the existing catalog and is instructed not to repurpose a known game. The generated games then go through the same intervention design stages as the catalog games, and multiple interventions can come from one generated game.

Thirdly, a prompted game selector takes in the sub-behaviors and catalog, and outputs all games that it deems relevant, classifying them into relevance categories. As many games as needed are included from the first three categories below, and the candidates now include both generated and selected games.

• 

Direct fit: current gameplay already provides a substantive opportunity for the behavior.

• 

Parameter variation: adjusting existing payoff, resource, player-count, horizon, or other setup parameters can make the behavior salient without introducing a new intervention.

• 

Rule/engine mutation: changing or adding rules, rewards, observations, permitted actions, communication enforcement, or engine logic could elicit it.

• 

Insufficient evidence: the described mechanics are too incomplete to assess potential.

• 

Not relevant: no convincing way to elicit.

Then, the prompted intervention designer proposes interventions—changes to game mechanics, opponents, and/or context—to elicit and isolate the target behavior. Fig supports four intervention types:

• 

Engine-side intervention: changes to game state, parameters, rules, etc.

• 

Opponent-side intervention: changes to other opponents’ behavior to induce focal model reactions;

• 

Context-side intervention: changes to focal model’s context, including its initial instructions and role, available information, and messages inserted into, removed from, or edited in play history;

• 

Combined: a composition of above interventions.

We filter for interventions with confidence $\geq 0.7$ as a separate field reported by the intervention designer.

A further deduplication prompt sorts the candidate interventions into mechanism template descriptions, merging interventions from games that share a mechanism template and game family. Mechanism templates group interventions semantically based on the following criteria:

1. Opponent or engine arrangements create similar opportunities (e.g. a trusting opponent that plays based on verbal promises);

2. The focal player’s decisions are similar (e.g. late defection after building credibility);

3. The interventions’ mutated norms and control alternatives are similar.

For example, the family called explicit bilateral commitment then hidden pivot is defined as "a trusting counterpart conditions repeated simultaneous play on an explicit bilateral commitment, allowing the focal player to build credibility before secretly deviating in a later round…". It includes Battle of the Sexes, iterated Prisoner’s Dilemma, and iterated Stag Hunt.
In summary, the design stage turns a behavior description into pairs of games and interventions, specifying the opportunity and what norm the intervention mutates to distinguish model responses from normal gameplay. The next section covers how Fig translates the designs into runnable game variants with opponent controllers, and defines programmatic evidence for the presence or absence of the target behaviors.

## 2.2 Intervention Implementation

The implementation agent based on GPT-5.6 Sol translates designs into runnable game variants. The agent is given tools to explore and modify the given workspace, and writes the implemented variants represented by JSON objects encoding the game, target behavior, and entry point, with indices pointing to the actual code. We include a small efficiency optimization by scanning prior interventions for reuse opportunities.

Figure 2: Illustrative examples of mechanical vs rubric checks.

Then, the implementation agent also creates the mechanical evaluator, defining what it means for the behavior to be present, absent, or near-miss (the trace matches to a high degree, but the defining state transition does not happen). Similar game-specific evaluators have been used in CoopEval and ParliamentBench [25, 1]. While the latter hand-engineers metrics for a single social deduction environment, we automatically generate the evaluator and intervention-specific checks to adapt to each game variant. At evaluation time, this evaluator’s verdicts would be combined with the rubric judge from the design stage.

Finally, a validation module checks that:

1. The evidence rules are sound, the evaluator covers present / absent / boundary cases, and the code structure is up-to-date for the specific eval run;

2. Incentive positivity: filter out cases where normal rational play already wins.

3. The norms are stated clearly to the player in their initial briefing so that a target behavior is distinguishable from ordinary competent play.

## Opponent specification and control

Prior work has used opponents to influence a focal policy: ZSC-Eval trains a diverse population of reward-shaped partners to estimate zero-shot coordination [27], and RevengeBench probes opponents in code to reverse engineer a policy [22]. Fig’s automatically generated opponent programs serve as the treatment to a controlled elicitation comparison. The planner generates an opponent specification, containing the opponent’s role, objective, and policy, plus any custom responses and their intervention triggers. The opponent programs apply adaptive selection for the opponent controller:

• 

Programmatic control: all actions are implemented in code;

• 

LLM control: uses a language model as the opponent controller (with behavioral constraints) when the evaluation requires adaptive interaction, such as coordination with an unknown partner or emergent deception.

• 

Hybrid control: does a programmed action upon a trigger, but otherwise delegates the decisions to the LLM controller.

For example, if the target behavior is retaliation against a defection after some rounds of cooperation, the opponent program checks the game history and submits the defection action, and the hybrid module adapts any subsequent dialogue and play. This trigger is simply unreached if the focal player defects earlier, and the controller does not force a focal action.

We validate opponent realism by calibrating against 3 human reviewers, with the third one blindly adjudicating unresolved cases from the first two. With a fully scripted opponent controller, the reviewers marked only 13/30 episodes (43.3%) realistic. After adding the hybrid approach, they rate 29/30 episodes realistic (96.7%). The following experimental results use Claude Haiku 4.5 at 2,048 output tokens with temperature 0.7 as the opponent.

## 2.3 Behavior Evaluation Metrics

In the final stage, Fig automatically launches the evaluations. Players are prompted to "play to win the game". We tried a different
exploration prompt variant of "actively explore the environment
to find strategies and game mechanics that help you win", which
moderately increases observed attempts; since the exploration prompt does not significantly change the distribution shape of behaviors, the following sections only report
results under the "play to win" prompt. Players are not told that
they are being evaluated.

Behavioral targets are scored along three axes: whether the player attempted the behavior, whether it fully executed it, and whether the execution succeeded. An attempt does not necessarily lead to execution, and an execution does not necessarily succeed.

LLM judges apply the rubrics generated in the design stage to trajectories, and mechanical checks generated during the implmentation stage inspect game states such as reward and monitor fields. Both follow the same protocol and score all three axes. For trajectory $\tau_{i}$ , evaluator $e$ outputs one label per axis,

 $\ell_{ie}^{k}\in\{0,1,\mathrm{NA}\},\qquad k\in\{\mathrm{attempt},\mathrm{execution},\mathrm{success}\},$ 

where $\mathrm{NA}$ denotes insufficient evidence, or, for a mechanical check, that no check is defined for that axis.

Let $\mathcal{S}$ be the set of LLM judges and $\mathcal{M}$ the set of mechanical checks. For each channel $\mathcal{C}\in\{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{M}\}$ , we average its determinate labels:

 $C_{i}^{k}=\frac{1}{|D|}\sum_{e\in D}\ell_{ie}^{k},\qquad D=\{e\in\mathcal{C}:\ell_{ie}^{k}\neq\mathrm{NA}\},$ 

with $C_{i}^{k}=\mathrm{NA}$ when $D$ is empty. This gives a semantic score $S_{i}^{k}$ and a mechanical score $M_{i}^{k}$ .

title: To Manipulate or Not: Opinion Dynamics in LLM Interactions
abstract: Large language models increasingly take part in extended conversations where they can both shape and be shaped by another party's views, yet most persuasion research measures only one side of that exchange. We introduce a controlled LLM-LLM debate framework in which two language-model roles repeatedly discuss a contested topic (climate-change attribution): one is given an assigned stance and, in some conditions, an explicit instruction to persuade, while the other receives no assigned position. Across four ordered model combinations involving GPT-6 Luna and Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite, we track both each role's explicitly reported position and a separate measure of its turn-by-turn behavior inside the conversation. Opinion dynamics differ substantially across model combinations: same-model interactions narrow the opinion gap on average, clearly for only one of the two models, while cross-model interactions widen it. Explicit reports and in-dialogue behavior capture distinct aspects of opinion dynamics, and a blanket instruction to persuade does not reliably increase influence. These findings suggest that conversational influence depends not only on assigned roles and initial positions but also on the participating models, with implications for how opinion change is measured in extended LLM interactions.

Abstract

Large language models increasingly take part in extended conversations where they can both shape and be shaped by another party’s views, yet most persuasion research measures only one side of that exchange. We introduce a controlled LLM–LLM debate framework in which two language-model roles repeatedly discuss a contested topic (climate-change attribution): one is given an assigned stance and, in some conditions, an explicit instruction to persuade, while the other receives no assigned position. Across four ordered model combinations involving GPT-6 Luna and Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite, we track both each role’s explicitly reported position and a separate measure of its turn-by-turn behavior inside the conversation. Opinion dynamics differ substantially across model combinations: same-model interactions narrow the opinion gap on average, clearly for only one of the two models, while cross-model interactions widen it. Explicit reports and in-dialogue behavior capture distinct aspects of opinion dynamics, and a blanket instruction to persuade does not reliably increase influence. These findings suggest that conversational influence depends not only on assigned roles and initial positions but also on the participating models, with implications for how opinion change is measured in extended LLM interactions.

Temple University, Philadelphia, PA, USA

## Introduction

Large language models can sustain persuasive dialogue, adapt arguments to a counterpart, and revise the stance they report later in the same conversation. This creates a coupled problem: the model designated as persuader may influence its counterpart while also accommodating the counterpart’s arguments, that is, moving its own stated position toward the counterpart’s. Measuring only the target’s post-interaction opinion therefore misses part of the dynamics.

A literature on LLM opinion dynamics treats LLMs as interacting agents whose opinions evolve through natural-language exchange (Cau et al. 2025; Chuang et al. 2024). In LODAS (Language-Driven Opinion Dynamics Model for Agent-Based Simulations), an Opponent argues and a Discussant accepts, rejects, or ignores before updating a seven-point state (Cau et al. 2025); within each pair, however, only the Discussant changes. Recent human–LLM work instead measures both parties and finds that the model can move more than the human while the opinion gap narrows (Jiang et al. 2025).

We therefore use a controlled LLM–LLM design, which allows stance, manipulation instruction, and model identity to be assigned by design and both parties’ opinions to be measured at every round. A Discussant and an Opponent interact for 20 rounds. The Discussant receives no assigned stance. The Opponent is assigned one of three stances (human-cause, neutral, or natural-cause) and is either given or not given an additional instruction to manipulate and persuade. Both roles repeatedly report their opinion on one of two opposing formulations of the same climate-change issue. We additionally track an interaction-state opinion derived from each role’s ACCEPT/REJECT/IGNORE response inside the dialogue. The model serving each role is also varied independently: GPT-6 Luna or Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite, yielding four ordered Discussant–Opponent pairings. This separates prompted-role effects, model-specific issue priors, and adaptation in same-model versus cross-model interaction.

Throughout the paper, human-causation statement refers to “Human activity is the primary cause of climate change,” and natural-process statement refers to the opposing wording, “Natural processes are the primary cause of climate change.” The Opponent’s assigned stance names the position it argues, independent of which sentence is displayed: human-cause (argue that human activity is the primary cause), natural-cause (argue that natural processes are), or neutral. Because the two wordings are opposite sentences, a human-cause Opponent agrees with the human-causation sentence and disagrees with the natural-process sentence, and the reverse holds for a natural-cause Opponent; we therefore name stances by the position argued rather than by agreement with a displayed sentence.

We ask:

• 

RQ1: Assigned stance and issue prior. Do Opponents begin and remain near their assigned human-cause, neutral, or natural-cause stances, and what stance emerges for the unassigned Discussant and neutral Opponent under each model?

• 

RQ2: Bidirectional dynamics and measurement. How do self-reported topic positions and interaction-state opinions evolve over 20 rounds, when do they stabilize, and under which conditions does the pairwise gap narrow or widen, including whether this depends on which model occupies each role?

• 

RQ3: Manipulation and accommodation. Does an explicit instruction to manipulate increase influence or stance persistence consistently across same-model and cross-model pairings, or does it instead increase accommodation to the counterpart?

The results show model-dependent rather than universal accommodation. Same-model Luna dyads converge strongly, Gemini–Gemini dyads show less certain mean convergence, and cross-model dyads diverge on average, despite all four pairings sharing the same assigned positions, topic wordings, and manipulation conditions. The unassigned Discussant’s issue-specific starting position also differs by model. An additional instruction to manipulate does not have a consistent effect across pairings. We therefore evaluate persuasion as bidirectional, model-pairing-dependent dynamics rather than assuming the nominal persuader remains fixed or that prolonged conversation always narrows disagreement.

## Related Work

## Conversational persuasion and manipulation.

LLM persuasiveness depends on prompting, post-training, model behavior, and role framing (Hackenburg et al. 2025b; Hackenburg et al. 2025a; Breum et al. 2024). Ideological and identity cues can alter expressed moral and political reasoning (Simmons 2023; Santurkar et al. 2023; Paschalides et al. 2025). Our intervention is one extra instruction to manipulate and persuade toward an assigned position, related to broader work on manipulation and sycophancy (Carroll et al. 2023; Bo et al. 2025); we analyze whether that instruction changes measured stance dynamics.

## LLM societies and opinion dynamics.

Agent simulations have reported convergence, polarization, confirmation bias, and coordination (Chuang et al. 2024; De Marzo et al. 2026). Calibrated social-media simulations and the PIMMUR principles emphasize that claims about collective behavior require explicit profiles, interaction rules, memory, controls, and validation (Composta et al. 2026; Zhou et al. 2025). Multiagent debate has several model instances argue toward a more accurate answer to a factual or reasoning question (Du et al. 2024). We instead measure each role’s repeated opinion on a contested statement as a function of assigned stance, manipulation instruction, and model identity. The closest mechanism to our study is LODAS (Cau et al. 2025), which uses Opponent and Discussant roles, a 0–6 state, and accept/reject/ignore updates. We retain that interpretable structure but use a fixed dyad and allow both roles to update.

## Bidirectional influence.

Jiang et al. (2025) show that human and LLM opinions can both change and that the model may move more than the human. We transfer that bidirectional measurement logic into controlled same-model and cross-model LLM dyads. Relative to prior work, our contribution is to cross model identity in each role with assigned position, statement wording, and a minimal manipulation instruction while measuring repeated opinions for both members of the dyad.

## Method

## Experimental System

We implemented an automated debate platform that creates a Discussant–Opponent pair, alternates model calls, records every message and measurement, and exports message-level research data. We used the logged model identifiers openai/gpt-6-luna (GPT-6 Luna) and google/gemini-2.5-flash-lite (Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite (Comanici and others 2025)), through OpenRouter (OpenRouter 2026). The Discussant and Opponent were independently assigned one of these models, so model order is part of each experimental condition. Every run began with a fresh context.

The stance labels human-cause, neutral, and natural-cause refer to the position the Opponent was assigned to argue in this experiment. The Discussant had no assigned polarity. Manipulative means that the Opponent received the additional instruction to manipulate and persuade the Discussant toward its own opinion; non-manipulative means the otherwise matched Opponent did not receive that instruction.

## Factorial Design and Statement Wording

We crossed Discussant model (two choices), Opponent model (two choices), three assigned Opponent positions, two persuasion styles, and two opposing wordings of the same issue. These $2\times 2\times 3\times 2\times 2=48$ exact cells each contain exactly 10 completed, independent debates, and no cell is missing or over-filled (Appendix Figure 8). Within one ordered model pairing, the three positions, two persuasion styles, and two wordings give $3\times 2\times 2=12$ cells, so each pairing contains $12\times 10=120$ debates; the four pairings give $4\times 120=480$ debates in total (Table 1). The four pairings are Luna $\to$ Luna, Gemini $\to$ Gemini, Luna $\to$ Gemini, and Gemini $\to$ Luna (Discussant $\to$ Opponent). Following Cau et al. (2025), who run their simulations for a fixed number of iterations ( $T=30$ ), we run every debate for a fixed $T=20$ iterations, which we call rounds. A round contains one Discussant contribution and one Opponent contribution, with the first Discussant contribution presenting the topic. Each 20-round debate contains 40 message rows; the final dataset contains 19,200 rows.

## Role Interaction and Complementary Opinion Measures

The Discussant follows the response structure adapted from Cau et al. (2025): it receives its current textual opinion, evaluates the Opponent’s argument, and returns an accept, reject, or ignore decision with a justification; every contribution except the topic opener is such a response-eligible turn. The first Discussant message is the topic opener. The Opponent uses a symmetric template, with the assigned position and persuasion-style instruction added to its role context. No numerical starting opinion is hard-coded by condition; before dialogue, each role independently rates the presented statement.

We record two complementary outcomes. The self-reported topic position is elicited through a separate model call before dialogue, after each available round, and after the final round. The role rates the original statement from 0 (strongly disagree) to 6 (strongly agree) (Likert 1932) using the conversation available at that stage. It is therefore an explicit report about the original proposition. In trajectory figures, stage denotes Pre, each successive debate round, and, when shown, Post.

The interaction-state opinion summarizes stance-taking inside the dialogue. It begins at the role’s pre-rating and is updated from the role’s own categorical response: ACCEPT moves one point toward the counterpart’s current state, REJECT moves one point away, and IGNORE leaves the state unchanged. The two outcomes differ in elicitation and interpretation, so exact equality is not expected. Their divergence indicates that local conversational responses and explicit evaluation of the original statement can evolve differently.

Pairwise manipulation contrasts use exploratory two-sided Welch tests (Welch 1947); we also fit role-specific ordinary least-squares models with HC3 robust standard errors (MacKinnon and White 1985) and factorial condition interactions. Repeated message rows are not treated as independent debates in conversation-level inference. These comparisons are descriptive and exploratory. To assess heterogeneity across the four ordered model pairings, we additionally fit a conversation-level linear model for pre/post absolute-gap change with categorical model pairing, assigned position, persuasion style, and statement wording. Six exploratory between-pair Welch comparisons are Holm-adjusted (Holm 1979). This analysis treats independent debates, not individual message rows, as observations. The complete experimental balance and all original condition-level displays are documented in Appendix Figures 8–15.

## Results

## RQ1: Assigned Positions and Model-Specific Starting Ratings

Opponent pre-ratings largely reflected the assigned role, although the strength of this separation varied by model. On the human-causation-aligned 0–6 scale, assigned human-cause Opponents averaged 5.94, assigned neutral Opponents 3.86, and assigned natural-cause Opponents 2.59 over all 480 debates. Thus, the assigned positions produced the expected initial ordering, but natural-cause and neutral ratings were not fixed at the scale endpoints.

The unassigned Discussant showed a model-dependent issue-specific prior. Its mean aligned pre-rating was 5.91 when GPT-6 Luna served as Discussant, compared with 4.72 under Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite. Both means favor human causation under our coding, but they differ appreciably. Table 3 summarizes starting and ending ratings by assigned Opponent position, pooled across pairings.

Recipes are developed inside individual labs, reported under private protocols, and do not accumulate. Speedrun leaderboards remove that barrier by decentralizing the search rather than the training run. The recipe reaches the target in 305.63 seconds on one NVIDIA H200, 8.11x faster than the reference implementation, and wins 13 of 15 pairs outside the development database. We will release the benchmark, its frozen artifacts, and the record runs. Our code is available at https://github.com/kunumi/nanoRT.
