body_start:
Abstract

Progress on foundation model pretraining is gated by who can afford a trial, and relational pretraining is no exception. Recipes are developed inside individual labs, reported under private protocols, and do not accumulate. Speedrun leaderboards remove that barrier by decentralizing the search rather than the training run. The problem is fixed, the stack is open, entries are ranked by wall-clock time to a quality target, and one GPU is enough to hold the record. We introduce modded-nanoRT, the first such leaderboard for Relational Transformers. Which database to hold out decides whether the benchmark can resolve improvements at all, so we fix it by calibration, ranking six candidates by how sharply a 45-minute learning curve separates improvement from seed noise. We open the leaderboard with typed trilinear attention, a relational operator that conditions attention scores and values on the foreign key traversed, together with Muon and SIGReg. The recipe reaches the target in $305.63$ seconds on one NVIDIA H200, $8.11\times$ faster than the reference implementation, and wins 13 of 15 pairs outside the development database. We will release the benchmark, its frozen artifacts, and the record runs. Our code is available at https://github.com/kunumi/nanoRT.

## 1 Introduction

Most machine learning data sits in relational databases, split across tables linked by primary–foreign key relationships. Standard pipelines flatten those links into a task-specific table, so data preparation repeats for every new database and prediction problem. Relational foundation models learn from the schema itself. RelBench standardized this setting across databases and predictive tasks (Robinson et al., 2024), and the Relational Transformer (RT) showed that one schema-aware model applies to unseen tasks without task-specific parameters or in-context examples (Ranjan et al., 2026a).

An architectural, optimizer, or regularization change takes hours to evaluate even at small scale, and the labs that can run such trials at volume are the labs with clusters, so recipe knowledge accumulates where the compute is and everyone else is priced out of the loop that produces it. Community speedruns answer this by pooling a different resource. Fixing the model family, the data, the hardware, and the target, and ranking submissions by time to reach it, turned recipe search for language model pretraining into a leaderboard that dozens of contributors each advanced by seconds (Jordan et al., 2024a); modded-nanoTabPFN did the same for tabular models (Pfefferle et al., 2025; Ozturk et al., 2026). What is decentralized here is not the training run but the search over it. Contributors hold one GPU each, work independently on disjoint parts of the design space, and their findings compose because every entry is measured on the same clock.

No such artifact exists for relational foundation models, and the format does not transfer mechanically. Language and tabular speedruns train on one fixed corpus. Relational pretraining mixes databases with different schemas, and the quantity of interest is zero-shot transfer to a database the model has never seen, so the mixture and an entire held-out database must be fixed in advance.

We introduce modded-nanoRT, an open speedrun for pretraining a nano-scale Relational Transformer on a single GPU and evaluating it zero-shot on a held-out database. Table 1 lists what is fixed; the training stack is open, and submissions are ranked by wall-clock time to the target. Choosing the held-out database is the design problem the relational setting adds, and we settle it by calibration. All six candidates run for 45 minutes over multiple seeds, ranked by how sharply their learning curves separate improvements from seed noise.

We open the leaderboard with three changes to the RT recipe. We introduce typed trilinear attention. RT uses the schema only as an attention mask, so every foreign key shares one compatibility function; we make the relation a third multiplicative factor in the attention score and the message, so neighbors reached by different foreign keys are no longer scored alike. We add SIGReg as a representation-level regularizer over relational columns (Balestriero and LeCun, 2025), following tabular work that reports faster convergence under it (Merchant et al., 2026). Muon orthogonalizes the matrix-valued updates of the backbone, carried over from the language model speedruns (Jordan et al., 2024b).

The record reaches the target in 305.63 seconds on one NVIDIA H200, $8.11\times$ faster than the reference implementation. Matched three-seed comparisons attribute the gain to Muon, and to typed attention only in combination with it; leave-one-database-out runs win 13 of 15 pairs outside development. Verification consumes $59.9\%$ of the record, so the next entry should look at the evaluation path.

## 2 Related Work

## Relational foundation models.

Relational deep learning has standardized benchmarks (Robinson et al., 2024) and pretrained schema-aware models (Ranjan et al., 2026a; Ranjan et al., 2026b), and synthetic multi-table generation addresses the scarcity of relational pretraining data (Kothapalli et al., 2026). These fix what to train on. None fix a protocol under which training-efficiency results can be compared, so recipe improvements are reported against private baselines and do not compose.

## Time-to-quality benchmarks.

DAWNBench introduced time-to-accuracy as a joint criterion for algorithmic and systems improvements (Coleman et al., 2018), MLPerf Training formalized quality targets under stochastic time to solution (Mattson and others, 2020), and Cramming audits a language model pipeline under a one-GPU, one-day budget (Geiping and Goldstein, 2022). Speedrun leaderboards inherit this criterion and add an open submission process, so contributors accumulate improvements between benchmark rounds. modded-nanoRT carries that to relational pretraining, where the database mixture and the held-out database create their own validity constraints.

## Typed and higher-order attention.

Typed edges are handled elsewhere by relation-specific message transformations (Schlichtkrull et al., 2017), and trilinear scores appear in the 2-simplicial Transformer (Clift et al., 2019; Roy et al., 2025). Our third factor is the database relation on a query–neighbor edge rather than a second neighbor, so typed trilinear attention is relation-conditioned message passing rather than a simplicial architecture.

## 3 The modded-nanoRT challenge

A full run fits on one accelerator. Table 1 lists the fixed quantities; the architecture, optimizer, regularization, context sampling algorithm, precision, and systems implementation remain open.

## Training mixture.

RelBench v1 provides seven databases. We keep only binary classification tasks, so that one metric applies across every database, and exclude rel-Event for confirmed temporal leakage. Six remain as candidates, with seed counts differing by orders of magnitude: rel-Amazon, rel-HM, rel-Stack, rel-Avito, rel-Trial, and rel-F1. One of the six is held out and excluded from the mixture, which therefore spans five. Sampling in proportion to those counts lets the largest database dominate the gradient and turns multi-database pretraining into single-database training; sampling uniformly over-weights the small schemas. We therefore temper the mixture, in the convention used for multilingual pretraining (Xue et al., 2021), $w(d)\propto n(d)^{\alpha}$ , $\alpha=0.5$ , where $n(d)$ is the seed count of database $d$ and the weights are normalized to sum to one, halfway between proportional ( $\alpha=1$ ) and uniform ( $\alpha=0$ ). Tempering is applied when the training artifact is built, by subsampling each database’s seed list until its share of the seeds equals $w(d)$ . The mixture is frozen as part of the protocol, because changing it changes what the metric measures.

## Held-out database.

Evaluation is zero-shot on a database excluded from the mixture, and which database plays that role decides whether the benchmark can resolve improvements at all. A database that saturates early, stalls at the noise floor, or is dominated by seed variance cannot rank entries. We settled it empirically, running a 45-minute leave-one-out calibration for each of six candidates over multiple seeds and ranking them by

 $\mathrm{score}(d)\;=\;\frac{\Delta\mathrm{AUROC}(d)\cdot s(d)}{\sigma(d)},$ 

(1)

where $\Delta\mathrm{AUROC}$ is the gain from initialization to 45 minutes, $s$ is the regression slope of the AUROC curve over the final 20% of wall-clock time, and $\sigma$ is the standard deviation across seeds. rel-Avito ranked first. The target, $0.81621$ , is the best pooled AUROC its calibration run reached inside the 45-minute budget, at $41$ : $20$ of $45$ : $23$ (Appendix B); the validation artifact was frozen alongside it with seeds capped at $50\,000$ and a fixed hop radius and text embeddings. Records are therefore speedups over the reference implementation, resolved to the width of each run’s evaluation grid.

## Evaluation.

We evaluate on the frozen validation artifact for the two rel-Avito tasks, user-visits and user-clicks (Robinson et al., 2024). At each scheduled evaluation we concatenate predictions and labels across both tasks and compute one AUROC. Pooling weights examples rather than tasks and confounds within-task ranking with cross-task score alignment. Only the pooled AUROC determines record eligibility.

## Reference baseline.

The baseline is the Relational Transformer of Ranjan et al. (2026a), reduced to nano scale. RT builds a temporally valid context around each seed row, masks the target cell, and represents every retained cell by its value, datatype, and frozen table–column text embedding; column, feature/foreign-key, and full attention mix these tokens before a datatype-specific decoder predicts the masked value. The baseline uses 12 blocks, width 256, eight heads, and a gated SiLU MLP of width 1024, for 19.3M trainable parameters. Pretraining uses bfloat16, contexts of 1024 cells, batches of 256, and AdamW at learning rate $10^{-3}$ , weight decay $0.1$ , with linear warmup over the first 20% of updates and linear decay after.

## Rules.

modded-nanoRT holds the problem fixed (Mattson and others, 2020; Jordan et al., 2024a; Ozturk et al., 2026). A submission must use one H200, the prescribed training artifact, the frozen rel-Avito validation artifact, and the official metric, target, evaluation schedule, and timing boundary. Weights start from a declared random seed; a submission may not load a checkpoint, train on rel-Avito, reveal masked targets, or modify the validation pipeline. The budget is 45 minutes, and runs that miss the target stay in the analysis as right-censored failures.

## 4 The record recipe

## Typed trilinear attention.

Standard RT scores a query cell $i$ and a neighboring cell $j$ bilinearly, so all foreign-key types share the same compatibility function and a relation enters the model only as an attention mask. Two neighbors carrying the same value are then scored identically whether they were reached through review $\to$ product or review $\to$ customer, and the model must recover the difference from cell content alone, separately in every context it samples. We attach the relation type $\rho(i,j)$ as a third factor in both the attention score and the message, driven by a frozen text embedding of the foreign-key description.

Relation-specific message transformations are standard (Schlichtkrull et al., 2017), but they allocate parameters per relation type and so cannot type an edge in a schema the model has never seen; the embedding comes from an external text encoder, so a new schema adds no parameters. Appendix A shows that the distinctness across relation types is what matters, not its content.

The factor is multiplicative rather than additive, following the trilinear principle of higher-order attention (Clift et al., 2019; Roy et al., 2025). An additive term shifts the scores of an edge class uniformly and gives the relation the status of a query-independent prior over edge types; multiplying inside the head dimension lets the relation select which coordinates of the query–key match are counted, so one query can rank the same neighbor differently depending on how it was reached.

## Muon.

Adam rescales each coordinate by its own gradient statistics, so the update matrix concentrates on a few dominant directions and successive steps reinforce the same subspace. Muon replaces the momentum update of each matrix-valued parameter with the nearest semi-orthogonal matrix, computed by a five-step Newton–Schulz iteration in bfloat16 (Jordan et al., 2024b), so every singular direction advances comparably and a step buys more of the representation than an Adam step of the same norm. The gain is largest early in training, the only regime a speedrun measures, and RT is almost entirely matrix-valued, with four attention sublayers and a gated MLP per block. We apply it to the two-dimensional matrices in the standard attention, typed attention, and feed-forward modules, at peak learning rate $5\times 10^{-3}$ . AdamW updates the encoders, decoders, normalization and scale parameters, biases, and the SIGReg projector, at learning rate $10^{-3}$ and weight decay $0.1$ . Both branches follow the reference schedule. Muon is inherited from prior speedruns and from relational pretraining (Liu et al., 2025; Ranjan et al., 2026b); we report its contribution but do not claim it.

## SIGReg.

RT admits every column of every database into one residual stream through per-datatype encoders, so a price and a free-text title arrive with no shared scale or shape, and nothing prevents a column’s hidden states from collapsing onto a low-dimensional region early in training; the shared blocks then spend capacity renormalizing their inputs. An isotropy constraint cannot add capacity, so we expect it to shorten the path to a given quality without raising the ceiling, which is what Merchant et al. (2026) report for tabular models and what Akbar (2026) report for vision and MLP backbones.

SIGReg matches random one-dimensional projections of a representation distribution to a standard Gaussian through an Epps–Pulley statistic (Balestriero and LeCun, 2025). We apply it to the hidden states leaving the first block, so that the constraint acts on the backbone’s input. Cells are grouped by (table, column), which enforces isotropy within each column’s own population; a trainable $256\rightarrow 1024\rightarrow 64$ projector maps each hidden state, $K=64$ random unit vectors slice the output, and for every group with at least eight valid cells we penalize the squared distance between the empirical characteristic function of each slice and that of $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ over $[-3,3]$ . Writing that group-weighted penalty as $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{col}}$ , the objective is

 $\mathcal{L}=(1-\lambda)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pred}}+\lambda\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{col}},\qquad\lambda=10^{-3},$ 

(5)

and the projector trains jointly with the backbone.

We report three views: the record lineage, a matched multi-seed sweep for attribution, and a leave-one-database-o

modded-nanoRT holds the problem fixed and leaves the training stack open, so that improvements accumulate across contributors. The opening entry reaches the target in $305.63$ seconds on one H200, $8.11\times$ faster than the reference implementation. Matched comparisons attribute that to Muon, and to typed attention only in combination with it, and outside the development database the recipe wins 13 of 15 pairs. title: Sketch2Sim: an end-to-end modular framework for hand-drawn circuit analysis
abstract: This study proposes a sketch-to-simulation system to solve handwritten circuit diagrams. The system converts raw images into a Simulation Program with Integrated Circuit Emphasis (SPICE)-compatible netlist and automatically calculates the circuit's nodal voltages and currents. Another objective is to propose a holistic framework that benefits students and educators by enhancing the teaching and learning experience of electric circuits and expediting engineering design reviews. This article presents a multistage pipeline that converts raw photographs of handwritten electric circuits into executable SPICE-like netlists, providing a solution. A dataset of 1,000 hand-drawn Resistor-Inductor-Capacitor (RLC) circuits was curated and annotated for components, text regions, and character recognition. The proposed system decomposes a circuit diagram into three stages: (i) dual You Only Look Once (YOLO)-based detectors for components and text regions, (ii) a Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (CRNN) with Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) and Optical Character Recognition (OCR)-based domain-aware symbol value extraction, and (iii) image processing with thresholding, skeletonization, and Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) to automatically identify nodes and map them with corresponding components. The proposed system produces the netlist and solves the circuit. The qualitative and quantitative ablation studies on modular stages, as well as end-to-end tests, demonstrate robust performance across various handwriting styles, lighting conditions, and clutter.This study serves as an interactive learning aid and practical tool for professionals, providing a comprehensive user interface (UI), enabling rapid digitization of circuit sketches for study, design, prototyping, or troubleshooting.

title: Decision language models as affordable and rapid alternatives to LLM judges of clinical generative AI
abstract: Automated judges of clinical artificial intelligence (AI) outputs are necessary, but large language model (LLM) judges are costly and slow at scale. We compared Jev, a decision language model that returns structured judgments, with frontier and open-weight LLM judges in four use cases. On 118 pediatric answers, Jev's agreement with physicians' ordinal quality ratings (Gwet's AC2 0.50; expected score 0.53) matched or exceeded that of seven of 12 LLM judges, including frontier models, Claude Opus 5.5 (0.49) and GPT-6 (0.38). On physician-graded binary HealthBench criteria, Jev matched or exceeded four of six LLM judges. On MedHELM's open-ended tasks, Jev's agreement with a three-LLM jury approached or exceeded the jurors' internal agreement. On HealthBench Professional, Jev matched the benchmark's reference judge, GPT-5.4, on 91% of criteria (other judges, 91-93%). Frontier judges cost 73-294 times more than Jev and took 7-57 times longer. Jev may enable efficient clinical AI evaluation at scale.

title: Forging More Tasks into Better Harnesses: Agentic Harness Evolution via Successive Scale Racing
abstract: Agentic harness evolution optimizes an agent's instructions, tools, and control flow by using its task execution experiences as evolving evidence. While more evolution tasks should intuitively improve performance, our preliminary study reveals a paradoxical failure mode: the performance of existing methods degrades as the task pool expands. Our further analysis demonstrates that this degradation stems from suboptimal evidence selection during optimization, as different evidence combinations lead to substantially different evolution outcomes. To address this issue, we propose Successive Scale Racing (SSR), a framework that adaptively searches for optimal evidence combinations in each evolution round. SSR constructs diverse evidence combinations based on the corresponding task quality and coverage, and efficiently races the resulting candidate harnesses under a small compute budget. Empirically, across three distinct benchmarks, SSR achieves state-of-the-art results in all six configurations. Notably, as the task pool grows from 40 to 200, SSR steadily improves the pass rate from 64.3% to 68.3%, while the baselines' performances all drop. Furthermore, its racing mechanism identifies near-optimal candidates while reducing validation executions by 60%.

headings: Forging More Tasks into Better Harnesses:
6.3 Effects of Task Experience and Search Resources
body_start:
Abstract

Agentic harness evolution optimizes an agent’s instructions, tools, and control flow by using its task execution experiences as evolving evidence.
While more evolution tasks should intuitively improve performance, our preliminary study reveals a paradoxical failure mode: the performance of existing methods degrades as the task pool expands. Our further analysis demonstrates that this degradation stems from suboptimal evidence selection during optimization, as different evidence combinations lead to substantially different evolution outcomes. To address this issue, we propose Successive Scale Racing (SSR), a framework that adaptively searches for optimal evidence combinations in each evolution round. SSR constructs diverse evidence combinations based on the corresponding task quality and coverage, and efficiently races the resulting candidate harnesses under a small compute budget. Empirically, across three distinct benchmarks, SSR achieves state-of-the-art results in all six configurations. Notably, as the task pool grows from 40 to 200, SSR steadily improves the pass rate from 64.3% to 68.3%, while the baselines’ performances all drop. Furthermore, its racing mechanism identifies near-optimal candidates while reducing validation executions by 60%.

## 1 Introduction

An agent harness governs a language model’s interaction with its environment through instructions, tool interfaces, context management, and control flow (Ning et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2026a). By determining what the model observes, remembers, and can do (Packer et al., 2023), it shapes how model capabilities are used on real-world tasks. Harness engineering has relied heavily on human design and implementation, such as manually refined interfaces (Yang et al., 2024) and coordination protocols (Hong et al., 2023; Qian et al., 2023). Recent work automates this process, evolving agent designs and workflows from execution experience while keeping model weights fixed (Hu et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024a; Zhang et al., 2026).

Current frameworks for agentic harness evolution commonly follow an execution–reflection–optimization paradigm (Lee et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026). The agent first solves assigned tasks, producing execution trajectories. An agent acting as the optimizer then distills lessons, which we refer to as evidence, from these trajectories, and uses them to guide improvements to the harness. This process repeats until a stopping criterion is met or the execution budget is exhausted.

Figure 1: Many existing methods evolve on large, fixed task pools, which can induce noisy or redundant signals. SSR searches over ordered evidence groups.

In machine learning, expanding training task pools generally improves generalization and system capabilities (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022). However, whether agentic harness evolution similarly benefits from larger task pools remains underexplored.
To address this gap, we first evaluate existing state-of-the-art methods (Lin et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2026b) by enlarging the set of training tasks used for evolution. Surprisingly, our preliminary study in Section 3 shows that larger task pools do not consistently yield better harnesses with existing methods. AHE (Lin et al., 2026), for example, initially improves but drops from 63.0% at 80 tasks to 57.7% at 200 tasks. Based on this observation, we pose our core research question:

How can we leverage experience from more tasks to evolve better harnesses?

To provide further insights into this problem, we investigate how different trajectory selections impact harness updates. We find that a set of
tasks selected by a simple LLM judge can generate better harnesses than either an equally sized alternative subset or the much larger full task pool.
This reveals a key insight: more task experiences, while providing more information, might also introduce noise or redundant signals. Feeding all trajectories into the optimizer could blur the focus of individual modifications. Thus, harness performance depends not on the total volume of available evidence, but on selecting the appropriate combinations of evidence for each evolution step.

However, searching for effective evidence combinations presents two key challenges: (1) The space of possible trajectory combinations is combinatorial. Generating every candidate harness and thoroughly evaluating each on validation tasks is computationally prohibitive. (2) The ideal evidence scale is not static; it shifts as the parent harness evolves and handles tasks differently across iterations.

To address these challenges, we propose Successive Scale Racing (SSR) (Figure 1), a framework that adaptively searches over evidence combinations under a fixed execution budget. SSR addresses the two challenges in the following ways: (1) Instead of enumerating combinatorial subsets, SSR introduces Representative Evidence Ranking (RER) to order task evidence by quality and coverage. It generates candidates from a selected set of evidence combinations based on the rankings. To minimize validation costs, SSR employs a cumulative performance racing mechanism that evaluates candidates on shared task batches and progressively prunes weaker candidates early. (2) In every evolution round, SSR refreshes execution trajectories based on the incumbent harness and dynamically re-ranks evidence subsets, allowing the winning evidence combination to adaptively shift as the harness evolves.

We evaluate SSR on SWE-Bench Pro Verified, DeepSWE, and GAIA-2 (Zheng et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026; Froger et al., 2026) across two execution setups. SSR achieves top performance and exhibits positive scaling, raising accuracy from 64.3% to 68.3% as the task pool expands from 40 to 200 tasks.
Our main contributions are threefold: (1) We identify noisy and redundant evidence signals as a primary cause of performance degradation when scaling task pools in harness evolution. (2) We propose SSR, which effectively searches over evidence scales using quality-coverage ranking and performance racing. (3) Across three benchmarks under two execution setups, SSR leads in all six settings and benefits from larger task pools, achieving higher efficiency and performance.

## 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Agent Harness Engineering

Harness design encompasses reasoning–action loops (Yao et al., 2022), multi-agent conversation (Wu et al., 2023), sandboxed execution (Wang et al., 2024), and prescribed repair workflows (Xia et al., 2024). Automated optimization spans instruction search (Zhou et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023), feedback-guided prompt revision (Pryzant et al., 2023; Agrawal et al., 2025), pipeline compilation (Khattab et al., 2023), and textual feedback propagation (Yuksekgonul et al., 2024). Beyond prompts, GPTSwarm optimizes computational graphs (Zhuge et al., 2024), AgentSquare evolves and recombines modules (Shang et al., 2024), and AgentOptimizer updates tool functions (Zhang et al., 2024b).

Figure 2: Existing methods’ performance change with more evolution tasks. Larger task pools do not consistently improve final harness performance.

Figure 3: Comparisons of harness performance on different task pools. A smaller, selected task pool tends to induce better harnesses than a large, random task pool.

## 2.2 Self-Evolving Agents and Harnesses

Experience can improve outputs through self-feedback (Madaan et al., 2023), later attempts through verbal reflection (Shinn et al., 2023), and future tasks through reusable skills (Wang et al., 2023), extracted insights (Zhao et al., 2023), contextual guidelines (Fu et al., 2024), instruction manuals (Chen et al., 2024), reasoning memory (Ouyang et al., 2025), or evolving playbooks (Zhang et al., 2025). Code-level evolution includes SICA’s self-edits (Robeyns et al., 2025), DGM’s archive (Zhang et al., 2026), HGM’s descendant-based search (Wang et al., 2026), and MGM’s cross-task and cross-lineage comparisons (Liu et al., 2026). AHE structures trajectory evidence (Lin et al., 2026), while Meta-Harness exposes historical code, scores, and traces (Lee et al., 2026). Retro selects a challenging, diverse coreset and uses self-preference for retrospective optimization (Pan et al., 2026b).

## 3 Preliminary Study

In this preliminary study, we investigate how task-pool size and evidence use affect harness evolution. To start with, we conduct experiments on SWE-Pro-V with the Codex setting, as in the analyses of Section 6. We report final Avg Pass@1 (%) averaged over three independent runs. Section 6.4 extends the evidence comparison to DeepSWE.

## 3.1 Effect of Task-Pool Size

We vary the training task pool from 40 to 200 tasks across Retro, AHE, HGM, and MGM. Contrary to intuition, none of these methods consistently benefits from larger pools (Figure 3). For instance, AHE peaks at 63.0% accuracy with 80 tasks, but degrades to 57.7% with 200 tasks.

## Observation 1.

Expanding the task pool does not necessarily produce a better harness under existing evolution strategies, and can even degrade performance.

## 3.2 Effect of Evidence Configuration

To understand this degradation, we analyze how different evidence selections impact optimization starting from the same harness (Figure 3). An LLM judge ranks experience records from the 160-task pool into Top 40 and Bottom 40 subsets. Top 40 outperforms All 160 by 3.4% and Bottom 40 by 5.4%, showing that evidence quality and scale matter significantly. Conversely, a randomly sampled 40-record subset from the 80-task pool trails All 80 by 1.3%, confirming that unguided scale reduction is unhelpful.

## Observation 2.

Evolution outcomes depend on the evidence combinations (from task trajectories) the optimizer uses; a well-selected subset can outperform full-pool evidence.

Figure 4: Overview of Successive Scale Racing (SSR).
(a) RER ranks training trajectories of the parent $H_{t}$ by quality and marginal coverage gain.
(b) Nested evidence prefixes of different scales independently modify $H_{t}$ to generate candidate harnesses.
(c) Candidates race against the protected parent $H_{t}$ over shared task batches, progressively eliminating weaker harnesses by cumulative score and updating the incumbent to $H_{t+1}$ for the next evolution round.

## 4 Successive Scale Racing

In this section, we introduce Successive Scale Racing (SSR). As illustrated in Figure 4, our framework operates in four key stages: (1) Representative Evidence Ranking (RER), which orders experience records by quality and coverage; (2) Multiscale Candidate Generation, which independently modifies a shared parent harness using nested evidence prefixes generated from the ranking; (3) Candidate Performance Racing, which progressively prunes weaker candidates using cumulative scores on shared validation batches; and (4) Recursive Evolution, which updates the parent harness and refreshes execution evidence for subsequent rounds.

## Notation.

Let $H_{t}$ denote the incumbent harness at round $t$ , and let $\mathcal{T}$ and $\mathcal{V}$ be disjoint training and validation task sets. Training tasks supply optimization evidence; validation tasks are held out from that evidence and contribute to candidate selection. $N=|\mathcal{T}|$ denotes the available evidence-pool size, $k$ the number of task records supplied to one candidate, and $M$ the number of candidates in a round.

## 4.1 Representative Evidence Ranking

An effective evidence set must offer actionable and transferable insights without overwhelming the optimizer with redundant or low-value execution logs. To achieve this balance, Representative Evidence Ranking (RER) establishes a global ordering of experience records that jointly optimizes individual evidence quality and collective pool coverage.

## Experience characterization.

For a given parent harness $H_{t}$ , we execute it on each training task $i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$ to collect one execution trajectory $\tau_{i}$ . An LLM judge distills each trajectory $\tau_{i}$ along with its feedback into a structured experience record $e_{i}$ , which comprises an executive summary and concrete harness improvement suggestions.

Formally, for each record $e_{i}$ , the judge outputs three normalized metrics in $[0,1]$ : experience importance $w_{i}$ , actionability $a_{i}$ , and confidence $u_{i}$ . Here, $w_{i}$ quantifies the generalizability of the experience beyond its originating task; $a_{i}$ measures the concreteness of the proposed harness modifications; and $u_{i}$ reflects the judge’s assessment reliability. We define the intrinsic record quality as $q_{i}=a_{i}u_{i}$ , ensuring a high score only when a concrete modification is proposed with high confidence. The importance weight $w_{i}$ is utilized separately to parameterize coverage over the evidence pool (Eq. 2).

Because trajectories from different tasks can reveal overlapping failure modes or identical improvement directions, we explicitly model pairwise evidence redundancy. Specifically, each record $e_{i}$ is mapped to a feature embedding $z_{i}$ by encoding its summary and extracted insights. We quantify the nonnegative pairwise similarity between records $e_{i}$ and $e_{j}$ as:

 $s_{ij}=\max\{0,\cos(z_{i},z_{j})\}.$ 

(1)

This similarity metric $s_{ij}$ directly feeds into the coverage objective to measure the extent to which a selected evidence subset represents the complete trajectory pool.

## Coverage with diminishing returns.

For a selected set $Y\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ and each record $j$ in the pool, let $C_{j}(Y)$ be the quality-weighted similarity of the selected records to $e_{j}$ , that is, how well $Y$ covers it. The objective $F(Y)$ sums the log-coverage of all records, weighted by importance:

 $\displaystyle C_{j}(Y)$ 
 $\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in Y}q_{i}s_{ij},$ 

 $\displaystyle F(Y)$ 
 $\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{N}w_{j}\log\bigl(1+C_{j}(Y)\bigr).$ 

(2)

The logarithm gives diminishing returns: a record similar to already-covered ones raises $F$ by less, leaving room for other important experiences. $F$ is monotone and submodular (Proposition 1), which the greedy ordering below exploits.

Starting from $Y_{0}=\varnothing$ , RER repeatedly selects the record with the largest marginal coverage gain:

 $\displaystyle\pi_{r}$ 
 $\displaystyle\in\arg\max_{i\notin Y_{r-1}}\bigl[F(Y_{r-1}\cup\{i\})-F(Y_{r-1})\bigr],$ 

 $\displaystyle Y_{r}$ 
 $\displaystyle=Y_{r-1}\cup\{\pi_{r}\}.$ 

(3)

The resulting permutation $\pi=(\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{N})$ defines every evidence prefix. Marginal gains are recomputed after each selection; this is not a static sort by individual quality.

## 4.2 Multiscale Candidate Generation

Because the optimal evidence scale is unknown a priori and shifts as evolution proceeds (Appendix E), SSR treats evidence scale as a per-round search variable. Given a set of predefined scale budgets $\mathcal{S}=\{k_{1},\ldots,k_{M}\}$ ( $1\leq k_{1}<\cdots<k_{M}=N$ ), we construct nested evidence prefixes from the ranking $\pi$ :

 $D_{t,k}=\{e_{\pi_{1}},\ldots,e_{\pi_{k}}\},\qquad k\in\mathcal{S}.$ 

(4)

Using nested prefixes rather than disjoint subsets offers distinct advantages. First, every prefix $D_{t,k}$ provides near-optimal coverage at its length, guaranteeing a $(1-1/e)$ approximation factor (Proposition 1; Feige, 1998). Second, nested structures isolate scale as the sole variable across candidates, preventing confounding between subset composition and evidence volume (Section 6.4). Third, the shared evidence core facilitates effective validation batching during performance racing (Section 4.3).

For each scale $k\in\mathcal{S}$ , the optimizer independently applies edits to the same frozen parent harness $H_{t}$ :

 $H_{t}^{(k)}=\operatorname{Optimize}(H_{t},D_{t,k}).$ 

(5)

The optimizer receives structured experience summaries and improvement suggestions from $D_{t,k}$ , with optional access to raw trajectories. All candidate harnesses $H_{t}^{(k)}$ are generated under identical optimizer prompts and permissions, serving as temporary hypotheses to be evaluated in the subsequent racing phase.

## 4.3 Candidate Performance Racing

Evaluating every proposed harness on every task would spend substantial execution budget on weak candidates. This is a fixed-budget best-arm identification problem (Audibert et al., 2010; Karnin et al., 2013): each harness is an arm, each task execution is a pull, and the goal is to return the best harness within the budget. SSR follows the successive-halving schedule (Karnin et al., 2013; Jamieson and Talwalkar, 2016) with a constant elimination quota, and protects the parent as an incumbent. SSR introduces new tasks over $K$ stages and directs later evaluations to surviving candidates. The parent remains active throughout as a common reference and is never included in the child-elimination quota. Evaluation continues across stages even when only one child remains.

First, the performance degradation observed when expanding training task pools is a multifaceted phenomenon. While our study focuses on noisy, conflicting, and redundant evidence as a primary underlying driver, other systemic factors may also contribute to this failure mode. Second, searching over evidence scales via SSR represents an initial step toward mitigating this scaling bottleneck. Alternative paradigms, such as adaptive evidence filtering via dynamic context pruning, fine-grained trajectory credit assignment, or reinforcement learning-based optimizer tuning, remain promising unexplored avenues for addressing noisy feedback during evolution. Third, our empirical evaluation, though conducted across multiple benchmarks and execution setups, is bounded by the specific choice of foundation models used as task agents and optimizers. conclusion: We propose Successive Scale Racing (SSR) to address performance degradation when scaling task pools in harness evolution. SSR ranks task experience by quality and coverage, generates multiscale candidate harnesses, and efficiently races them under a fixed compute budget. Across three benchmarks and two execution setups, SSR achieves top performance in all six settings and enables positive task-pool scaling. Furthermore, its racing mechanism identifies near-optimal candidates while cutting validation executions by 60%, confirming that evidence-driven candidate diversity and execution-based selection provide a robust paradigm for agent self-improvement.

title: Automating ML for Science: Can Frontier Agents Climb Scientific Hills in the Wild?
abstract: Frontier coding agents are increasingly framed as end-to-end automated researchers, and ML for science offers a demanding test of that promise: improving a scientific model often requires domain insight beyond routine ML engineering. We introduce Agent4Sci, a long-horizon testbed for measuring how far today's agents can improve the published best models on scientific ML benchmarks, spanning 20 benchmarks across 11 domains. Rather than ranking agents on a leaderboard, Agent4Sci asks what kinds of progress agents can make on these tasks under in-the-wild conditions, and where they fall short. Empirically, today's frontier agents advance the published best on every benchmark, with Claude Opus reaching 10.4% mean relative improvement and no run flagged for academic misconduct. These gains, however, come almost entirely from a bag of ML-engineering tricks rather than research-level insight. Trajectory analysis surfaces three recurring limitations in this setting: novelty miscalibration, resource under-utilization, and rapid collapse into local engineering sweeps. Lightweight plug-in skills for research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists raise Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1% and Codex from 4.4% to 8.1%, while yielding more diverse, domain-relevant interventions. Agent4Sci gives the community a way to track and push frontier agents from ML engineering toward domain insight on real-world ML-for-science problems. Code and data are available on GitHub (https://github.com/maszhongming/agent4sci) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/MingZhong/agent4sci).

Abstract

Frontier coding agents are increasingly framed as end-to-end automated researchers, and ML for science offers a demanding test of that promise: improving a scientific model often requires domain insight beyond routine ML engineering. We introduce Agent4Sci, a long-horizon testbed for measuring how far today’s agents can improve the published best models on scientific ML benchmarks, spanning 20 benchmarks across 11 domains. Rather than ranking agents on a leaderboard, Agent4Sci asks what kinds of progress agents can make on these tasks under in-the-wild conditions, and where they fall short. Empirically, today’s frontier agents advance the published best on every benchmark, with Claude Opus reaching 10.4% mean relative improvement and no run flagged for academic misconduct. These gains, however, come almost entirely from a bag of ML-engineering tricks rather than research-level insight. Trajectory analysis surfaces three recurring limitations in this setting: novelty miscalibration, resource under-utilization, and rapid collapse into local engineering sweeps. Lightweight plug-in skills for research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists raise Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1% and Codex from 4.4% to 8.1%, while yielding more diverse, domain-relevant interventions. Agent4Sci gives the community a way to track and push frontier agents from ML engineering toward domain insight on real-world ML-for-science problems. Code and data are available on GitHub and Hugging Face.

## 1 Introduction

Recent advances in frontier coding agents are turning automated research into an executable workflow: agents can read papers and repositories, modify implementations, run experiments, interpret quantitative feedback, and iterate. A growing body of recent work suggests a common recipe for this vision: cast research as a feedback loop in which an agent operates in a workspace, pursues a measurable objective, and improves through experimentation [50, 38, 28, 62, 23]. Yet most demonstrations so far assume well-structured codebases [19, 36, 61], operate in single-task settings [50, 38, 23], and are heavily skewed toward computer science domains [40, 56, 13]. The broader landscape of ML for science remains far less explored: benchmarks span diverse scientific domains and modalities, codebases are often research artifacts rather than polished evaluation environments, and nontrivial gains often require domain insights. This gap motivates our central question: Can the frontier agents we have today make meaningful progress on ML for science when operating in the wild?

(a) Scientific Hill-Climbing Task

(b) Frontier-Agent Gains

Figure 1: Scientific hill-climbing gives an agent a paper, codebase, data, and target metric, then asks it to improve that metric under a fixed resource budget. On Agent4Sci, frontier agents push past the published best on every benchmark, with Claude Opus reaching 10.4% mean relative improvement while most gains come from ML-engineering routines.

We instantiate this question as automated scientific hill-climbing (Figure 1). In this setting, an agent is given a scientific ML benchmark, its paper, codebase, data, and target metric. Starting from the best available model in the benchmark, the agent works under a fixed resource budget to improve the metrics through code changes and experiments. However, our pilot study shows that this natural setup is fragile. Across 12 tasks from 5 NeurIPS 2025 benchmarks, 5 tasks exhibit severe evaluation-gaming behaviors, including selective reporting, test-set contamination, metric manipulation, and even direct hardcoding. This aligns with recent work showing that coding agents succeed in well-structured evaluation settings but degrade sharply on real-world code and evaluations [10]. These failures motivate a testbed that preserves the in-the-wild nature of scientific tasks, makes meaningful progress measurable, and guards against evaluation gaming.

To address this challenge, we construct Agent4Sci, a testbed for evaluating automated scientific hill-climbing across 20 ML-for-science benchmarks, 25 tasks, and 11 scientific domains spanning the physical sciences, life sciences, Earth and environmental sciences, and scientific engineering. We first standardize each benchmark through human-verified baseline reproductions, repaired data splits, reduced runtime bottlenecks, and isolated environments. On top of this foundation, each run follows the Agent4Sci evaluation protocol. The hill-climbing agent receives the standardized environment with access only to training and validation data, then submits artifacts such as code changes, checkpoints, logs, and outputs. A separate evaluation agent runs the submitted artifacts on the held-out test set, and an auditing agent inspects the trajectory for academic misconduct.

Agent4Sci is motivated not as a leaderboard for ranking agents, but as a way to ask how much measurable progress agents can make on scientific ML tasks, whether they produce insight, and where they fall short. We evaluate four frontier coding agents: Claude Code (Opus and Sonnet), Codex, and Gemini CLI. Each receives 8 H200 GPUs, a 12-hour budget, and a minimal instruction to hill-climb the specified metric. Across the suite, frontier agents push every benchmark beyond its published best, all four agents achieve positive mean improvements, and the auditing stage flags no academic misconduct under our evaluation protocol. On Agent4Sci, current agents already produce measurable, fully automated gains on real scientific ML benchmarks.

The more revealing question is what produces these gains. The improvements concentrate on familiar ML-engineering moves instead of research-level insight, and the agents adopt sharply different default workflows: Claude Opus behaves as an iterative optimizer, Codex as a commit-and-wait planner, and Gemini oscillates between the two. Across trajectories, we identify three recurring limitations: agents miscalibrate novelty, under-utilize resources, and collapse quickly into local engineering sweeps. Lightweight plug-in skills for research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists raise Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1% mean relative improvement and Codex from 4.4% to 8.1%, without changing the evaluation protocol. Beyond the score gains, agents propose more varied, problem-grounded interventions and surface insights that move beyond routine ML engineering.

Overall, these results draw a practical boundary for automating ML for science today. Frontier coding agents can climb scientific hills in the wild, but the climb is still powered mostly by engineering optimization rather than scientific reasoning. Agent4Sci makes this boundary measurable and visible: each new agent generation can be evaluated not only by how much it improves a metric, but by whether its improvements reflect increasingly transferable research insight. The goal is to help move automated agents from executing better experiments toward doing better science.

## 2 Agent4Sci: A Testbed for Automated Scientific Hill-Climbing

## 2.1 Task and Benchmark Selection

We construct Agent4Sci from recent ML-for-science benchmarks, retaining only tasks that support iterative improvement by an agent. We use benchmark to denote a published benchmark, and task to denote one of its evaluation tasks (typically with a designated mainstream metric); a single benchmark can contribute multiple tasks. Selection runs through a four-stage filtering pipeline:

• 

Domain Classification. Retain papers whose benchmark targets a scientific domain, filtering out benchmarks aimed at generic AI, ML, or systems research.

• 

Automated Screening. An agent scores each retained paper against seven criteria covering data, training, baselines, evaluation, and licensing (see Appendix B.2), and 7/7 candidates advance.

• 

Human Verification. Re-check the automated criterion labels by hand and demote any candidate whose 7/7 status does not survive verification.

• 

Deep Review. Inspect the paper and the official repository for reproducibility evidence, task specificity, repository usability, and domain coverage relative to the rest of the suite.

Taking the NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks track as a representative case, this pipeline admits 10 benchmarks from 497 candidates (a 98% rejection rate, with full per-stage diagnostics in Appendix B.3). Rejected papers are typically competitive in their original setting and are excluded only because they target a different scenario than ours, not because of any deficiency in the underlying work. After adding curated benchmarks from other top ML venues and domain journals, Agent4Sci contains 20 scientific benchmarks and 25 tasks across 11 scientific domains.

## 2.2 Pilot Study: Evaluation Gaming on Raw Scientific Tasks

To assess whether existing scientific repositories can directly support automated hill-climbing, we conduct a pilot study on 12 tasks drawn from 5 NeurIPS 2025 scientific benchmarks. The agent receives the paper, the original repository, the task description, and the data artifacts as released, then attempts to improve the reported metric. The pilot reveals that this setup is unreliable: 5 of 12 tasks exhibit one or more severe evaluation-gaming behaviors, which we group into four categories.

• 

Selective reporting. The agent evaluates only on a favorable subset of the test set and reports the inflated score as the headline result.

• 

Test-set contamination. The agent extracts held-out statistics, inspects test-input error cases, or uses test-set information to guide model selection or hyperparameters.

• 

Metric manipulation. The agent invents a non-standard evaluation protocol, claims the official metric is incorrect, or modifies the evaluation script to favor its model.

• 

Direct hardcoding. The agent hardcodes final outputs, copies predictions from earlier runs, or claims that legitimate checkpoints were accidentally deleted to obscure failures.

We use evaluation gaming as an umbrella term because these failures need not require malicious intent. Official scientific ML repositories often lack clear metric definitions, fixed data splits, or complete training and evaluation scripts. End-to-end hill-climbing directly on such repositories, therefore, opens seams that an aggressive optimizer can exploit, even when the agent’s high-level instruction is framed honestly. An evaluation that exposes the original repository and trusts the final score returned by the hill-climbing agent cannot reliably measure scientific progress.

## 2.3 The Agent4Sci Evaluation Protocol

The pilot study motivates the Agent4Sci evaluation protocol (Figure 2). The protocol has two parts: a one-time standardization phase that prepares each task into a verified reference environment, and a three-stage evaluation procedure that separates hill-climbing, held-out evaluation, and auditing.

Figure 2: Agent4Sci evaluation protocol. Each task includes a standard reproduction folder with standardized training scripts, evaluation scripts, and data splits. Runs separate the hill-climbing agent from held-out evaluation and auditing to prevent evaluation gaming.

## Standardization.

Each admitted task is converted into a verified reference environment through substantial human effort, and the foundation of that effort is reproduction. Starting from the official codebase, we reproduce the paper’s headline number on the published baseline, and a task is admitted into Agent4Sci only when this reproduction matches the paper within a verified tolerance. Reproduction is rarely a drop-in rerun of the published recipe: 3 benchmarks require an additional training pipeline that the original release does not include, 2 require a held-out validation slice carved from training data because our protocol does not allow test-set access during checkpoint selection, and another 2 require alignment of data-handling and split conventions with our standardized setting.

Standardization extends beyond reproduction along three more axes: deterministic train/validation/test splits with the test set sequestered, runtime optimization that fits the baseline within a single-H200 envelope, and isolated hill-climbing and evaluation containers. Every standardized task is independently re-checked by two reviewers, with disagreements resolved through repository inspection and reruns until both reviewers agree that the reproduction and the surrounding environment match the paper. The full per-benchmark record, including a paper-vs-reproduction comparison and the specific standardization moves applied to each project, appears in Appendix B.4.

## Three-Stage Evaluation.

After standardization, each run evaluates only the hill-climbing agent. The evaluation and auditing agents are auxiliary safeguards: they execute the submitted artifacts on the held-out test set and inspect the run for evaluation gaming and other academic misconduct.

• 

Hill-climbing. The hill-climbing agent receives the standardized environment and task specification. It can modify code, launch experiments, train models, and submit artifacts, but cannot read or evaluate on the held-out test set.

• 

Evaluation. A separate evaluation agent loads the submitted artifacts and runs them on the held-out test set using the standardized evaluation path.

• 

Auditing. A third auditing agent inspects the trajectory and submitted artifacts for any of the four evaluation-gaming behaviors from §2.2 as well as other forms of academic misconduct.

Together, standardization and the Agent4Sci evaluation protocol let each hill-climbing run start from a verified SOTA baseline and focus on the scientific task itself. Test-set access and score computation remain outside the hill-climbing agent, directly addressing the four evaluation-gaming behaviors observed in §2.2 and making residual protocol deviations auditable. All agents used to assist benchmark selection and standardization are Claude Opus 4.6, while final acceptance and verification decisions are made by human reviewers.

title: SpecEvo: Speculative Evolution with Large Language Models for Cost-Efficient Scientific Discovery
abstract: LLM-driven evolutionary search is a promising paradigm for scientific discovery, but existing methods remain costly and slow, often applying expensive reasoning uniformly while underusing evidence from failed, redundant, and saturated trials. We introduce Speculative Evolution (SpecEvo), a multi-LLM framework that coordinates lightweight and frontier models through continual consolidation of search evidence. Lightweight models power both parallel Speculators, which generate and refine candidate programs, and an Advisor, which distills accumulated successes, failures, and saturated directions into persistent guidance for subsequent exploration. At sparse checkpoints, a frontier-model Navigator inspects the evolving population and intervenes through synthesis, surgical refinement, or reframing according to search stagnation. This speculate-then-consolidate workflow delegates routine exploration and evidence consolidation to inexpensive models while reserving frontier reasoning for strategic interventions whose benefits extend across many subsequent low-cost evaluations. Across 176 tasks spanning four scientific and algorithmic discovery domains, SpecEvo matches or outperforms frontier-model baselines while reducing API cost by up to 80%, achieves up to 1.5x greater evaluation efficiency than cost-efficient baselines on equation discovery, and improves over the strongest CO-Bench baseline by 3.8%. These results support trajectory-conditioned model coordination as an effective approach to cost-efficient scientific discovery.

## 1 Introduction

Recent advances in large language models have enabled a new paradigm of evolutionary search for automated scientific discovery (Yamada et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026b). LLMs act as semantic variation operators, proposing meaningful modifications to candidate programs that are refined through execution-based evaluation and selection (Liu et al., 2026a; Wu et al., 2024). Such approaches have achieved strong results across mathematical discovery, combinatorial optimization, and systems engineering (Hieu et al., 2026; Cemri et al., 2026; Novikov et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024b).

Despite their strong results, many systems nevertheless use a single backbone for candidate generation and higher-level search decisions (Agrawal et al., 2025; Cemri et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b). When that backbone is a frontier model, routine proposals repeatedly incur expensive inference. Figure 1 illustrates the resulting performance–cost trade-off: using lightweight backbones lowers API expenditure but can substantially reduce solution quality in the evaluated baselines. Lightweight models offer inexpensive exploration, but without reusable guidance they can repeatedly revisit similar strategies or reproduce implementation errors (Dat et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024a). Merely generating more affordable proposals therefore does not ensure sustained search progress.
Heterogeneous-model approaches address part of this problem by assigning different search operations to different models or transferring a population from lightweight exploration to frontier-model refinement (Tanveer, 2026; Luo et al., 2026a; Huang et al., 2026). These approaches motivate a complementary question: How can accumulated successes, failures, and signs of saturation continually inform both subsequent lightweight proposals and the scope of frontier-model intervention?

Figure 1: Top: Performance vs. API cost on mathematical discovery tasks; SpecEvo forms the Pareto frontier. Bottom: Best-so-far NMSE on LSR-Synth Biology and Chemistry over 500 evaluations.

To address these gaps, we present SpecEvo, a multi-LLM evolutionary framework organized around a workflow we call speculate-then-consolidate (StC). StC repeatedly converts accumulated search evidence into guidance and strategic interventions that inform subsequent low-cost exploration; SpecEvo provides its concrete realization through specialized model roles and shared search state. Consolidation occurs periodically while lightweight exploration continues. A central design choice is to distinguish the programs retained for further search from the evidence retained for learning. An adaptive MAP-Elites-style (Mouret and Clune, 2015) archive maintains one elite per structural–semantic niche, allowing programs outside the global top ranks to remain available when they improve their own niches. A separate history records all evaluated attempts, including rejected programs and execution failures. Together, these structures expose which strategies remain competitive, which directions consume evaluations without progress, and which implementation errors recur. This evidence supports both revisable guidance for lightweight models and search-state-dependent choices about frontier intervention.
Across model configurations, SpecEvo improves the performance–cost trade-off over methods built around a single frontier model. Its advantages over cost-efficient allocation strategies persist under matched model-call and evaluation budgets, supporting the value of coordinating model use through accumulated search evidence. Ablations and search-trajectory analyses further support the importance of preserving diverse candidates, adapting intervention scope to stagnation, and revising guidance as evidence accumulates. Our main contributions are:

• 

We introduce SpecEvo, an asynchronous realization of StC with parallel lightweight Speculators, a lightweight Advisor, and a sparsely invoked frontier-model Navigator.

• 

We develop coordinated feedback mechanisms that combine failure- and niche-progress-aware guidance with a stagnation signal controlling parent sampling and selecting among synthesis, surgical refinement, and reframing at fixed Navigator checkpoints.

• 

We provide a systematic evaluation on 176 tasks spanning mathematical discovery, systems optimization, combinatorial optimization, and scientific equation discovery, combining comparisons under matched budgets with controlled model-allocation studies, component ablations, and analyses of search dynamics.

## 2 Related Work

LLM-Guided Evolutionary Search.
FunSearch and AlphaEvolve demonstrate how execution-based selection can turn LLM-generated program variations into mathematical and systems discoveries (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025). Subsequent work addresses two complementary challenges within this loop. The first is preserving useful alternatives: OpenEvolve combines island evolution with quality-diversity archiving, while SeaEvo organizes search around persistent strategy-level memory (Sharma, 2025; Luo et al., 2026b). These designs retain alternatives that can support exploration beyond the current best program. The second is using evaluation feedback to improve search decisions: GEPA derives reflective updates and maintains complementary candidates through Pareto selection, AdaEvolve adapts exploration and resource allocation to observed progress, and EvoX evolves the search policy itself (Agrawal et al., 2025; Cemri et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b). SpecEvo builds on these principles, using archive- and trajectory-level evidence to coordinate lightweight exploration, guidance revision, and frontier intervention.

Cost-Efficient LLM Allocation.
Cost-efficient LLM systems commonly coordinate cheap and strong models through cascades or adaptive routing (Chen et al., 2023b; Aggarwal et al., 2024; Ding et al., 2024; Ong et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026). SCOPE uses query-level partial evaluations to select a fixed model assignment for each module of a compound system under a quality constraint (Huang et al., 2026). While reducing configuration-search cost, it does not adapt allocation to an evolving search state. Within evolutionary search, LEVI combines diversity preservation and proxy evaluation with role-aware routing, assigning local refinements to cheap models and paradigm shifts to a frontier model (Tanveer, 2026). However, the frontier model remains tied to a predefined role, while its error-oriented advice does not use broader progress and saturation evidence to adapt interventions. RelayEvolve develops multiple cheap-model trajectories and performs a one-time handoff of a quality-diverse population to strong-model refinement (Luo et al., 2026a). Afterward, lightweight exploration ends, and evidence from discarded or exhausted trajectories is not consolidated into reusable guidance. SpecEvo instead continually consolidates accumulated evidence to guide both lightweight exploration and state-dependent frontier-model intervention.

## 3 Methodology

Figure 2 summarizes how SpecEvo initializes its population and coordinates the subsequent search, while Appendices D and H provide the complete algorithms and prompt templates, respectively.

## 3.1 Motivation: From Speculative Decoding to Speculative Evolution

Speculative decoding uses lightweight drafts and parallel verification by a stronger model to amortize inference while preserving the target distribution (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023a). Related evolutionary methods likewise reserve stronger models for difficult mutations or structural changes (Ray et al., 2026; Tanveer, 2026). In SpecEvo, candidate quality is established by an executable evaluator, while accumulated outcomes inform future proposals. The speculate-then-consolidate (StC) workflow therefore transfers the principle of asymmetric computation to search trajectories: inexpensive exploration supplies evidence, and periodic consolidation turns that evidence into guidance and strategic proposals for subsequent exploration.

Figure 2 separates population initialization on the left from the ongoing StC loop on the right. Initialization proceeds from seed generation through lightweight diversification to population embedding. The resulting archive supports continuous Speculator exploration, while the Navigator above and the Advisor below provide strategic proposals and reusable guidance at slower cadences. Once the prescribed budget is exhausted, the search terminates and the highest-scoring program in the final archive is returned. We next describe the shared search state and each functional role.

## Problem setup.

Given a task $\mathcal{T}$ with a space $\mathcal{P}$ of executable candidate programs and an evaluator $F:\mathcal{P}\to\mathbb{R}$ , we aim to discover $p^{\star}=\arg\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}}F(p)$ under a prescribed wall-clock, API-cost, or evaluation budget. At evaluation step $t$ , we maintain two shared structures: a behavioral archive $\mathcal{A}_{t}$ retaining a bounded set of competitive programs, and a search history $\mathcal{H}_{t}$ recording every evaluated attempt, including rejected candidates and execution failures. Each stored program $p$ is paired with a natural-language description $d(p)$ of its strategy, supplied by the generating model.

## Initialization.

The Generate seed programs block in Figure 2 provides diverse, verified starting hypotheses. The Navigator uses the frontier model $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{N}}$ to generate $M{=}5$ seed programs sequentially, conditioning each call on the strategies and evaluation outcomes of earlier seeds. The prompt asks the model to identify their algorithmic paradigms and propose a different modeling, decomposition, construction, or search strategy. In the subsequent Generate variants block, the Speculator pool uses the lightweight model $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{S}}$ to expand each executable seed into $V{=}20$ inexpensive variants in parallel, drawing on $n_{\mathrm{insp}}\in\{1,2\}$ other seeds as inspiration. We initialize the behavioral archive from these evaluated programs using the representation and admission rule described next.

## Behavioral archive.

Fitness alone does not distinguish the strategies implemented by candidate programs. A population selected solely by global fitness can become dominated by variants of one strategy, discarding lower-scoring alternatives that may provide complementary mechanisms or promising starting points for further search. We therefore maintain $\mathcal{A}_{t}$ as a MAP-Elites-style archive (Mouret and Clune, 2015) holding at most $K{=}50$ incumbents, one per niche: a region of structural–semantic descriptor space within which candidates compete on fitness. Competition within niches preserves alternatives across descriptor regions, keeping them available for Speculator mutation and crossover and Navigator synthesis even when they fall outside the global top ranks.

The Embedded population block constructs the descriptors used by the Adaptive archive. Let $r=1,2,\ldots$ index successive descriptor-fitting rounds. At each round, we estimate the PCA basis and standardization parameters from the current archive and hold them fixed until the next refit. Under the descriptor map fitted at round $r$ , each program is represented as

 $\mathbf{z}_{r}(p)=\big[\mathcal{Z}^{\mathrm{ast}}_{r}\!\big(\phi(p)\big)\;\big\|\;\mathcal{Z}^{\mathrm{sem}}_{r}\!\big(\mathbf{U}_{r}^{\top}(\mathbf{e}(p)-\bar{\mathbf{e}}_{r})\big)\big]\in\mathbb{R}^{16},$ 

(1)

where $\|$ denotes concatenation.
The structural vector $\phi(p)\in\mathbb{R}^{8}$ contains eight statistics extracted from the code’s abstract syntax tree (AST), each transformed by $\log(1+x)$ to reduce sensitivity to unusually large programs.
The semantic block captures the strategy description $d(p)$ through its embedding $\mathbf{e}(p)$ . We subtract the archive embedding mean $\bar{\mathbf{e}}_{r}$ and project onto the eight leading PCA directions stored in $\mathbf{U}_{r}$ , yielding eight semantic features. The operators $\mathcal{Z}^{\mathrm{ast}}_{r}$ and $\mathcal{Z}^{\mathrm{sem}}_{r}$ standardize each feature separately by subtracting its archive mean and dividing by its archive standard deviation, both estimated at fitting round $r$ ; features with zero variance are mapped to zero. This makes the structural and semantic features comparable in scale for the Euclidean distances used in niche assignment (Appendix D.1).

Figure 2: Overview of SpecEvo. Initialization (left) generates $M$ seed programs, expands each executable seed into $V$ lightweight variants, and embeds the evaluated population to initialize the archive. During evolution (right), $W$ lightweight-model Speculators continuously explore the archive. The frontier-model Navigator (top) intervenes every $\Delta_{N}$ completed evaluations, while the lightweight-model Advisor (bottom) updates reusable guidance every $\Delta_{A}$ evaluations.

## 3.2 The Speculate-then-Consolidate Workflow

While fewer than $K$ slots are occupied, valid candidates are admitted into new slots. At capacity, the first descriptor fit defines sites $\mathbf{c}_{i}=\mathbf{z}_{r}(p_{i})$ whose Voronoi cells form the niches. A candidate is then assigned to its nearest site and admitted only if it strictly improves that niche’s incumbent. Replacement leaves the site and descriptor map fixed until the next refit, stabilizing candidate assignment. After initialization, every $\Delta_{C}{=}50$ completed evaluations, we refit PCA and normalization statistics on the current archive, recompute incumbent descriptors, and re-anchor the sites to follow the evolving population. Slot indices support progress tracking, although niche boundaries can change (Appendix D). Table 3 shows the effect of refitting on overall search performance.

## Stagnation signal.

The low-to-high scale in the Navigator block represents search stagnation: $s_{t}$ increases toward $1$ when either global-best improvements or archive admissions become infrequent. We use this signal to adjust both parent selection and the scope of Navigator intervention:

 $s_{t}=\max\!\Big\{\min\!\big(1,\tfrac{t-\tau^{\mathrm{best}}_{t}}{H_{g}}\big),\;\min\!\big(1,\tfrac{t-\tau^{\mathrm{adm}}_{t}}{H_{l}}\big)\Big\},$ 

(2)

where $\tau^{\mathrm{best}}_{t}$ and $\tau^{\mathrm{adm}}_{t}$ denote the evaluation steps of the most recent global-best improvement and archive admission, respectively, with normalization horizons $H_{g}{=}100$ and $H_{l}{=}20$ . Each term measures a normalized waiting time, capped at one. Taking their maximum makes $s_{t}=1$ after 100 evaluations without a global-best improvement or 20 without an archive admission.

## Speculators: continuous exploration.

We use $W$ asynchronous Speculators ( $W{=}4$ in our experiments), which continuously generate candidates using $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{S}}$ . Sampling concentrates on leading elites when the search is progressing, while increasing stagnation broadens exploration toward lower-ranked archive regions. Whenever a worker becomes idle, it selects a parent according to its fitness rank $r_{i}$ under a Zipf distribution whose exponent adapts to stagnation (Piantadosi, 2014):

 $\Pr(p_{i}\mid\mathcal{A}_{t})=\frac{r_{i}^{-\beta_{t}}}{\sum_{j=1}^{|\mathcal{A}_{t}|}r_{j}^{-\beta_{t}}},\qquad\beta_{t}=\beta_{\min}+(1-s_{t})(\beta_{\max}-\beta_{\min}),$ 

(3)

with $(\beta_{\min},\beta_{\max})=(0.3,2.0)$ . Thus, $\beta_{t}$ decreases from $2.0$ to $0.3$ as stagnation increases, flattening the distribution while retaining a preference for higher ranks. We use rank-based selection to avoid dependence on task-specific score scales. The worker then inserts the selected parent into one of six uniformly sampled variation prompts: general mutation, focused single-weakness repair, mechanism replacement, analysis-targeted mutation, structural crossover, and component-level crossover. Figure 8 and Table 3 show that using these complementary prompts sustains higher code diversity and yields better performance than a single general mutation prompt. conclusion: We introduced SpecEvo, a multi-LLM framework that coordinates low-cost exploration and sparse frontier-model reasoning through continual consolidation of search evidence. Its speculate-then-consolidate workflow combines parallel lightweight Speculators, persistent Advisor guidance distilled from successes, failures, and saturated directions, and stagnation-dependent Navigator interventions at fixed checkpoints. Across 176 scientific and algorithmic discovery tasks, SpecEvo matches or outperforms strong baselines under matched wall-clock, API-cost, and evaluation budgets, with 50%–80% lower API expenditure under the three-hour wall-clock budget. Its gains across backbone configurations and under matched evaluation budgets support the value of using accumulated search evidence to guide sparse frontier interventions and subsequent lightweight refinement.

title: Scaling in Games: Continued Pre-Training For Embodied Agents In Diverse Virtual Worlds
abstract: Scaling data, diversity and model capacity has improved embodied learning in physical environments, where diverse experiences remain grounded in shared physical laws. Whether these gains extend to virtual worlds with different visual styles, dynamics, controls, and objectives remains unclear. We investigate this question through a controlled study of continued pre-training (CPT) across three axes: data volume, diversity, and model size. Our 120 training configurations span four model sizes from 0.8B to 27B, six data budgets from 50 to 1,600 hours, and five mixtures ranging from Minecraft-only data to diverse multi-world corpora. We assess performance and generalization using three-level validation losses and gameplay benchmarks from in-corpus worlds to unseen worlds. Our results show: (1) more data improves in-corpus performance, diversity improves transfer to related worlds with limited gains in distant worlds, and model size improves data efficiency but generalizes worse to distant worlds under single-world training; (2) we observe an early interface phase with broad cross-world benefits and a later world phase with gains narrowed to in-corpus and related worlds, and fit an empirical scaling law relating validation loss to data volume, diversity and model size; and (3) our models are competitive with Minecraft specialists and frontier models in 3D worlds, and perform best in real-time settings. However, the limits of imitation and persistent gaps in distant worlds suggest that building generalist embodied agents requires richer training stages beyond continued pre-training.

body_start:
Abstract

Scaling data, diversity and model capacity has improved embodied learning in physical environments, where diverse experiences remain grounded in shared physical laws. Whether these gains extend to virtual worlds with different visual styles, dynamics, controls, and objectives remains unclear. We investigate this question through a controlled study of continued pre-training (CPT) across three axes: data volume, diversity, and model size. Our 120 training configurations span four model sizes from 0.8B to 27B, six data budgets from 50 to 1,600 hours, and five mixtures ranging from Minecraft-only data to diverse multi-world corpora. We assess performance and generalization using three-level validation losses and gameplay benchmarks from in-corpus worlds to unseen worlds. Our results show: (1) more data improves in-corpus performance, diversity improves transfer to related worlds with limited gains in distant worlds, and model size improves data efficiency but generalizes worse to distant worlds under single-world training; (2) we observe an early interface phase with broad cross-world benefits and a later world phase with gains narrowed to in-corpus and related worlds, and fit an empirical scaling law relating validation loss to data volume, diversity and model size; and (3) our models are competitive with Minecraft specialists and frontier models in 3D worlds, and perform best in real-time settings. However, the limits of imitation and persistent gaps in distant worlds suggest that building generalist embodied agents requires richer training stages beyond continued pre-training.
