## 1 Introduction

Embodied agents are expected to perceive, reason, and act across changing environments. Recent scaling studies in robotics suggest that broader experience can improve such generality (Lin et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026a; Abe et al., 2026). Real-world scenes share one coherent physical reality, i.e., gravity, contact, and object permanence remain consistent, and the physical effect of an embodiment’s controls changes relatively little across tasks. This shared structure makes experience collected in one setting potentially reusable in another.

In Figure 1, virtual worlds remove much of this consistency. Different worlds may vary simultaneously in entirely different visuals, rules, physics, action spaces and goals (Wang et al., 2025b; Tan et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b). Humans adapt to the heterogeneity quickly: they easily figure out unfamiliar rules, adjust to different controls, and apply past experience to new visuals and mechanics. A generalist virtual embodied agent should exhibit the same ability. Interactive video games provide a diverse and controlled subset of such worlds, making them a particularly demanding test of embodied generality (Abi Raad et al., 2024; SIMA Team, 2025; Zhang et al., 2026a).

Figure 1: One physical world versus diverse virtual worlds.
Left: Agents learn from varied physical scenes sharing common dynamics, where they can scale and generalize with broader experience (Wang et al., 2026a).
Right: Agents play diverse games with varying dynamics. We want to investigate the question that whether continued pre-training scales and generalizes in virtual worlds.

Recent work studies this broader goal by training models to perceive visual input from games and output native keyboard–mouse controls across different virtual game worlds (Baker et al., 2022; Magne et al., 2026; Yue et al., 2026). Across these systems, continued pre-training (CPT) on gameplay trajectories has become a common stage for generalist embodied intelligence (Abi Raad et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025b; SIMA Team, 2025; Tan et al., 2025). However, virtual embodied continued pre-training remains largely a recipe: existing studies change the data volume, diversity and models together, leaving the effect of each factor unresolved. Most importantly, it remains unclear whether heterogeneous experiences help to build embodied agents that can generalize across different worlds, or if it just causes interference that ruins what they learned in any individual worlds.

We address this question with a controlled grid study spanning four model sizes from 0.8B to 27B, six data budgets from 50 to 1,600 hours, and five data mixture settings from Minecraft-only to broad multi-game corpora. The resulting 120 configurations are evaluated through three-level validation loss and benchmark ladders from in-corpus worlds, such as Minecraft (Zheng et al., 2025) and Doom (Wydmuch et al., 2019), to unseen near and distant worlds, such as OmniGameArena (Lin et al., 2026), and GameWorld (Ouyang et al., 2026). Our study reveals how data volume, mixture diversity, and model capacity affect embodied agents in these three levels of worlds, and whether heterogeneous experience becomes complementary as it scales.

Our contributions are mainly three-fold:

• 

A controlled study of scaling CPT in virtual worlds.
We quantify how data volume, mixture diversity, and model size affect CPT of generalist embodied agents in virtual worlds.
More relevant data improves performance on in-corpus worlds where model performance multiplies in Minecraft. Diversity improves transfer to related worlds but provides limited gains in distant worlds. Larger models improve data efficiency and achieve larger early gains, while generalizing worse under single-game training.

• 

An empirical two-phase learning dynamics and scaling law.
We observe an empirical early interface phase: model learns basic self-control and action primitives, which are shared and improved across worlds; and a world phase then follows: further gains are obtained in trained and unseen related worlds.
We fit an empirical scaling law to relate validation loss to data volume, mixture diversity and model size, achieving $R^{2}=0.982$ and $R^{2}=0.995$ on Minecraft and in-corpus loss, respectively.

• 

Three-level evaluation of model performance and generalization.
We evaluate models in a three-level setting covering in-corpus, related, and distant worlds. This anchors our models among game and general foundation models, providing the community a reliable reference. Our models are competitive with Minecraft specialists and frontier models in 3D worlds, and outperform frontier models in real-time settings by up to $5\times$ .

## 2 Related Work

Virtual Embodied Models. Early models were trained as environment-specific specialists. Deep reinforcement learning achieved superhuman performance in Atari, Go, StarCraft II, and Dota 2 while relying on a fixed environment, objective, and action interface (Mnih et al., 2015; Silver et al., 2016; Vinyals et al., 2019; OpenAI et al., 2019). Recent work instead focuses on large foundation models. VPT learns a Minecraft control prior from internet video, while NitroGen and OpenP2P extend pixel-to-action learning across broader game corpus (Baker et al., 2022; Magne et al., 2026; Yue et al., 2026). LLM and VLM based agents further reuse pre-trained language and visual knowledge for instruction following, planning and control (Abi Raad et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b; Tan et al., 2025; SIMA Team, 2025). Across these approaches, CPT has become a common mechanism for turning a general backbone into an interactive model for virtual embodied agents. To our knowledge, we conduct the largest controlled CPT study of virtual embodied models.

Virtual Worlds as Test Environments. Games provide a controllable subset of virtual worlds for evaluating perception, reasoning, and action under diverse rules and dynamics (Ouyang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a; Wang et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026b). Minecraft and Doom suites measure capabilities within a familiar in-corpus world (Wydmuch et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2025); OmniGameArena tests transfer to unseen 3D worlds (Lin et al., 2026); and GameWorld extends evaluation to visually and mechanically distinct 2D, 2.5D, and 3D environments (Ouyang et al., 2026). Training in one kind of virtual worlds may transfer to others, but there is no previous study to investigate which factor is critical to the transfer.

Scalability of Continued Pre-training. Classical scaling laws relate model performance to capacity, data, and compute, while studies of domain-adaptive and repeated pre-training show that source composition can alter both adaptation and retention (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022; Que et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2026). Related evidence appears in computer-use and embodied learning: GUI studies find that task composition can matter as much as sample count (Liu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025; Raoof et al., 2026), and robotic imitation studies report diversity scaling, negative transfer, and capacity-dependent interference (Lin et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026a; Abe et al., 2026). Virtual worlds sharpen this problem because visual style, dynamics, controls, and objectives change across sources. Existing research on CPT in virtual worlds alters model size, training data, and duration simultaneously. No prior work systematically isolates these three axes while measuring held-out loss and transfer capabilities at varying distances from training.

## 3 Preliminaries and Experiment Framework

## 3.1 Data construction

Figure 2: Adaptation to the keyboard–mouse interface during CPT. Smoothed training losses for key, mouse, and format tokens, and eight-direction mouse prediction accuracy for three model capacities trained on mixtures S1 and S4.

Gameplay trajectories.
Following the setting in previous works (Wang et al., 2025b; Tan et al., 2025; SIMA Team, 2025; Lin et al., 2026), we formulate gameplay as visual decision-making process. At step $t$ , the model takes prompt context $c$ , the current observation $o_{t}$ , and interaction history $\mathcal{H}_{t}$ as the input $x_{t}$ and produces a reasoning trace $r_{t}$ and then an executable action $a_{t}$ :

 $r_{t}\sim p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{t}),\qquad a_{t}\sim p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{t},r_{t}),\qquad x_{t}=(c,o_{t},\mathcal{H}_{t}).$ 

(1)

Reasoning and action have distinct roles. The possibly empty $r_{t}$ is internal textual reasoning. The mandatory $a_{t}$ is structured text chunks that are parsed into low-level device commands, which further changes the environment. Each chunk covers 200 ms (Tan et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2026):

 $a_{t}=\texttt{<|action\_start|>}~\Delta x_{t}~\Delta y_{t}~\Delta z_{t};K_{t}^{(1)};\ldots;K_{t}^{(6)}~\texttt{<|action\_end|>},$ 

(2)

where $(\Delta x_{t},\Delta y_{t})\in[-1000,1000]^{2}$ are discretized relative mouse moves, $\Delta z_{t}\in[-5,5]$ is the scroll delta, and each $K_{t}^{(j)}$ contains 0-4 keys or mouse buttons held for 33 ms. The model receives observations at 5 Hz and controls at 30 Hz. History is modeled as interleaved image–action turns. Each trajectory has 20 turns. During training, preceding think and action are visible to later turns.

Three scaling axes.
Our study evaluates a $4\times 6\times 5=120$ configuration grid across four Qwen3.5 backbones $\mathcal{M}=\{\text{0.8B},\text{2B},\text{9B},\text{27B}\}$ (Qwen Team, 2026), six data budgets $\mathcal{T}=\{50,100,200,400,800,1600\}$ , and five data-diversity mixtures $\mathcal{S}=\{\mathrm{S1},\ldots,\mathrm{S5}\}$ . This yields total $3.5\times 10^{11}$ training tokens and $2.2\times 10^{22}$ FLOPs via the “ $6ND$ rule” (Hoffmann et al., 2022).

Data diversity mixtures.
Our training data consists of two components: (1) 85% gameplay trajectories sampled from VPT, D2E, and OpenP2P (Baker et al., 2022; Choi et al., 2025; Yue et al., 2026), and (2) 15% general data covering vision–language, embodied and egocentric settings (Li et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2026; Tong et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026c; Yang et al., 2026). We construct five data mixtures ( $\mathrm{S1}$ – $\mathrm{S5}$ ) with increasing mixture diversity by setting the Minecraft trajectory proportion in the gameplay data to 100%, 51.4%, 27.1%, 2.8%, and 0%, respectively. The remaining trajectories are sampled from a diverse pool of other games. We also augment a small fraction of gameplay turns with retrospective reasoning generated by GPT-5.6-Luna (OpenAI, 2026) based on the recorded observation and action, to preserve the backbone’s native reasoning capabilities without altering action targets. See Appendices A.1 and A.2 for further details about scaling on mixture diversity.

## 3.2 Training and Evaluation

Training objective and validation sets.
All models are continued pre-trained using a causal next-token prediction loss over assistant responses conditioned on interleaved histories. All parameters, including those of the ViT, are updated using AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) with a Warmup–Stable–Decay schedule (Hu et al., 2024). The resulting models are evaluated on three levels of validation data: Minecraft-only data, data from in-corpus games covered during training, and data from unseen games not covered in training. We also record key, mouse, and format losses. Apart from data volume, data diversity, and the choice of base model, all experimental settings are held fixed across training configurations. See Appendix A.4 for further details.

Three-level gameplay evaluation.
We evaluate gameplay competence across three categories of virtual worlds that are increasing distant from the training distribution. (1) In-corpus worlds: we use the MCU benchmark (Zheng et al., 2025) to evaluate performance on multiple tasks in Minecraft, and ViZDoom (Wydmuch et al., 2019) to evaluate performance on single shooting tasks in DOOM. Both games are covered in our training corpus. (2) Unseen related worlds: we evaluate our model in OmniGameArena (OGA) (Lin et al., 2026), which consists of seven unseen 3D worlds. Although their scenes and tasks are absent from training, action primitives such as navigation, aiming, jumping, shooting, and interaction have semantic counterparts in the training corpus. (3) Unseen distant world: we evaluate our model in GameWorld (GW) (Ouyang et al., 2026), which primarily covers 2D and 2.5D games, alongside a small portion of 3D games. These games differ substantially from the training data in visual styles, physics, controls and objectives.

## 4 Scaling and Generalization in Heterogeneous Virtual Worlds

We investigate how three scaling axes: data volume, data diversity, and model size, affect performance and generalization across all 120 configurations. Figure 2 illustrates the action component losses. Figure 3 presents the three-level training and validation losses alongside our scaling law predictions. Figure 4 details benchmark evaluations. The next three subsections concentrate on each axis and the last subsection derives an empirical scaling law that unifies them.

Figure 3: Loss scaling across data volume, model size and data diversity. Rows report the smoothed training loss and three-level validation loss. Columns 1–4 denote the 0.8B-27B backbones; colors denote the training mixtures S1–S5; markers denote the six checkpoints from 50 to 1,600 hours. The base model loss is annotated in each validation panel. All plots in a given row shares a common y-axis scale. Column 5 plots the loss predicted by the fitted scaling law (Section 4.4) against the observed loss.

Figure 4: Benchmark performance across data budget, model size and data diversity. Rows report MCU, ViZDoom, OmniGameArena, and GameWorld performance. Columns denote the six checkpoints from 50 to 1,600 hours. Colors denote S1-S5 and the base-model reference, while each curve spans the 0.8B-27B backbones. All plots in a given row shares a common y-axis scale.

## 4.1 Data Scaling

Early training brings broad cross-world gains.
Figure 2 shows the training loss of key, mouse, and format tokens. These losses drop rapidly during the initial tens of hours of training data before tapering into a more gradual decrease. Mouse direction prediction accuracy continues to improve. After exposure to 50 hours of training data, validation losses drop below those of the base models on all three validation sets (Figure 3), even for games absent from the training mixture. We refer to this early stage as the interface phase. This cross world improvement indicates that the model gradually acquires shared formats, representations and action patterns that can transfer across games.

Later gains depend more on the worlds seen during training.
After the interface phase, further performance gains depend heavily on exposure to relevant game worlds. We term this stage the world phase. From 50 to 1,600 hours, the mean Minecraft validation loss decreases by about 10.4% across four model sizes under the MineCraft-heavy mixtures S1–S3, correlating with substantial gains in MCU performance (Figure 3). Conversely, scaling total data volume without sufficient Minecraft trajectories yields negligible further reduction in this specific validation loss. For the in-corpus validation set, diverse multi-game training consistently reduces loss across all model sizes, whereas Minecraft-only training causes the loss to plateau or even increase. Similarly, out-of-distribution (OOD) loss stagnates or rises, although it remains below base model levels. At the largest model size, GameWorld performance degrades across all five mixtures as data volume increases. Thus, more data improves performance on in-corpus and related environments, but fails to drive continued gains in distant worlds.

## 4.2 Diversity Scaling

The best training mixture depends on the evaluation set.
Across all 24 configurations of model size and data volume, Minecraft validation loss is lowest with S1, whereas in-corpus loss is minimized with S3 or S4 (Figure 3). Increasing

title: A Small Model Asks Better: Fine-Tuning Query Clarification for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Query clarification is essential for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems that face ambiguous user queries. We consider multi-turn grounded conversational scenarios where a user query is either ill-formed or ambiguous in the context of the prior dialog or, more interestingly, it may be well-formed but when posed against retrieved documents there are multiple relevant interpretations. The task is to recognize both such cases and then generate an appropriate clarification request to the user. We present ClariEdge, a new dataset of approximately 3,900 examples that include such ambiguous queries along with negative examples that do not require clarification. We also show that a lightweight fine-tuned LoRA achieves 96.6% classification accuracy and outperforms prompted baselines of many larger models on both classification and quality of clarification generation. Our study shows that hard negatives are an essential ingredient to separate out queries that are truly ambiguous from queries that may look ambiguous but are not (i.e., can be resolved from the context). The same LoRA achieves high performance in both pre-retrieval and post-retrieval scenarios; thus, it can be used in two places in a RAG pipeline as a check before answer generation. The ClariEdge dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ibm-research/ClariEdge.

body_start:
Abstract

Query clarification is essential for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems
that face ambiguous user queries.
We consider multi-turn grounded conversational scenarios where
a user query is either ill-formed or ambiguous in the context of the prior dialog or,
more interestingly, it may be well-formed but when posed against retrieved documents there
are multiple relevant interpretations. The task is to recognize
both such cases and then generate an appropriate clarification request to the user.
We present ClariEdge, a new dataset of approximately 3,900 examples
that include such ambiguous queries along with negative examples that
do not require clarification.
We also show that a lightweight fine-tuned LoRA achieves
96.6% classification accuracy and outperforms prompted baselines of many larger models on
both classification and quality of clarification generation.
Our study shows that hard negatives
are an essential ingredient
to separate out queries that are truly ambiguous from queries that
may look ambiguous but are not (i.e., can be resolved from the context).
The same LoRA achieves high performance in both pre-retrieval and post-retrieval
scenarios; thus, it can be used in two places in a RAG pipeline as a check before
answer generation.
The ClariEdge dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ibm-research/ClariEdge.

## 1 Introduction

Ambiguity in user queries can come in two distinct forms. The first is the
ill-formed query, where the user mentions an entity or attribute that the
conversation has not narrowed down to a single choice. Figure 1(a)
shows such a case: after the assistant has surfaced two credit cards, the user
asks “What are the potential rewards of this credit card?” The system
must decide whether to attempt an answer under uncertainty or ask which card the
user means; a useful clarification lists the candidates already on the table
(a pattern we call hedging over list).

U: I’m applying for a credit card for personal travel and business expenses. What would you suggest?

A: Two strong options: (1) Gold Card — travel rewards and lounge access; (2) Business Card — cashback on office expenses.

U: What are the rewards of this credit card?

A: Which credit card are you asking about: the Gold Card or the Business Card?

(a) Ill-formed query: “this credit card” has multiple referents in the conversation. Clarification lists the candidates (hedging over list).

U: Is the language that descended from Common Brittonic still spoken today, or has it become extinct?

Retrieved: passages on Welsh, Breton, and Cornish as descendants of Common Brittonic.

A: Several languages descended from Common Brittonic: Welsh, still widely spoken in Wales; Breton, still spoken in Brittany; and Cornish, extinct in the 19th century but since revitalized. Which one are you referring to?

(b) Well-formed query: user thinks there is only one choice, but the retrieved corpus shows several. Clarification pairs each option with a brief grounded answer (hedging with answers).

Figure 1: Ambiguity forms in conversational RAG. Ambiguous user query and clarification response are highlighted.

The second form arises when the query is well-formed in
isolation but becomes ambiguous once grounded in a set of retrieved
documents. In Figure 1(b), the user asks whether
“the language that descended from Common Brittonic” is still spoken, a question that sounds well-defined - but the retrieved passages surface several possible descendants (Welsh, Breton, Cornish). In retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) (Rosenthal et al., 2026), this is a common occurrence, and a useful clarification should both flag the ambiguity and also
enumerate the grounded options with a brief answer for each (hedging with
answers). The quality of clarification, that is,
naming the right options and choosing the pattern of communication
(see Table 7 for details)
matters as much as the
decision of whether to clarify at all. Both use cases - ambiguity before retrieval, and after - can occur in the same deployment.
Therefore we need a unified clarification functionality that handles both, usable before retrieval, based only on the conversation
(Cao et al., 2025; Sahay et al., 2025), and after retrieval, when documents become available
(Kim et al., 2023).

Existing benchmarks address only one slice of this picture. CLAMBER
(Zhang et al., 2024) evaluates ambiguity detection on standalone questions (no conversational context, no retrieved documents) and finds that
chain-of-thought and few-shot prompting yield only marginal gains over a base
classifier. AmbigQA (Min et al., 2020) grounds ambiguity in a corpus, but
treats a question as ambiguous whenever retrieval surfaces multiple atomic
factual answers, even when they are part of the same larger answer. This is a
notion that current conversational LLMs largely subsume by responding with
a composite answer that includes the atomic facts: for example, ‘‘Who took control of the Italian government in 1922?’’11
 1

 This question, along with many similar ones, comes from the AmbigQA dataset and is considered ambiguous there.
yields “Benito Mussolini” and “the Fascists” in one response –
so the AmbigQA ambiguity rarely surfaces as a clarification need.
Neither CLAMBER nor AmbigQA capture the joint conversation-plus-corpus setting
that real RAG deployments face.

Problem Statement.

Given a multi-turn conversation between a user and an
AI assistant, together with optionally retrieved documents for the last user turn, our goal is to determine
whether the user’s last turn is ambiguous, that is, whether it admits either no
clear interpretation or multiple valid interpretations. When it is ambiguous,
the system should generate a clarification request that elicits additional information from the user.

Towards addressing this problem, we make the following specific contributions:

1. ClariEdge: Clarification Grounded Dataset with Hard Negative Edge Cases.
We release ClariEdge, a dataset of approximately 3,900 examples with multi-turn
conversations, retrieved documents, and explicit hard negatives, that is,
queries that look ambiguous but are resolvable from context via coreference
resolution or query rewriting. The dataset is built
through direct human annotation and synthetic LLM generation followed by human
validation.

2. Lightweight Fine-Tuning Substantially Outperforms Prompting.
Against seven prompted baselines that include substantially larger models, our
lightweight LoRA achieves the highest classification accuracy
and the best clarification-generation quality on the queries it
correctly flags.
Whereas prompted baselines tend to either over-clarify or under-clarify, the
fine-tuned model handles both directions reliably.
An ablation study further
confirms that the hard negatives present in ClariEdge are essential for query clarification, since removing
them causes a sharp drop in accuracy on boundary cases.

3. Multi-Setting Handling in a Single Model. Unlike approaches that rely on
separate models or dynamic strategy selection (Sahay et al., 2025), one LoRA model handles
both pre-retrieval (conversation-only) and post-retrieval (conversation plus
documents) scenarios, with classification accuracy ahead of larger prompted models.
As shown in Figure 2, the same LoRA is invoked once on the
conversation alone (gating retrieval) and once on the conversation plus retrieved
documents (gating answer generation), asking a clarifying question whenever either
invocation flags ambiguity.

Figure 2: Deployment in a RAG pipeline.

## 2 Related Work

Ambiguity and clarification have been studied across many information-seeking
settings: open-domain factual QA (AmbigQA, Min et al., 2020; ASQA,
Stelmakh et al., 2022; CAmbigNQ, Lee et al., 2023; CondAmbigQA,
Li et al., 2025), standalone questions (CLAMBER,
Zhang et al., 2024), conversational QA (Abg-CoQA,
Guo et al., 2021; PACIFIC, Deng et al., 2022; CANARD,
Elgohary et al., 2019), and conversational search (Qulac,
Aliannejadi et al., 2019; ClariQ, Aliannejadi et al., 2020;
MIMICS, Zamani et al., 2020). Table 1
compares our dataset against four of these
benchmarks. On the modeling side, LLMs gain only marginal benefits from
chain-of-thought or few-shot prompting on ambiguity identification
(Zhang et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2023), motivating work that exploits
models’ own uncertainty signals (Kim et al., 2024; Testoni and Fernández, 2024) or
resolves ambiguity via retrieval-grounded disambiguation without asking the
user (Kim et al., 2023).

On the method side, prior systems specialize clarification along three axes:
when to clarify, using LLM uncertainty or calibration
(Kuhn et al., 2023; Zhang and Choi, 2023; Cole et al., 2023); how to
ask, via facet-driven or reasoning-trace supervision
(Sekulić et al., 2021; Andukuri et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Rahmani et al., 2024); and which deployment setting to target
(Sahay et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2024; Cao et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2025). These systems
typically rely on prompting or uncertainty rather than task-specific
supervision, and each remains tied to the prompts, models, or iterations of
its setting.

In contrast, we show that a single LoRA fine-tuned with hard negatives covers
both pre- and post-retrieval, draws an explicit boundary between genuine
ambiguity and context-resolvable references, and outperforms substantially larger
prompted baselines. This indicates that training-data quality dominates raw model
scale on this task.

## 3 ClariEdge Dataset

Effective query clarification requires training data that captures the nuanced
decision boundaries between clarification-worthy and clear queries. This section describes our ClariEdge dataset and its creation.
Conversations span the same four domains as MTRAG (Katsis et al., 2025): ClapNQ (Wikipedia), Cloud (technical documentation), FiQA (finance), and Govt (government).

Table 1 compares our ClariEdge dataset against four widely used
clarification benchmarks, each covering a complementary slice:
AmbigQA (Min et al., 2020) targets answer-set ambiguity in open-domain factual QA; CLAMBER (Zhang et al., 2024) introduces a Epistemic Misalignment / Linguistic Ambiguity / Aleatoric Output
typology for LLM evaluation on standalone questions; ClariQ (Aliannejadi et al., 2020) captures
web-search facets; and Abg-CoQA (Guo et al., 2021) addresses
referential ambiguity in conversational QA. None of these combines
multi-turn conversation, retrieved documents, and explicit hard negatives in a
single resource. Our dataset targets entity-option ambiguity, where the
user query may be referring to one of several candidate entities surfaced by either the conversation or the retrieved documents, and is the first to include systematic hard
negative edge cases that look ambiguous but are resolvable from context.

Our dataset comprises three categories: (1) Ambiguous (positive examples),
where user queries genuinely require clarification due to multiple plausible
interpretations; (2) CLEAR-random (easy negative examples), which are queries
that do not require clarification and are straightforwardly clear; and (3) CLEAR-hard
(hard negative examples), which are queries that appear superficially ambiguous
but can be resolved from conversation context. Table 2 presents
the data size and Table 3 illustrates some examples for the three categories.

The distinction between CLEAR-hard and CLEAR-random is critical:
hard negatives appear ambiguous due to referential expressions but
can be resolved from conversation context, while easy negatives are straightforwardly
clear queries. Training with hard negatives teaches the model the precise boundary
between genuinely ambiguous queries and those with resolvable references.

Additional dataset statistics (pre-/post-retrieval split, turn counts,
document counts) are reported in Appendix A.

## 3.2 Data Creation Process

Ambiguous examples.

Following the methodology for creating underspecified
questions in MTRAG-UN (Rosenthal et al., 2026), the final user query in each
conversation was designed to admit multiple plausible interpretations. Conversations
were constructed via two parallel approaches: (1) annotators writing ambiguous
questions inspired by entity types and instances drawn from the underlying
corpus; each such question was then stitched, in a subsequent step, as the last
turn onto an existing human-annotated multi-turn conversation, or (2) synthetic
generation of ambiguous questions appended as the final turn to existing
human-created multi-turn conversations, followed by a manual validation step. The latter approach is also the same one used for CLEAR-hard examples (see more details later): the major difference is that here the manual validation decides that these are truly ambiguous questions, while for CLEAR-hard it decides the converse.

For approach (1), relevant passages were added to each conversation using two
retrieval strategies: direct retrieval with the ambiguous question, and query
expansion with a context relevance filter, which yields a richer set of passages
to simulate scenarios where significantly more interpretations exist; these
examples form the post-retrieval portion of the Ambiguous category. Further details on the human annotation guidelines for this approach are given in Appendix B.1. For approach
(2), no passages were retrieved: this branch shares the synthetic-then-validate
pipeline used for CLEAR-hard (described below), and produces conversation-only
(pre-retrieval) Ambiguous examples. In both cases, reference clarification
responses were generated using an LLM with pattern-based prompting to include
relevant disambiguation options (see Section 3.3), followed by
human correction.

CLEAR-random examples.

The easy negative examples in this category were
constructed by randomly sampling clear, unambiguous user queries from existing
multi-turn conversations. For some examples, retrieved documents were paired with
the query to represent clear post-retrieval scenarios; for others, documents were
deliberately removed to create conversation-only examples where the query remains
unambiguous without external context.

CLEAR-hard examples.

A key contribution of our dataset is the systematic
construction of hard negatives, which are queries that may appear ambiguous to an LLM but can
be resolved from conversation context.
By construction, these examples are for the conversation-only (pre-retrieval) setting: their ambiguity-or-resolvability hinges on linguistic cues in the
dialogue rather than on retrieved passages.
We describe their creation next.

We prompted an LLM
on multi-turn conversations to generate questions targeting
entities discussed in the conversation, where the last user query is intended to be ambiguous.
In the basic variant, the model was given 793 conversations and asked to produce questions
where a user asks about an entity type with multiple instances occurring in the conversation. In
an advanced variant, 228 longer conversations (>6 turns with multiple entity types)
were processed using chain-of-thought reasoning with self-verification and iterative
refinement. Human annotators then manually reviewed all LLM-generated queries,
classifying each as genuinely ambiguous or resolvable from context. Conversations with
last user query determined to be truly ambiguous were moved to the Ambiguous category, while
the remaining ones, where queries appear ambiguous but can be resolved through conversation
context, became hard negatives.

We collected additional patterns of hard negatives where the synthetic generation model incorrectly generated clear queries as ambiguous. These included: “which one” patterns where the phrasing appears ambiguous but the question is just a comparison across the previously mentioned entities; follow-up questions resolvable through the regular conversation flow; and terse or keyword queries that appear ambiguous but are clear in context.

The human manual review was essential for this. Further details on the manual review process, including an illustrative example, are given in Appendix B.2.

limitations:
Despite the strong empirical results reported above, our study has several limitations
that circumscribe its scope and suggest directions for future work.

Single-turn clarification.

Our model generates a single clarifying question
rather than engaging in multi-turn clarification dialogues. Practical deployments may
benefit from iterative clarification strategies that progressively narrow the user’s
intent across multiple exchanges. Extending our approach
to multi-turn clarification remains an open direction.

English-only evaluation.

Both the dataset and evaluation are restricted to
English. The cross-lingual transferability of our method remains unexplored.
conclusion:
In this work, we introduce ClariEdge, a new dataset for clarifying ambiguous questions in RAG settings, and show that LoRA fine-tuning on a small model is more beneficial than prompting larger LLMs. Hard negatives are an essential
ingredient, suggesting that teaching a model what not to do is as important as
teaching it what to do. The resulting LoRA works well in both pre-retrieval and post-retrieval settings, although the pre-retrieval regime is a more challenging one.

title: Think Harder Where It Matters: Item-Level Adaptive Recursion for Sequential Recommendation
abstract: Existing sequential recommenders usually allocate a fixed computational budget to every item in a user's interaction history, regardless of the item's contribution to the final prediction. We challenge this de facto design with two diagnostic findings. (1) Non-uniform computational need: items within the same sequence vary drastically in how much computation they require. Most converge after shallow processing while a critical minority only stabilizes at full depth. (2) Suboptimality of fixed allocation: given oracle access to the target item, a non-uniform depth assignment consistently outranks the fixed one, indicating that existing uniform computation both wastes capacity on already-converged items and sacrifices overall recommendation quality. These observations motivate a shift from fixed-depth computation to item-level adaptive reasoning. To this end, we propose LoopRec. LoopRec recursively applies a single weight-shared block and introduces a lightweight gate at each recursion boundary that makes a binary exit-or-continue decision for every item independently. Items whose representations have sufficiently matured exit early, while those requiring deeper reasoning continue to subsequent recursions. This design converts the fixed global depth into a learned, per-item property without auxiliary depth labels, and is readily adaptable to diverse backbone architectures. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks with four backbone families demonstrate that LoopRec consistently outperforms matched fixed-depth counterparts. Further analysis reveals that LoopRec's learned allocation exhibits interpretable patterns aligned with our post-hoc oracle analysis: lower-frequency items and more recent interactions naturally receive deeper computation. Our code is available at https://github.com/Elpmis117/LoopRec.

headings: Think Harder Where It Matters: Item-Level Adaptive Recursion for Sequential Recommendation
body_start:
Abstract.

Existing sequential recommenders usually allocate a fixed computational budget to every item in a user’s interaction history, regardless of the item’s contribution to the final prediction. We challenge this de facto design with two diagnostic findings. (1) Non-uniform computational need: items within the same sequence vary drastically in how much computation they require. Most converge after shallow processing while a critical minority only stabilizes at full depth. (2) Suboptimality of fixed allocation: given oracle access to the target item, a non-uniform depth assignment consistently outranks the fixed one, indicating that existing uniform computation both wastes capacity on already-converged items and sacrifices overall recommendation quality.

These observations motivate a shift from fixed-depth computation to item-level adaptive reasoning.
To this end, we propose LoopRec.
LoopRec recursively applies a single weight-shared block and introduces a lightweight gate at each recursion boundary that makes a binary exit-or-continue decision for every item independently. Items whose representations have sufficiently matured exit early, while those requiring deeper reasoning continue to subsequent recursions. This design converts the fixed global depth into a learned, per-item property without auxiliary depth labels, and is readily adaptable to diverse backbone architectures. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks with four backbone families demonstrate that LoopRec consistently outperforms matched fixed-depth counterparts. Further analysis reveals that LoopRec’s learned allocation exhibits interpretable patterns aligned with our post-hoc oracle analysis: lower-frequency items and more recent interactions naturally receive deeper computation. Our code is available at https://github.com/Elpmis117/LoopRec.

Keywords: 
Sequential Recommendation, Adaptive Depth, Looped Transformer

## 1. Introduction

Sequential recommendation models temporal patterns in user interaction histories to predict the next item of interest, supporting personalized ranking on e-commerce and online content platforms (Kang and McAuley, 2018; Sun et al., 2019; Shin et al., 2024). The dominant paradigm processes a user’s interaction history through a fixed number of stacked layers, producing item representations that are then scored against candidates for next-item prediction. This paradigm has driven steady progress over the years, from attention-based models (Kang and McAuley, 2018; Sun et al., 2019; Hou et al., 2022) to architectures incorporating frequency-domain inductive biases (Shin et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2022; Du et al., 2023) and linear recurrences (Yue et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2026). Despite their architectural diversity, these methods share a common and largely unquestioned design choice: every item in the history receives exactly the same computational depth.

We argue that this uniform allocation mismatches the nature of user behavior. A real-world interaction history is inherently heterogeneous (Zhang et al., 2024; Rang et al., 2023): it mixes routine repeat purchases that carry minimal predictive signal with rare, exploratory, or pivotal interactions that critically shape the user’s evolving intent. Intuitively, these items should not demand the same amount of reasoning, yet current models are structurally incapable of differentiating between them, leading to suboptimal performance.

To move beyond intuition, we design two diagnostic experiments on a trained three-layer SASRec model (Section 2). First, we find that $76.14\%$ of items already stabilize their contribution to the recommendation after a single layer, while $6.72\%$ remain sensitive through all three layers, and these two extremes frequently coexist within the same sequence. Second, a restricted oracle equipped with ground-truth target information finds the original fixed-depth allocation optimal in only $4.6\%$ of sequences, achieving up to $8.8\%$ relative Hit Rate improvement through flexible reassignment. These findings show that: uniform depth both wastes capacity on items that have already converged and under-serves the critical minority that benefits from deeper computation. This motivates us to reframe sequential recommendation as a per-item computation allocation problem.

Realizing per-item adaptive computation in sequential recommendation, however, introduces two intertwined challenges. (1) Representation alignment across depths: since different items may exit at different depths, their output representations still need to reside in a shared feature space for downstream computation and scoring. Allowing depth to vary without careful architectural design can lead to misaligned representations that are incomparable at prediction time. (2) Progressive depth determination: how much computation each item needs cannot rely on a single upfront decision, because an item’s readiness only becomes apparent as it progressively absorbs context from surrounding items. Premature commitment risks either wasting computation on already-converged items or prematurely halting those that have not yet formed a reliable representation.

We propose LoopRec, a framework for sequential recommendation with item-level adaptive recursion. For representation alignment, LoopRec uses a recursive architecture (Dehghani et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2026; Bae et al., 2026),
reusing a single weight-shared block across all depths. Since every recursion maps through the same parameters, items exiting at any depth naturally produce representations in the same feature space. For progressive depth determination, LoopRec places a lightweight binary gate at each recursion boundary that evaluates each item’s current state after absorbing the latest round of context, and decides whether it is ready to exit or should proceed to the next recursion. Items exit progressively as they converge, while those that benefit from deeper reasoning remain active. This design requires no auxiliary depth labels, introduces minimal additional parameters, and is readily adaptable to diverse backbone architectures.

We conduct extensive experiments on three public benchmarks with four different backbone families. LoopRec consistently outperforms the matched fixed-depth counterpart. Beyond accuracy gains, in-depth analysis of the learned routing reveals interpretable allocation patterns aligned with our post-hoc oracle analysis: the model naturally devotes deeper computation to lower-frequency items and more recent interactions, precisely the groups that an oracle would also allocate more computation to.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

• 

We use two complementary diagnostics to reveal variation in item-level computational demand and the limitations of fixed-depth processing in sequential recommendation.

• 

We propose LoopRec, which combines a shared recursive backbone with learned item-level stopping decisions to adapt computation depth within each interaction history.

• 

Experiments on three datasets and four backbones show consistent ranking improvements, with routing analyses revealing deeper computation for less frequent and more recent items.

## 2. Diagnostic Analysis

Before presenting LoopRec, we empirically probe the uniform-depth assumption with two diagnostic experiments on Amazon Office Products (Hou et al., 2024) using a three-layer SASRec (Kang and McAuley, 2018). We investigate:

• 

RQ1: How is computational demand distributed across items within the same sequence under fixed-depth processing?

• 

RQ2: To what extent does the fixed-depth allocation affect recommendation quality relative to flexible per-item alternatives?

## 2.1. Probe 1: Item-Level Saturation Depth

To quantify the computational demand of individual items, we introduce the following diagnostic quantity:

Definition (Saturation Depth). For a trained $L$ -layer model, the saturation depth of item $i$ is the earliest layer $\ell$ at which its hidden representation can be frozen (i.e., excluded from all subsequent layer computations) without altering the model’s final Top- $K$ recommendation set:

(1)

 $\ell_{i}^{\star}=\min\!\left\{\ell\in\{1,\dots,L\}\,:\,\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{trunc}}^{(i,\ell)}=\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{full}}\right\},$ 

where $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{full}}$ is the full-depth Top- $K$ set, and $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{trunc}}^{(i,\ell)}$ is the Top- $K$ set produced when item $i$ ’s representation is frozen after layer $\ell$ while all other positions continue through the remaining layers normally.

Intuitively, a smaller $\ell_{i}^{\star}$ indicates that item $i$ contributes a “settled” signal early, while a larger $\ell_{i}^{\star}$ means it remains sensitive to deeper processing. We set $K{=}30$ and evaluate on all test sequences. We use this as a diagnostic statistic for the trained model. Additional details are in Appendix A.3.

Results.

Figure 1(a) reveals substantial variation in saturation depth: $76.14\%$ of items reach $\ell_{i}^{\star}=1$ , and $93.28\%$ satisfy $\ell_{i}^{\star}\leq 2$ . Yet $6.72\%$ only saturate at full depth ( $\ell_{i}^{\star}=3$ ). The sequence-level view in Figure 1(b) further shows that shallow- and deep-saturating items frequently coexist within the same history, with many sequences spanning all three saturation depths.

Finding 1: Non-uniform computational demand. Items within the same sequence exhibit highly heterogeneous computational demands. Most items converge after minimal processing, while a non-trivial minority requires full depth. Since both groups frequently coexist within the same sequence, no single fixed depth can simultaneously serve all items well.

## 2.2. Probe 2: Item-Level Depth Allocation

Probe 1 establishes that items differ in how much computation they need, but does not tell us whether this mismatch actually hurts recommendation quality. To bridge this gap, we design a controlled experiment: keeping model parameters frozen, we ask whether a per-item flexible depth assignment can produce better rankings than the original fixed allocation.

Specifically, we construct a counterfactual search over the five most recent items in each test sequence. Each of these items is allowed to exit after depth 1, 2, or 3, while earlier positions retain the original full-depth pass. The original fixed-depth assignment is included as a candidate. An offline oracle with access to the ground-truth target then selects the assignment that achieves the best target rank. Construction details are in Appendix A.3.

Results.

Figure 2 and Table 1 present the oracle’s findings. (a) Aggregated over the test set, the flexible oracle improves over the fixed-depth baseline by $7.1\%$ on NDCG@20, $6.5\%$ on MRR@20, and $8.8\%$ on HR@20. (b) Concrete examples show that the oracle-selected assignments achieve rank improvements while often consuming less total tail-side computation than the fixed baseline. In addition, the fixed-depth assignment is the oracle’s preferred choice in only $4.6\%$ of test sequences. In the remaining $95.4\%$ , a non-uniform allocation ranks the target higher.

Finding 2: Suboptimality of fixed allocation. The fixed-depth allocation is locally suboptimal in the overwhelming majority ( $95.4\%$ ) of sequences. A flexible per-item assignment improves ranking quality while often reducing total computation, demonstrating that uniform depth actively leaves performance on the table.

These two findings establish a strong empirical case for treating depth as a per-item computation allocation variable in sequential recommendation, motivating the design of LoopRec.

## 3. The Proposed LoopRec

To address the inefficiency of fixed-depth computation in sequential recommendation, we propose LoopRec, an adaptive routing framework built on a single shared backbone. LoopRec recursively reuses the same backbone block and lets a depth router assign different history positions to different recursion depths, so that computation is dynamically allocated item by item while the standard next-item prediction objective remains unchanged. Sec. 3.1 formulates the task, Sec. 3.2 presents depth-routed recursion, and Sec. 3.3 describes the training objective.

## 3.1. Task Formulation

We consider the standard next-item prediction task in sequential
recommendation over an item set $\mathcal{V}$ . Each training instance is an interaction sequence $\mathbf{s}=[v_{1},\dots,v_{n}]$ , where $v_{t}\in\mathcal{V}$ and the items are ordered by interaction time.
Given the prefix $\mathbf{s}_{1:t}=[v_{1},\dots,v_{t}]$ , the goal is to predict the next item $v_{t+1}$ , where $1\leq t<n$ .

Each item $v_{t}$ is mapped to an input token
 $\mathbf{x}_{t}=\phi(\mathbf{e}_{v_{t}}+\mathbf{p}_{t})$ , where
 $\mathbf{e}_{v_{t}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and
 $\mathbf{p}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ are the item and positional embeddings.
Stacking the positions yields
 $\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d}$ for the padded sequence length
 $T$ .
For each prefix $\mathbf{s}_{1:t}$ , the model outputs a probability distribution over candidate items, denoted by
 $p(v\mid\mathbf{s}_{1:t})$ . Given the training set $\mathcal{D}$ of prefix–target pairs, the recommendation objective is the standard cross-entropy loss:

(2)

 $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}=-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{(\mathbf{s}_{1:t},\,v_{t+1})\in\mathcal{D}}\log p(v_{t+1}\mid\mathbf{s}_{1:t}).$ 

Figure 2. Restricted tail-5 oracle on Office. (a) Relative gains of the flexible oracle over the fixed-depth baseline. (b) Oracle-selected tail depths for sample sequences. Numbers denote depths, and columns 0–4 are the five most recent positions.

## 3.2. LoopRec Architecture

Section 2 shows that different historical items within the same sequence can require different amounts of computation, making uniform fixed-depth processing restrictive for sequential recommendation. Motivated by this observation, LoopRec allocates computation depth at the item level while keeping the standard
next-item prediction objective unchanged. For each position $t$ , let $\mathbf{e}_{v_{t}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and $\mathbf{p}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ denote the item and positional embeddings, and let $\mathbf{x}_{t}=\phi(\mathbf{e}_{v_{t}}+\mathbf{p}_{t})$ be the corresponding input token. Stacking these tokens gives the padded input sequence $\mathbf{X}=[\mathbf{x}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{T}]\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d}$ .

To realize this adaptive-depth mechanism within a single model, LoopRec treats the backbone block as a reusable computation unit and shares it across recursions. Let $\mathcal{B}(\cdot)$ denote a shared backbone block with $L$ layers, and let $R$ be the maximum number of recursions. We denote this layer–recursion configuration as LxRy. For example, L2R3 uses a two-layer shared block for up to three recursions. Given $\mathbf{X}$ , LoopRec proceeds through three components. Initial Context Encoding first applies $\mathcal{B}(\cdot)$ to the full sequence to obtain contextualized states for all positions. Depth-Routed Recursion then applies adaptive depth routing at each recursion boundary: the depth router makes a stop-or-continue decision for each active position and re-applies the shared block only to positions that continue, until all positions stop or the recursion budget is reached. Finally, Depth-Specific Readout forms the representation used for next-item prediction from the state at the selected depth. A position that stops after recursion $r$ has effectively received $rL$ layers of sequential encoding. Figure 3 provides an overview.

Figure 3. Overview of LoopRec. At each recursion boundary, depth-routing gates decide which positions stop and which continue through the shared block.

Initial Context Encoding.
LoopRec begins with a shared shallow pass over the full sequence:

 $\mathbf{H}^{(1)}=\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{X}),$ 

where
 $\mathbf{H}^{(1)}=[\mathbf{h}^{(1)}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{h}^{(1)}_{T}]$ .
This initial pass provides the common contextualized states on which
subsequent routing decisions for individual history items are based.

Depth-Routed Recursion.
Starting from the contextualized states $\mathbf{H}^{(1)}$ , LoopRec performs depth-routed recursion for up to $R-1$ additional steps. At recursion boundary $r\in\{1,\dots,R-1\}$ , the depth router examines the current state of each active position and decides whether that position should stop at the current depth or continue to a deeper recursion. For position $i$ , let $\mathbf{h}_{i}^{(r)}$ denote its state after recursion $r$ . The depth router computes a routing score

 $s^{(r)}_{i}=g(\mathbf{h}^{(r)}_{i}+\boldsymbol{\rho}_{r}),$ 

where $g(\cdot)$ is the router head and $\boldsymbol{\rho}_{r}$ is a learnable embedding of the recursion index. This score is converted into an exit probability

 $q^{(r)}_{i,\mathrm{exit}}=1-\sigma(s^{(r)}_{i}),$ 

where $\sigma(\cdot)$ is the logistic sigmoid. A position stops at boundary $r$ if $q^{(r)}_{i,\mathrm{exit}}\geq 0.5$ . Otherwise, it is sent to the next recursion.

Let $\mathcal{A}^{(r+1)}$ denote the positions that continue after boundary $r$ . Then

 $\mathcal{A}^{(r+1)}=\{i\in\mathcal{A}^{(r)}:q^{(r)}_{i,\mathrm{exit}}<0.5\}.$ 

Only these continuing positions are updated by re-applying the shared block to their states from the previous recursion:
conclusion:
We revisited fixed-depth computation in sequential recommendation
through diagnostic experiments that reveal heterogeneous depth sensitivity
across history items. Motivated by these findings, we proposed LoopRec,
which uses weight-shared recursion with learned item-wise routing to
allocate computation adaptively. Across three Amazon benchmarks and
four backbone families, LoopRec consistently improves ranking performance
over fixed-depth counterparts. Its learned routes allocate greater depth
to recent and less frequent items, consistent with the patterns observed
in these diagnostics.
LoopRec also reduces the encoder computation budget in the measured
configurations, although latency gains vary. Future work includes
developing sparsity-aware kernels and learning the maximum recursion budget,
which is currently fixed per configuration before model training begins.

title: PhysiCalWorld: In-Context Physics Calibration for World Models
abstract: Existing world models typically perceive a scene through current visual frame or a narrow history window. However, these observations may not reveal the physics properties that determine transition dynamics, such as an object's mass distribution, joint damping, or surface friction. Without calibrating these physics factors for world models, predictions tend to regress toward an empirical prior and induce severe drift in novel test scenes. To this end, we propose PhysiCalWorld, which calibrates action-conditioned world models to the instance-specific dynamics via in-context prompting, without fine-tuning or analytical physics modeling. Our method encodes an exploratory interaction clip collected within the test scene into a compact physics descriptor token, which grounds subsequent predictions in the scene's actual physical behavior. PhysiCalWorld is trained end-to-end with the latent prediction loss alone, without physics labels. At inference time, the descriptor token is extracted once and can be reused across rollouts with negligible compute overhead. We evaluate PhysiCalWorld across four environments covering diverse physics variations and show that it substantially improves rollout prediction accuracy and visual planning success rate. The learned descriptors also form a physically structured latent space and generalize beyond the physics ranges seen during training.

## PhysiCalWorld: In-Context Physics Calibration for World Models

Yunhao Luo*  Wentao He*  Yinpei Dai  Hyelin Nam  Hongze Fu

Affiliation: Joyce Chai  Nima Fazeli†  Jeong Joon Park†

Affiliation: University of Michigan
headings: PhysiCalWorld: In-Context Physics Calibration for World Models
3.1 Physics Calibration via Physics Descriptor Token
body_start:
Abstract

Existing world models typically perceive a scene through current visual frame or a narrow history window. However, these observations may not reveal the physics properties that determine transition dynamics, such as an object’s mass distribution, joint damping, or surface friction. Without calibrating these physics factors for world models, predictions tend to regress toward an empirical prior and induce severe drift in novel test scenes.
To this end, we propose PhysiCalWorld, which calibrates action-conditioned world models to the instance-specific dynamics via in-context prompting, without fine-tuning or analytical physics modeling. Our method encodes an exploratory interaction clip collected within the test scene into a compact physics descriptor token, which grounds subsequent predictions in the scene’s actual physical behavior.
PhysiCalWorld is trained end-to-end with the latent prediction loss alone, without physics labels. At inference time, the descriptor token is extracted once and can be reused across rollouts with negligible compute overhead.
We evaluate PhysiCalWorld across four environments covering diverse physics variations and show that it substantially improves rollout prediction accuracy and visual planning success rate.
The learned descriptors also form a physically structured latent space and generalize beyond the physics ranges seen during training.
Project page at https://physical-world.github.io/.

††footnotetext: *Equal contribution.  †Equal advising.

## 1 Introduction

World models predict how a scene evolves given its current state and
the intended actions of the agents within it.
Trained on internet-scale data, video-based world
models (Bruce et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2023; Team et al., 2026; Agarwal et al., 2026)
are now able to generate photorealistic visual predictions of complex scene dynamics that are difficult to model with traditional physics engines.
Modeling the world in image space is thus becoming a promising alternative to hand-built physics modeling in such areas as robotics (Hou et al., 2026) and autonomous driving (Feng et al., 2025).

Existing world models usually generate predictions from the current frame or a short visual history. However, such observations may leave the underlying physical properties unconstrained, forcing the world models to guess a future state among multiple possible ones. For example, an opaque bottle appears identical whether or not it is filled with water, yet it will respond differently under identical actuation. A world model that relies only on empirical priors over object category or appearance will produce incorrect predictions in such scenarios, limiting its applicability in downstream applications that require accurate dynamics (Zhou et al., 2025; Quevedo et al., 2026). This motivates calibrating the world model to the hidden physical properties of each scene.

A natural way to resolve this physics ambiguity is to physically interact with the scene to infer its hidden properties, similar to how we humans would do for an object with unknown properties.
Inspired by this,
prior system identification methods (Wu et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2017; Kumar et al., 2021) attempt to construct accurate physical models with closed-form equations and fit the predefined physics parameters to the in-situ interaction data. However, real-world systems exhibit complex, coupled physics factors, thus building a geometric model or formulating closed-form equations can be challenging.
Hence, to adapt to each deployment setting, existing world models (Gao et al., 2026) are typically finetuned on a small set of in-house data, which is computationally expensive.

To this end, we propose PhysiCalWorld, a method for in-context Physics Calibration for World models.
Inspired by the in-context learning capabilities of large sequence models (Brown et al., 2020; Bar et al., 2022), we prompt world models with a sequence of observation-action pairs
collected in the test environment (i.e., an environment whose physics configuration is unknown) for physics calibration.
Our in-context prompting method sidesteps both the need for human effort to build analytical physics simulators for system identification and expensive model finetuning. Our method requires only an exploratory interaction clip without any gradient descent steps.
PhysiCalWorld compresses the interaction sequence into a compact physics descriptor token that conditions the world model. The entire system is trained end-to-end with only a video prediction objective, requiring neither ground-truth physics parameters nor a simulator.

At test time, PhysiCalWorld first extracts the descriptor from a few exploratory interactions with the test scene (e.g., via random exploration or scripted policies).
This descriptor then conditions all subsequent rollouts in that scene, enabling the world model to generate physically consistent predictions in novel configurations without any test-time weight updates.

In summary, our contributions are three-fold:

• 

In-Context Physics Calibration: We formulate physics calibration of generative world models as in-context conditioning: from a short interaction sequence, the model adapts zero-shot to instance-specific dynamics, with no test-time weight updates.

• 

Physics Descriptors Learned from Video Alone: We introduce a physics descriptor token that grounds the world model in hidden physical properties. It is learned end-to-end from video prediction alone, requiring neither ground-truth physics parameters nor a simulator.

• 

Performance and Analysis: Across four environments with single and coupled physics variations, PhysiCalWorld consistently improves rollout accuracy and planning success on two world model backbones. Its single-token descriptor matches or exceeds raw-context conditioning at a fraction of the cost. Without physics labels, the descriptors form a physically structured latent space and extrapolate beyond the training parameter range.

Figure 1: In-Context Physics Calibration for World Models.
In a test environment with unknown transition dynamics, an embodied agent first executes exploratory actions to collect an in-context interaction sequence. This sequence is then provided as prompt to calibrate the world model such that future predictions adhere to the actual dynamics of the test environment.

## 2 Related Work

World Models for Robotics.

World models predict future states conditioned on current observations and agent actions, serving as an increasingly foundational framework for robotics (Li et al., 2025c; Hou et al., 2026). For example, they are scalable neural simulators, enabling low-cost policy evaluation without real-world execution (Guo et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026e; Team et al., 2025; Tseng et al., 2025).
Through future imagination, world models can also substantially improve sample efficiency in reinforcement learning (Hafner et al., 2019; Hansen et al., 2022; Seo et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2023) and facilitate policy learning (Saxena et al., 2026; Luo & Du, 2025).
Moreover, optimizing action sequences with world models enables embodied agents to complete novel tasks via visual trajectory planning (Zhou et al., 2025; Assran et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024).
However, existing methods typically condition only on the current frame or a narrow observation history, assuming that these observations suffice to identify the underlying transition dynamics of the test scene.
As a result, predictions tend to suffer from severe drift if latent physical properties vary across test scenes.
In this work, we ground model predictions in the actual test-scene dynamics by introducing an additional in-context interaction prompt collected within the test scene as input to the world model, substantially enhancing the prediction accuracy and visual planning performance.

In-Context Learning in Physical AI.

Context can serve embodied agents in various forms. For example, it can adapt a robot policy to test-scene dynamics by conditioning directly on execution history or by explicitly recovering physical parameters (Lee et al., 2020; Kumar et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). Another role is in-context policy learning, where task demonstrations steer actions either through structured representations such as keypoints and graphs (Di Palo & Johns, 2024; Vosylius & Johns, 2025; Hwang et al., 2024) or raw video-action pairs (Fu et al., 2024; Shah et al., 2025; Ding et al., 2026),
and in-context reinforcement learning (Lee et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2023).
Most recently, context has been applied to action-conditioned world models by prepending context prefixes to adapt to new camera viewpoints or embodiments (Yang et al., 2026).
However, prior works focus on policy adaptation, require privileged physical priors, or prepend raw context frames at high computational cost. In contrast, we use context to enable physics-grounded future prediction in world models, introducing a compact physics descriptor token to minimize computational overhead while maintaining high prediction accuracy and rollout efficiency.

Physics-Aware Video Generation.

Video generative models have advanced rapidly (Yang et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026), with widespread commercial deployment (Seedance et al., 2026; Wan et al., 2025).
However, their adherence to physical laws remains limited (Motamed et al., 2026; Upadhyay et al., 2026; Bansal et al., 2025; Meng et al., 2024).
Recent efforts seek to improve physical awareness in video models by incorporating explicit physics equations or parameters in the generation process (Zhang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026a; Yuan et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b),
coupling with external physics simulators (Liu et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2025; Foo et al., 2026),
leveraging foundation models (Xue et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b), or optimizing handcrafted rewards (Zhang et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2025a).
However, these approaches either rely on analytical formulations and are restricted to a pre-defined set of physics properties, or focus on learning general physics and tend to fail in scenarios that require fine-grained instance-level physics grounding.
In comparison, our work focuses on calibrating action-conditioned world models to the instance-specific dynamics of a test scene from an exploratory interaction prompt, operating entirely end-to-end without prior assumptions or ground-truth supervision of the environment’s underlying physics.

## 3 Method

We consider an embodied agent interacting with an environment over discrete timesteps $t$ . At each step, the agent receives a high-dimensional visual observation $o_{t}\in\mathcal{O}\subset\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3}$ (and an optional proprioceptive state $p_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{p}}$ ) and executes a control action $a_{t}\in\mathcal{A}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}}$ . Our objective is to learn an action-conditioned world model that predicts future observations directly in a compact latent space and enables both long-horizon rollout and visual planning.

Latent World Models.

While our proposed in-context prompting framework is a plug-and-play module applicable to different world model architectures, we base the proposed method on two recent latent world models, DINO-WM (Zhou et al., 2025) and LeWM (Maes et al., 2026), due to their efficiency and strong trajectory planning performance.
In these latent world models, each input RGB frame $o_{t}$ is encoded by a visual encoder $E_{\text{v}}$ into a set of visual tokens $z_{t}$ :

 $z_{t}=E_{\text{v}}(o_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{z}\times d_{z}},$ 

(1)

where $N_{z}$ denotes the number of visual tokens per frame and $d_{z}$ is the feature dimension.
Meanwhile, actions $a_{t}$ are mapped into action embeddings $e_{t}^{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}^{\prime}}$ via a learned MLP $E_{\text{a}}$ :

 $e_{t}^{a}=E_{\text{a}}(a_{t}).$ 

(2)

The latent dynamics predictor $f_{\theta}$ (a causal transformer with weights $\theta$ ) models temporal transitions over a history window of $K$ steps. At step $t$ , the predictor takes a sequence of past visual tokens and action embeddings to predict the next latent tokens:

 $\hat{z}_{t+1}=f_{\theta}\left(\{z_{i},e_{i}^{a}\}_{i=t-K+1}^{t}\right).$ 

(3)

For visual evaluation and pixel-space rollouts, we train a lightweight convolutional decoder $D_{\text{v}}$ that reconstructs images $\hat{o}_{t}$ from latent tokens, $\hat{o}_{t+1}=D_{\text{v}}(\hat{z}_{t+1})$ , while downstream visual planning can be conducted directly within the latent space $\mathcal{Z}$ .

Figure 2: 
Method Overview.
PhysiCalWorld calibrates action-conditioned world models to the actual dynamics of a test scene via prompting with in-context interaction.
In (a), the current visual observation alone cannot identify the physical dynamics of the test scene $\mathcal{T}$ , forcing the world model to guess among multiple potential future states.
In (b), starting from the top left, exploratory actions $a_{1:T_{c}}^{c}$ are first executed in the test scene $\mathcal{T}$ , yielding observations ${o}_{1:T_{c}}^{c}$ . The context encoder $g_{\phi}$ then extracts physics information from this obs-action sequence and compresses it into a physics descriptor token $\mathbf{z}_{\text{phy}}$ . Conditioned on $\textbf{z}_{\text{phy}}$ , the world model is able to generate future predictions $\hat{o}_{t+1}$ consistent with the test scene’s dynamics.

## 3.1 Physics Calibration via Physics Descriptor Token

Physics Ambiguity in Visual World Models.

The forward transition function $\mathcal{T}$ of an environment depends not only on the current states and actions, but also on a set of underlying physics properties $\xi\in\mathcal{X}$ (e.g., mass, surface friction, or joint damping).
Because many of these physics properties rarely correlate with surface appearance,
a static visual frame $o_{t}$ or a brief observation window can hardly identify $\xi$ and hence leaves the true transition dynamics underdetermined.

Consequently, action-conditioned future prediction becomes an ill-posed, one-to-many problem.
Without sufficient interaction data from the test scene to calibrate the future predictor $f_{\theta}$ , its prediction may collapse to the expectation over the training distribution with compounding dynamic drift when the test environment deviates from the nominal mean.
While one could explicitly estimate and feed the test-scene physics parameters to $f_{\theta}$ , this usually relies on ad-hoc analytical modeling (as one must know in advance which physics properties determine the dynamics) and also introduces cascading estimation errors.
An alternative strategy is to scale up the history window $K$ of world models, so that the future predictor $f_{\theta}$ can directly extract the physical transition dynamics from previous interaction.
However, self-attention complexity in transformers scales quadratically with sequence length, making long-history conditioning computationally prohibitive. Furthermore, continuously carrying long raw frame histories (e.g., thousands of tokens) in every inference step introduces substantial redundancy, as the underlying physics configuration can usually be represented far more compactly.

Physics Descriptor Token.

To address these challenges, our method calibrates world models through a single compact representation, termed physics descriptor token $\mathbf{z}_{\text{phy}}$ , which is extracted from an exploratory interaction sequence collected in the test scene.
Formally, given an interaction clip $\mathcal{C}=\{(o_{i}^{c},a_{i}^{c})\}_{i=1}^{T_{c}}$ of length $T_{c}$ , the context encoder $g_{\phi}$ maps it to a descriptor token
 $\mathbf{z}_{\text{phy}}=g_{\phi}(\mathcal{C})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{phy}}}$ .
Internally, a lightweight visual encoder $E_{c}^{v}$ extracts per-frame visual features and an action encoder $E_{c}^{a}$ maps the control actions into action embeddings.
At each timestep $i$ , the two are concatenated along the channel dimension into a joint transition token $[E_{c}^{v}(o_{i}^{c})\mid E_{c}^{a}(a_{i}^{c})]\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}+d_{a}^{\prime}}$ .
A transformer $E_{c}^{\text{fuse}}$ then fuses these transition tokens across time and pools them via a learnable query token $\mathbf{z}_{\text{cls}}$ :

 $\mathbf{z}_{\text{phy}}=g_{\phi}(\mathcal{C})\coloneqq E_{c}^{\text{fuse}}\Bigl(\mathbf{z}_{\text{cls}},\;\bigl\{\bigl[\,E_{c}^{v}(o_{i}^{c})\;\big|\;E_{c}^{a}(a_{i}^{c})\,\bigr]\bigr\}_{i=1}^{T_{c}}\Bigr)_{0},$ 

(4)

where $[\,\cdot\mid\cdot\,]$ denotes channel-wise concatenation and $(\cdot)_{0}$ denotes the output at the query-token position. We use $\phi$ to collectively denote the parameters of $g_{\phi}$ , including $E_{c}^{\text{fuse}}$ , $E_{c}^{v}$ , $E_{c}^{a}$ , and $\mathbf{z}_{\text{cls}}$ .
The world model’s latent dynamics predictor $f_{\theta}$ is subsequently conditioned on
 $\mathbf{z}_{\text{phy}}$ alongside the default observation-action history window $K$ , predicting future latents $\hat{z}_{t+1}$ as:

 $\hat{z}_{t+1}=f_{\theta}\Bigl(\bigl\{(z_{i},e_{i}^{a})\bigr\}_{i=t-K+1}^{t},\;\mathbf{z}_{\text{phy}}\Bigr).\vskip-5.0pt$ 

(5)

Efficiency and Reusability. The design of physics descriptor token provides two practical advantages. (1) minimal rollout overhead: adding a single additional token $\mathbf{z}_{\text{phy}}$ into the predictor $f_{\theta}$ introduces only a constant and almost negligible computational cost, circumventing the quadratic attention overhead compared to using longer history or simply prepending raw context frames to $f_{\theta}$ (see +Long-History and +Context-Prefix in Section 4 and Figure 6 for comparison);
(2) one-pass extraction and in-context reuse: $\mathbf{z}_{\text{phy}}$ is computed via a single forward pass of a lightweight context encoder and can then be cached.
If the dynamics of the test scene remain unchanged, the same descriptor can be reused across arbitrarily many future rol
conclusion:
Limitations.
Our approach has several limitations.
First, training PhysiCalWorld requires grouping trajectories by the physics configurations under which they were collected. While partitioning data by environment identity is far less demanding than deriving analytical equations, curating grouped data from in-the-wild video remains non-trivial. One potential direction to relax this is leveraging self-supervised representation learning to automatically
cluster latent transition dynamics into environment groups.
Moreover, the proposed test-time calibration depends on the quality of the interaction prompt given to the model. While we find that simple playful or even random policies often suffice, future work could explore active or curiosity-driven exploration to collect more informative prompts.
Finally, our framework assumes the physics properties are stationary: the dynamics remain unchanged within an episode. Extending this approach to non-stationary environments (e.g., fluctuating wind fields) may require additional techniques such as reactive prompting or online descriptor updates.

Conclusion.
We believe that world models should go beyond generic visual fidelity toward instance-specific physics-grounded prediction.
In this work, we take a step toward this goal by introducing an in-context calibration framework that grounds action-conditioned world models in the actual physics dynamics of novel test scenes.
We achieve this by prompting the model with an interaction sequence collected within the test scene, enabling zero-shot calibration without finetuning or analytical physics priors.
Evaluations across diverse environments demonstrate that our approach substantially improves predictive accuracy and downstream visual planning.

title: Environment Duels: A Microcosm of LLM Co-Evolution
abstract: Through a tangle of real-world interactions, from synthetic training pipelines to data shared on the open web, frontier LLMs absorb what their predecessors and competitors create. How well does each model play its role in this ecosystem, as a creator and as a solver? We introduce Environment Duels, a dynamic agentic benchmark that evaluates both capabilities on interactive environments. Each model writes environments, each with a privileged hint, aiming for tasks that capable solvers fail without the hint and pass with it. Across nine frontier LLMs, solving and authoring prove to be distinct skills: the strongest solvers are not the strongest authors, while smaller models learn more from how others played and write the hardest environments and the most useful hints. Beyond the scores, the pairwise interactions form a microcosm of how models affect one another. Head-to-head outcomes are transitive and so yield a stable ranking; independent authors converge on the same designs; and in a reinforcement-learning study with Qwen3.8-27B, the learner's hint lift on an author's environments tracks how much training on those environments improves it on held-out reasoning and agentic benchmarks, whether the environments are its own or another model's. Each of these patterns has a counterpart in how models shape one another outside the duel. By staging these interactions under controlled conditions, Environment Duels offers a window onto how LLMs teach, challenge and learn from one another. Code is available at https://github.com/LLM-Duels/EnvDuels.

## Environment Duels:

A Microcosm of LLM Co-Evolution

Shibo Jin
